channel.title: Podcast — The world is too loud. Read what matters.
channel.description: Every day, the judgements worth remembering from 197 Chinese- and English-language podcasts. Points and quotes carry timestamps — tap one and you are back at the second it was said. Quotes are checked word for word and figures back to the source; anything unverifiable is cut, not published.

item.title: Silicon Valley Makes Too Much Money, and That's Why California's Government Has No Incentive to Get Better
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-allin-硅谷太赚钱-反而让加州政府没有变好的动力/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-allin-硅谷太赚钱-反而让加州政府没有变好的动力/
item.description: California has been a one-party state for 16 years — not because voters want big government, but because Silicon Valley's tax payments are so generous that the government doesn't need to survive on results. Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton says the price is the highest poverty rate, unemployment rate and cost of living in the country.
item.content:encoded:
California has been a one-party state for 16 years — not because voters want big government, but because Silicon Valley's tax payments are so generous that the government doesn't need to survive on results. Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton says the price is the highest poverty rate, unemployment rate and cost of living in the country.

What's worth listening to are two verifiable causal chains: how Sacramento's bill assembly line has piled up 420,000 regulations, and how Silicon Valley's tax revenue lets the government skip improving.

5:04 The rules aren't written, they're piled up every year
Hilton gives a countable form to the consequences of one-party rule: Sacramento passed 1,118 bills last year, and when he printed them out, the stack was twice his height. "No one is reading this" — do you think Gavin Newsom reads them all before signing? The result is that California has accumulated more than 420,000 regulations, and he promises to cut that below 200,000 within his first term. Who are the bills written for? He says for the narrow interest groups that control the process: unions, plaintiff lawyers, and the people who donate to politicians. That's why California is the highest litigation-risk place in the country, and why starting a company in California carries a 90% chance of ending up in court. Structurally, over those 16 years Democrats took all eight statewide elected offices, a two-thirds majority in the state legislature, every big county and big city, and a 6-to-1 majority on the state Supreme Court.

13:08 The key is that 26% of undecided voters
What he offers isn't a "Republicans flip it" story but an arithmetic problem: his internal poll at the start of the campaign was 33% firmly for him, 41% firmly for Becerra, 26% undecided. That 26% is the key — mostly people who have voted Democratic but aren't die-hards, overwhelmingly non-college-educated working people who are financially maxed out, and whose top concern is the cost of living. So the platform is all priceable line items: cancel high-speed rail, cut the government payroll by 10%, stop funding the nonprofits that make homelessness worse, and put together a "first $150,000 free of state income tax"; gas goes from $6 toward $3, because the low carbon fuel standard and cap and invest add roughly 150 dollars to the price of gas, and cap and invest money is flowing to high-speed rail; cap the vehicle registration fee at 73 dollars by abolishing the DMV. The polling gap has narrowed from 30 points on primary night to 8 points recently.

19:14 Silicon Valley's money removes the pressure to perform
This is the most counterintuitive stretch of the whole piece. One host cites Peter Thiel's observation from years ago: Silicon Valley is like a resource curse for California — it generates so much wealth and tax revenue that the place doesn't need a good government, and that's also why one-party rule can persist. Hilton adds the evidence: before the primary, Becerra was asked on CNN what policy he would change given homelessness, the highest poverty rate, the highest unemployment rate and a terrible cost of living. His answer was that this is the world's fourth-largest economy, people still love coming to Disneyland and the beaches, so things must be heading in the right direction. Hilton's rebuttal is that the fourth-largest economy figure includes the size of the government itself — which has doubled in a decade — while net private-sector job creation in California since the pandemic is basically zero.

23:19 What works is the content, not the AI
Spencer Pratt is running for mayor of Los Angeles as an independent and got a mountain of free media off a batch of AI-generated videos. He breaks down the mechanism himself: what actually worked was what the videos said — he went on every platform and just told the truths he knew, and then creative people across the country threw ideas into this "machine." "I don't think it's the AI that worked, it's just one piece of a lot of puzzle pieces." He thinks there's evidence for this: most of the people who voted for him are Democrats. He also claims that if Los Angeles's 200,000 registered Republicans had actually turned out to vote, he would have won.

27:21 Taxpayers are paying for needles handed out in the park
Hilton and Spencer together describe MacArthur Park: last Tuesday at 10:30 in the morning, sunny in downtown Los Angeles, and in every direction people are smoking crack, injecting drugs, some bent over from fentanyl. The reason is that four nonprofits show up every day handing out crack pipes, needles and drug supplies, and the money comes from taxpayers. Spencer adds the follow-up: one of the needle distributors was found to also be selling drugs. Hilton stresses this isn't a case of no one being in charge — Los Angeles has a new DA cracking down on drugs and crime, and there are federal prosecutors chasing gangs and cartels — but the scene in the park is the same every Tuesday.

29:22 Do the right thing and you're punished, do the wrong thing and you're rewarded
A Latino couple in South Los Angeles have run a shoe store for 14 years. The store is spotless, and they pay every tax, license, electricity bill and permit that gets more expensive every year. They asked Hilton to step outside and look two blocks of sidewalk: all of it is vendors selling shoes, clothing and T-shirts who pay no taxes, no electricity, no rent, no license. That's why the couple is closing. When did it start? In the last six or seven years — in 2018 Sacramento passed a bill legalizing street vending statewide, and cities and counties have no power to regulate it. His conclusion: here doing the right thing is punished and doing the wrong thing is rewarded, the whole thing is upside down. Spencer adds the numbers: 50,000 food vendors, a permit costs just 21 dollars, yet the city council allocated 500,000 dollars to buy them carts, while the unbuilt Palisades reservoir cover would cost only 200,000 dollars.

42:32 Ballot collection is legal, so it can't be audited
Spencer's claim is: it's not fake ballots, it's ballot harvesting, which California law allows. The mechanism has three steps: a witness signature can be a smiley face or an X; the same witness can witness 43,000 ballots, and there's no verification allowed; once ballots reach the counting center they're separated from their envelopes, the signatures stay on the envelopes, and the chain of custody is broken — so even if you know who these people are, you can't audit it, and a recount just recounts the same batch. The other side's rebuttal: voter fraud is a felony and is prosecuted regularly; after Trump lost last time he filed 60 such lawsuits and lost them all. Asked directly whether he believes he lost because of fraud, Spencer's answer is "without evidence I'd say no," and he lists the 200,000 registered Republicans who didn't vote as one of the reasons.

47:35 The empty reservoir and the reconstruction lawsuit
Spencer's house, his parents' house and his neighbors' houses all burned. Reconstruction is stuck on two things. First, that empty reservoir is still empty — even the one across from his house, the one he thought would never burn, is empty, and Palisades is now supplied by a hose run all the way from Tanga through regrown dry brush. Second, they're pursuing a mass tort suit with 10,000 victims, naming Gavin Newsom's state parks, the city and the city's water and power department as defendants. His chain of allegations: on New Year's Eve there was an 8-acre fire in Pacific Palisades, state parks was supposed to monitor it per the manual but didn't, letting embers smolder into the known high-wind weather of January 6 and 7; firefighter whistleblowers told him there were visibly smoldering coals on the hillside, and state parks employees produced photos in testimony showing the hillside smoking.

item.title: Individual productivity triples, but company delivery only shrinks from 20 days to 17
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-lightstar-个人提效三倍-公司交付只从20天缩到17天/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-lightstar-个人提效三倍-公司交付只从20天缩到17天/
item.description: AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weak link in the barrel isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform process and organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.
item.content:encoded:
AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weak link in the barrel isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform process and organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.

A frontline CEO talks about building his own CEO AI, canceling weekly meetings, and using token consumption to identify elite performers — the mechanisms and numbers are concrete, and the decision hub section in the second half is the most valuable.

16:07 Individual productivity triples, but delivery only speeds up by three days
NetEase did a study last year: a software requirement, from the product manager receiving it and producing a design draft to the feature going live, averaged 20 working days. After AI coding crossed the inflection point, many engineers doubled or even tripled to quintupled their personal efficiency, some tenfold. But for features of the same scope, the entire process only shrank from 20 days to 17. The reason is that a team completing a complex task is like a barrel: of 20 staves, 10 are engineers, 3 are product, 3 are testing. The engineer and product manager staves rise rapidly, but some staves aren't people — they're process — and they haven't improved at all. So AI adoption must clear three hurdles: cognition, applying it to individual short-range tasks, and transforming process and organization. The third is the hardest.

20:11 Cancel weekly meetings: AI syncs information, humans only solve problems
Ruan Liang asked friends who run companies whether they still hold weekly meetings; 99% said yes. Weekly meetings usually serve three purposes: sync information, discover problems and opportunities, and make decisions. Previously they ran 2.5 hours a week, but the time spent for that meeting could be ten times 2.5 hours — every department prepares materials layer by layer, and information sync itself isn't done well because no one listens attentively the whole time and may miss a sentence relevant to them. After the reform: the general manager and management agree on what information is needed, everyone fills in a template and stores it in the knowledge base, AI scans and integrates it into a focused, interactive HTML report where people can leave comments and follow up; an AI agent produces a preliminary list of problems and opportunities, which human brains confirm and supplement; problem-solving and decision-making become dedicated meetings.

28:20 SaaS isn't dead, but ordinary SaaS will die
Ruan Liang doesn't think SaaS is dead: SaaS is essentially Service, and Service always exists, it just changes form. AI as a Service and Agent as a Service are themselves software. But ordinary SaaS may indeed die. Truly good SaaS that has entered a company's critical processes will only get better, because it becomes internal infrastructure. Previously humans used software, limited by time and energy; in the future, large numbers of Agents will call databases, APIs, security APIs, audit APIs, HR APIs, CRM APIs. The call volume will far exceed the number and actions of humans, will increase enormously, and the more it's called, the more entrenched it becomes. The premise is that the Service itself is critical enough within the enterprise.

32:21 Distill top salespeople into skills and distribute them to everyone
Bosses have two headaches: the sales team has only one or two strong performers and the rest are mediocre; or a salesperson is too strong and what if they leave? Previously there was no solution, but now you can distill or extract the actions, scripts, and behaviors of good salespeople into skills. Two uses: distribute them to other salespeople for direct use; and have AI turn elite salespeople into teachers to train ordinary salespeople. What training should distill isn't the salesperson, it's the customer — take the customer interaction data the salesperson has had, such as calls, WeChat, emails, and let AI simulate various customers to train salespeople. Online sales are purely digital and on record; for offline sales, it's recommended or even required to equip them with a recording card. After a visit, while memory is fresh, record a two-to-three-minute voice note. Salespeople dislike CRM (they think CRM is for managing them), but they don't mind recording cards, because it's also useful for their own customer review.

44:31 Fewer middle managers, strong individuals lead Agent legions back to the front line
Ruan Liang judges that middle managers will become fewer, but not necessarily eliminated — rather, they'll go to the front line, and the front line can also lead a bunch of agents. Middle managers with management responsibilities will become fewer; elite individuals with strong skills will become more numerous. He gives the example of an engineering team: previously socialized division of labor split software development ever finer — frontend, backend, algorithm, test engineers; in the last half year it has clearly reverted to full-stack, everyone becoming full-end engineers. In the future, organizations will look more like a distributed structure: countless engineering capabilities are strong, a mother peak commands some engineering, and countless agents fight a battle. He imagines a future interview negotiation scenario: the candidate says I'm not one person, I bring an AI team, a summary of all my past experience and skills, and the premium the company pays might be some kind of OPC.

50:35 AI value formula: quality times time saved
Ruan Liang gives a formula referencing a paper: AI value = quality of AI completing the task (as a ratio of human quality) × time saved × the company's economic value per unit time. For example, a human makes a cup of coffee at eight out of ten, AI also makes it at eight out of ten, so the quality coefficient is 1; a human takes 20 minutes, AI takes only 10 seconds, saving 14 minutes 50 seconds; multiply by the company's economic value per unit time, and you can calculate ROI. Prioritize four types of tasks for AI: time-consuming, high-frequency, unavoidable, and tasks where different people produce roughly the same result. Once calculated, you can immediately decide whether to use AI. He also suggests first using the most expensive AI (Cloud, GPT) to prove the task can be done, solidify the process, then switch to cheaper ones — if the most expensive can do it, within two months the cheaper ones can too.

59:40 Token consumption leads by a landslide, output also leads by a landslide
NetEase started a points system in 2024, trying to quantify engineers' work tasks into points with work value. In the AI era, they found a group of people whose token consumption is astonishing, and whose work output and work value are also astonishing, forming a statistical pattern: people whose token consumption leads by a landslide are most likely building systems for themselves, saving their own work time and increasing thinking time, so their work quality and work results also lead by a landslide. Many bosses worry about waste from AI abuse; Ruan Liang's hot take is that truly excellent or elite people won't waste — the company has audits but doesn't tell colleagues, and through statistics they found elite colleagues don't waste. He also says small companies are more likely to fully embrace AI, because there are fewer organizational relationships, the boss uses it first, there are fewer layers, and the chain is shorter.

1:11:50 The core of a decision hub is decision history, not the model
Building an AI decision hub essentially requires a high-quality knowledge base; what really matters is the historical decision processes and decision bases. This year NetEase preserved past decisions and included them in the knowledge base. Combining the two types of knowledge to train an agent or skill, then feeding back hundreds of original cases for the agent to judge, achieved accuracy over 90%. Ruan Liang also mentions that Bridgewater gave researchers and analysts agents they built themselves, precipitating decision processes and decision history into a decision knowledge base; what Bridgewater did better was making the agent a learnable, evolvable part — after a person adjusts it, the confirmed adjustment actions enter the next round of reinforcement, advancing with the times, equivalent to human-machine collaborative self-evolution.

item.title: Mooncakes sell for only two months a year, yet they've become a 28.2 billion yuan business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.description: Being bound to Mid-Autumn Festival actually traps mooncakes' selling window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from gifting scenarios and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.
item.content:encoded:
Being bound to Mid-Autumn Festival actually traps mooncakes' selling window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from gifting scenarios and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.

Worth listening for food industry practitioners and anyone wanting to understand the holiday consumption business, but information density is low — much of the runtime is spent on explaining regional styles and flavors, with the business mechanics concentrated in the middle and later sections.

6:06 Zongzi can sell year-round, mooncakes cannot
Zongzi is tied to Dragon Boat Festival, but once vacuum-sealed for long shelf life it can sell all year round — Wufangzhai even opened restaurants to put zongzi into everyday scenarios. Mooncakes' problem isn't that the craft can't achieve long shelf life, it's that they're defined as "traditional festival pastries mainly eaten during Mid-Autumn Festival" — the national standard GB19855 writes the season directly into the definition. So of two festival foods, zongzi can decouple from its festival through shelf life and channels, mooncakes cannot.

12:12 The national standard draws hard lines on fillings
Lotus paste mooncakes must contain no less than 60% lotus seeds, fruit mooncakes must contain no less than 25% fruit products, and five-kernel mooncakes must use the five kernels: walnut, almond, olive kernel, melon seed, and sesame. The purpose of these lines is to push up ingredient costs and prevent cheap candied winter melon, red and green shreds, and inferior nuts from being used as filler. For consumers, reading the order of ingredients on the label tells you how much of what is actually in there.

26:30 Why custard lava mooncakes are made so small
Custard lava mooncakes are small not out of stinginess but because of structure. Outside is pastry, the middle is a custard layer, and the innermost is the lava layer — the custard layer acts as a moisture barrier. Production requires two rounds of baking to keep the lava semi-solid, and the lava's melting point must be engineered: solid during transport, then a few seconds in the microwave turns it into flowing liquid. If heated too long, the lava gets absorbed by the pastry and it reverts to an ordinary custard mooncake.

37:34 Five preconditions for "everything can be a mooncake"
Not everything can be stuffed into a mooncake. First is water content — hot and sour soup mooncakes can't be made because there's too much water to contain. Second is safety — meat, egg, and dairy are also favored by microorganisms, so processing temperatures and sterilization processes must be repeatedly tested. Third is particle size — too large and the pastry can't contain it, too fine and you can't taste it. Fourth is flavor retention after high-temperature baking — some aromas simply disappear once baked. Fifth is whether the cost can be handled. So long-term stable flavors are ones confirmed by generation after generation.

44:40 Choosing an OEM isn't a matter of bigger is better
When big brands make branded mooncakes through OEM, there's a common misconception: you must pick the best OEM in the country. But the top OEM's production scale actually doesn't match yours. Indicators you can screen on include registered capital, tax payment records, number of employees with social insurance contributions, and accumulated days without safety incidents. Also, the nine major regional styles correspond to different factories — you can't ask Guangzhou Restaurant to produce Shanxi egg-skin mooncakes; they don't have that capability or production line.

48:44 Flexible production lines can take orders of a few hundred boxes
Mooncake production is semi-automated and semi-manual — wrapping and forming machines can do their part, but brushing egg wash, pressing patterns, and stamping require human hands, which actually makes it favorable for OEM and customization. Flexible factories can go as small as a few hundred boxes, and can do thousands or tens of thousands of boxes too. If a company has only 50 employees, they can use the factory's existing mooncakes directly and only need to design the box. This small-batch quick-response capability is the core of why mooncakes can do corporate custom business.

51:47 The 28.2 billion yuan scale is propped up by gifting
In 2025 China's mooncake output was 518,000 tons, with sales of 28.2 billion RMB, both down from the previous year. At 80 grams each that's about 6.4 billion pieces; at 100 grams, about 5.18 billion pieces — across a population of 1.4 billion, an average of three to four per person. For comparison, Dragon Boat Festival zongzi annual sales are about 10 to 11 billion, and instant noodles about 68 to 120 billion. Mooncakes selling for only two months a year yet reaching 28.2 billion is fundamentally about the gifting attribute — brands prepare large amounts of PR gifts at the two nodes of Chinese New Year and Mid-Autumn Festival, and zongzi's gifting attribute is far weaker than mooncakes'.

58:55 499 yuan is a number forced out by the regulatory line
In 2022 the National Development and Reform Commission and three other departments jointly issued an announcement placing boxed mooncakes priced above 500 yuan per unit under key supervision. So the highest price on the market is 499. The calculation logic: a box of mooncakes costs about 70 yuan per box, and adding channel commissions and allocated expenses, it's impossible to exceed 500. Back when the economy was good there were sky-high mooncakes with very expensive tea or liquor inside, even wooden gift boxes, with both cost and price very high.

item.title: AI for Science Is Stuck on the Last 0.001 Points, Not on Compute
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.description: ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap on the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to say "you got this paper wrong."
item.content:encoded:
ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap on the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to say "you got this paper wrong."

High information density, but it takes a little patience: the first half covers ERA's mechanics, the second half covers contrails, wildfires and quantum computing, all first-hand detail.

9:24 ERA takes chat as input and returns a scored notebook
ERA's product form isn't having people write config files — you just start chatting. Because mapping a scientific problem onto a scorable task is itself non-obvious, Michael Brenner wrote an agent specifically to conversationally help you define what score to optimize. When the conversation ends, it generates a Python notebook underneath containing a function that produces a score, and then the system starts mutating that notebook in a "clever way," continually proposing new code to push the score higher.

10:24 It doesn't always pick the best candidate
ERA runs Monte Carlo Tree Search internally, holding hundreds or thousands of notebook candidates at once in a tree-shaped pool. Selection uses the upper confidence bound from reinforcement learning: estimate the 95th percentile outcome of a mutation and pick the one with the highest optimistic upper bound. So it doesn't always greedily pick the currently best-performing notebook; sometimes it picks the fifth-best, in order to explore more efficiently. It has also tried combining the ideas of two candidates to generate a third.

18:38 Evolutionary coding was stuck for decades because random mutation is useless
Platt says people have been doing evolutionary coding since the 1970s — mutating Lisp code and the like — but it never took off, because random mutation in code space is basically worthless: just like DNA, the vast majority of mutations are harmful. ERA works because the inner loop is itself an AI that knows which direction to try, which amounts to having a meaningful gradient underneath. The price is that it also overfits, and it also goes off the rails in "genie wish" fashion.

22:44 Predictive models and descriptive models are two different things
John Platt splits scientific modeling into two kinds: a predictive model only seeks the lowest error rate on some dataset; a descriptive model is what science actually wants — it contains some internal description of reality, so it can extrapolate. His example is Newton: an apple falling can be fit, but gravity isn't about apples, and if you take a model that only fits apples and ask it about planets, it has no planetary data and knows nothing. He admits the line is blurry, because the scientist themself also constrains the model with a pile of known facts and intuitions.

31:59 This is a power tool, and it will cut your fingers off
Faced with multiple hypothesis testing and overfitting, Platt's answer isn't a new method but a harsher version of an old one: because ERA is a power tool, you have to be stricter than ever, with a holdout hidden so deep you never look at it yourself. He states plainly that no system yet discovers entirely new physics or entirely new science, and scientists are still responsible for judging whether a conclusion is descriptive.

39:18 AI is stuck on the last 0.001 points
Ira pushed the score very close, but it couldn't close the last 30 places or so, because nobody goes and scrapes out that final 0.001 points. This exposes the system's real structure: the inner layer is a machine running for hours to produce candidates, and the outer layer is a human making judgments like "you got this paper wrong." Platt compares it to a graduate student who never sleeps and is extremely eager — you tell it a direction, it goes and tries, but when it gets stuck a human has to change the approach.

48:08 The counterfactual model stalled the team for two years
To judge which contrail to avoid, you need to know how much warming it actually causes, and that's a counterfactual problem: you can't enter the universe where the contrail doesn't exist. The team built a version of a counterfactual model that worked for outgoing longwave radiation, but they could never build one for the part that reflects sunlight, and it stalled them for two years. They even self-tested with a dataset where contrails were artificially injected, and their own attempt couldn't pass their own test. In the end ERA found a simple model that searches over all confounders, passed the test, and cracked the problem.

1:24:27 A wildfire is best put out before it's room-sized
Google has a crisis resilience effort, and one project in it is called Firesat: a wildfire is extremely easy to extinguish when it's only as big as "this room," and once it reaches an acre it's far harder, while the growth from room-sized to an acre may be exponential. The plan is a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation using mid-wave IR (which corresponds to blackbody radiation, exactly the temperature of fire) for detection; about 50 to 80 satellites could cover the globe, spot a fire roughly 5 meters across, and raise an alarm within 15 to 20 minutes. The partner is the nonprofit Earth Fire Alliance, the satellites are built by Muon Space, and one prototype has already launched.

item.title: Trump Invites Xi to a Show. What Did the US Get in Return?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-特朗普请习近平看戏-美国换到了什么实质东西/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-特朗普请习近平看戏-美国换到了什么实质东西/
item.description: This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question is not whether something goes wrong, but what the US traded symbolism for in substance. So far: nothing.
item.content:encoded:
This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question is not whether something goes wrong, but what the US traded symbolism for in substance. So far: nothing.

The first half covers the summit and US-China relations; the middle and later sections on China after Xi and fifty years since Mao's death are denser with information and worth hearing.

6:06 This visit has no substantive agenda at all
Gewirtz's judgment is that this state visit has "there is not a very deep substantive agenda at all." Trump invited Xi mainly because he wants to put on a show, wants the pomp and the cameras, and incidentally wants to push issues like the Iran war out of the news. For Beijing, this actually makes them less nervous — because if it were a more confrontational meeting, they would be more anxious. But Gewirtz flags two things: Trump himself is extremely unpredictable, and Beijing has internalized that; and Beijing watches the chaos in Washington and sees the American president himself often in a position they would never want Xi to be in — going to the wrong place, being photographed in unflattering images, being pressed by reporters. So the real question is not whether someone deliberately sets a trap, but whether things slip into the very scenario they are desperate to avoid.

9:25 Symbolism for substance: where is the trade
Gewirtz characterizes this visit as "we are in a space of symbolism and optics." He says that in US-China relations, trading symbolism for substance is itself a reasonable play: give Beijing the pomp and cameras it craves, and get back something concretely useful to Americans and American interests. That was the model for US relations with the Soviets during the Cold War and after — the US gave symbolism, legitimacy, and that handshake photo, and got a step back from the other side on Third World countries or nuclear issues. But the problem this time is that the Trump administration does not even seem to have tried to design a set of "deliverables." Gewirtz says "it doesn't even seem like they're trying." So what to watch is not where things go wrong, but "where is the trade happening."

11:37 The direction of concessions has been flipped entirely
Gewirtz points to a counterintuitive dynamic: concessions the US might once have given China have now been flipped into "gifts" from China to the US. Pomp and cameras were what Beijing wanted, but in Washington they are treated as Xi's visit being a concession to the US. The same flip happens on advanced semiconductors: the US used not to sell these things, and opening up products like the H200 would have been a huge concession; now, if Beijing agrees to buy, many in Washington would see it as Beijing conceding to Trump. Gewirtz says this flip keeps recurring, and the reason it matters is not to score points for the administration but because it reflects what happens when the power gap in superpower competition narrows — very small differences, interpersonal dynamics, can produce much larger shifts in the overall strategic picture.

12:39 US-China relations are also K-shaped, held up by the upper leg
Gewirtz uses "K-shaped" to talk about US-China relations: one upward leg is the leader-level channel — dense mutual visits, friendship, cameras; one downward leg is the competitive reality and the actions certain parts of both governments keep taking. The system is currently held up by the upward leg, but it is very fragile. He stresses the metaphor is not just a parallel analogy: saying "truce" or "detente" sounds too static, like a state already reached, but US-China relations are actually quite dynamic, quite unstable, moving in two directions at once. He applies the same K-shaped logic to China's economy — manufacturing and AI are flying, real estate and consumer demand are struggling, the upward leg is pulling the whole system forward, and the question is whether it can keep holding as the K widens.

22:03 The bipartisan consensus on China policy has shattered
Gewirtz argues that Trump changed the tone of America's China discussion in the 2016 election and became the symbol and standard-bearer of that turn; but now, after helping create that turn, he has helped destroy or transform it. He cites David Feith's article in the Reagan Institute on "a new cold war in an age of doubt" — that great rethink on China was not as great as many assumed. Gewirtz's conclusion: if the political dynamics are more complicated than imagined and the bipartisan consensus some people talk about does not exist, then this is a moment of "incredible fluidity." He says he has no confidence in the direction of either Democratic or Republican China policy in the medium term, and Beijing has no confidence either.

31:24 Chinese officials cannot talk about risks they have no solution for
Gewirtz offers a different read on how the US should interpret Chen Yixin's article. On the surface, Americans are panicking about existential risk and China is panicking about regime security, and that is correct. But he says: heads of American AI model companies can talk at length about risks they have no solution for, and they all do; China's minister of state security cannot. In China, when you point out a risk in public, you are simultaneously saying "we the Communist Party see it, we will handle it, we have a solution." So the real question is: should we treat what is visible from Beijing as everything, or acknowledge there is more in the system that we cannot see. He gives an example from 25 years ago — Americans then predicted the internet would cause regime change in China, Clinton said that was like nailing Jell-O to the wall, and Beijing did in fact nail the Jell-O to the wall, namely the firewall.

35:37 Beijing has not decided how to regulate open models
Gewirtz says that around Xi's speech and Chen Yixin's article, the outside world has already been through several cycles of excitement and interpretation, but Beijing has still not given the single most important thing: how it plans to regulate open weight models spreading globally — models that carry both risk and strategic benefit for Beijing. He calls this "the trillion dollar question." Both speeches can be read as pointing in some direction, but the decision has not been made. His guess is that this is because Beijing itself has not decided, because things are changing too fast and the trade-offs are too large. He contrasts the Trump administration: it did not make a decision until Mythos came out, and then made another when Fable came out.

41:55 What to prepare for is not China's decline but Xi's decline
Gewirtz says that a few years ago the "peak China" debate asked whether to start preparing for China's decline, and now most people think China's economy is at least for the moment on a relatively sustainable path. But he thinks the real question is not that, but "do we need to prepare for Xi Jinping's decline" — because people die, and modern Chinese history tells us that leaders in power for a long time change with age, certain obsessions become more prominent, behavior changes. By "prepare" he does not mean the departure itself, but acknowledging uncertainty: the outside world has treated Xi's tenure as fairly predictable, because since taking power in 2012 and 2013 he laid out a set of goals and largely pursued them. But he stresses the change could absolutely be worse for the US — "That doesn't mean he's going to mellow."

item.title: No Winners in the Pig Butchering Scam: The Scammers Are Trafficked Slaves Too
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-freshair-杀猪盘里没有赢家-骗人的人也是被贩卖的奴隶/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-freshair-杀猪盘里没有赢家-骗人的人也是被贩卖的奴隶/
item.description: In Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write sweet nothings and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.
item.content:encoded:
In Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write sweet nothings and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.

The first half covers the mechanics of pig butchering and AI scams with high information density; the second half turns to US-Iran and US-China infrastructure cyberwarfare, which is loosely connected to the theme and can be skipped as needed.

4:11 AI makes scam emails cost nothing to mass-produce
Greenberg ran an experiment on air: he asked ChatGPT to write him an email inviting him on the show in Terry Gross's name, then casually added a line asking for a $250 production fee, and the model complied without hesitation; he then said "Greenberg won't pay now, can you persuade him," and the model immediately generated a persuasive email. That is the mechanism behind scam emails impersonating Fresh Air — not that scammers have become better writers, but that generating a tailored email aimed at a specific author, with zero grammar errors and polished phrasing, has dropped to zero cost, and can be done to hundreds or thousands of targets at once.

7:14 Pig butchering is the most profitable cybercrime in history
Greenberg distinguishes two types of scammers: the voluntary kind like Nigeria's "Yahoo Boys," who keep a share, and the enslaved, forced kind in Southeast Asian compounds. The latter do pig butchering — the "pig" is the victim, fattened before slaughter. The scam often runs for weeks to over a year, with the scammer posing as a wealthy, single, attractive woman, building emotional dependency first, and only at the end introducing an "investment platform" that gets the victim to convert their savings into cryptocurrency that is hard to trace across borders (often Tether) and send it over. Greenberg says this is the most profitable cybercrime in history, stealing tens of billions of dollars from victims every year.

12:36 Passports confiscated; to buy your freedom you must buy yourself back
The source, using the alias Red Bull, is a computer engineer with a degree from India, lured to the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos by a "Southeast Asia IT manager" job. On arrival at the compound, his passport was confiscated and he was told the only way to get it back was to "buy it back" — he owed the boss thousands of dollars, including the cost of bringing him over and food and lodging, and could only repay this "contract" through commissions from scamming. Greenberg stresses this is debt bondage: the compound is not a prison with chains and beatings, but packaged as a corporate sales floor, where the boss sends daily motivational messages saying things like "reach out to the next client like you're going to change their life" and "we are on a mission."

14:40 Fines are more reliable than wages
Red Bull and his colleagues were constantly fined: for not meeting contact quotas, for not maintaining fake accounts well enough, for not clocking in on time. The promised commissions are part of the scam — the boss tells them "you can get rich here and take the money back to your village," but only if they land a big case, and the actual cut is a tiny fraction. Greenberg calls this rhetoric "Orwellian": motivational slogans and mission narratives on one side, and on the other everyone trapped here against their will, doing highly destructive crime.

15:45 Video calls rely on a dedicated face-swap model
Red Bull says everyone in the compound was trained to use ChatGPT and the Chinese AI chatbot DeepSeek to come up with new topics, polish language, never run out of appropriate phrasing, even write little motivational poems, and find the perfect goodnight line. More crucial is video: the boss required them to discourage victims from video calls as much as possible, making excuses to delay; if they couldn't put it off, the compound had a dedicated room and a model whose full-time job was video calls, using face-swap software to change the model's face into the photo originally sent to the victim. Greenberg says this kind of software isn't perfect, but by the video call stage, the victim wants to believe it so badly that they actively ignore the flaws.

18:54 The next step is fully autonomous AI pig butchering
Greenberg judges that AI is currently just a tool for human scammers, but the next step — already emerging — is fully autonomous AI scams. He cites a case from an Anthropic report last week: a Chinese group made 20 dating apps, all filled with AI, where victims had to keep paying to continue the conversation, and the "majority" on the other side were actually fully autonomous large models. He also mentions a study showing that in most parts of the scam process, AI is better than humans at building relationships — more timely, more engaged, more focused — and that is exactly what the scam does for the vast majority of the time before it reaches the endgame of asking for money.

23:08 Thirty people, three months, only $2.2 million
Greenberg gives a concrete scale: Red Bull's group of about 30 people earned only about $2.2 million in total over the three months that Red Bull recorded and leaked to Wired. This shows pig butchering is a game of probability — a single group's output is limited, but there are dozens of such compounds in Laos alone, and more in Cambodia and Myanmar, and together they add up to the scale of tens of billions of dollars a year. Greenberg also notes that Red Bull himself was a "very inefficient scammer," so he was penniless, eating only rice from the compound canteen and vegetables that tasted of strange chemicals, constantly sick, and disgusted by what he was doing.

24:12 Forged police letter escape attempt, beaten after being exposed
Red Bull's escape attempt was to forge a letter from the police in his home state in India, saying he was under investigation and had to return home to deal with it, or the boss would also be in trouble. Greenberg advised him not to do it, but he went ahead, and the forgery was immediately exposed. The boss locked him in a room, beat him, kicked him, denied him food, interrogated him, and even gave him a glass of water with white powder dissolved in it and forced him to drink it — Greenberg guesses it was some kind of stimulant to make him talk more, while his skin broke out in hives. They never found out he was in contact with a journalist, and Greenberg says if they had, he would certainly have been killed.

item.title: Supersonic Passenger Flight Stalled for Fifty Years — the Blocker Was the Engine, Not Aerodynamics
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-allin-超音速客机没落五十年-卡在发动机不在空气动力学/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-allin-超音速客机没落五十年-卡在发动机不在空气动力学/
item.description: Concorde was banned not because the technology failed but because the sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and that engine is now going to power data centers first.
item.content:encoded:
Concorde was banned not because the technology failed but because the sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and that engine is now going to power data centers first.

A founder's first-person account of the full path from being turned down by Bezos to building his own engine and pivoting into data-center power generation, with concrete numbers and regulatory detail, at high information density.

5:12 Bend the boom and the ban disappears
Boom's answer to the sonic boom is not to make the aircraft quiet but to use the atmosphere's own refractive capacity to redirect the boom back up into the sky. Blake calls it boomless cruise; engineers call it Mach cutoff. The boom is still generated at the aircraft, at normal strength, but it bends sharply in the air and never reaches the ground. This works below Mach 1.3 — that is, 50% faster than today. So you can't go full speed over land, but a 9am departure from New York and a 9:30am landing in San Francisco still holds. Over the ocean nobody is listening, so full speed is fine. Pushed to its logical extreme, it comes down to this: if there is no boom at all, there is nothing to argue about.

5:12 From executive order to act of Congress, unanimous
The US ban on overland supersonic flight, in place since 1973, ended last June 6. But Blake knew an executive order can in theory be reversed by the next person, so he turned to pushing Congress. The Supersonic Legalization Act passed the House unanimously and recently cleared a Senate committee unanimously as well. He put the significance plainly: supersonic is not a partisan issue, which is the only way to get that kind of vote count. For a hardware company that has to span multiple administrations on a timeline measured in decades, upgrading regulation from executive order to statute turns policy risk from a variable into a constant.

6:12 Getting stood up by a big company saved the company
Blake says one of the dumbest things he ever did was outsource engine development to an established large company; the plan failed, the split with Rolls-Royce was public, and everyone said Boom was finished. So they decided to do what everyone said was impossible: build the engine from scratch, and not just design it — even the hardest parts, like turbine blades, they make themselves. His judgment: engineering and manufacturing have to be done together, and if you want to reindustrialize America you have to invent the next generation of manufacturing technology here, not bring back what was offshored to China. That forced choice later became the source of the company's valuation — because an engine designed to run at full power for long periods at Mach 1.7 temperatures, with the fan removed and a generator bolted on the back, is a power generation device.

8:13 The supersonic engine's first customer is a data center
Boom's engine's first application is not in the sky but on the ground. Take off the fan, put a generator on the back, drop it into a few trailers, and you can do 42 megawatts of behind-the-meter generation — and because the engine core was designed to run at high temperature, it needs no water. Blake pointed out specifically that water is a common objection, so just make it disappear. The factory has already started producing the first parts, with a target of multiple gigawatts a year and more than 10 gigawatts added to the grid over the next five years. The financial point of this path: before the supersonic airliner ever gets its airworthiness certificate, the company already has a product it can sell — and it is selling to the buyer that is least short of money right now.

10:14 Run on the ground first, then fly
Boom putting the engine into ground power first has an engineering side effect: it will be the most-tested new jet engine in history, because it will have run for enormous numbers of hours on the ground before ever being installed and flown. Blake admits plenty of hard problems remain and success is not guaranteed. The promise to passengers: twice as fast over water, 50% faster over land with no sonic boom. The sequencing itself is worth noting — normally an aviation engine's validation comes from accumulated flight hours, and Boom has moved validation to the ground and to data-center scenarios, effectively having another market pay the test bill for the aviation business.

10:38 Transatlantic round trip, breakeven fare $3,500
The numbers Blake gives: a Mach 1.7 transatlantic round trip in 3 hours, breakeven fare around $3,500, with the actual fare most likely higher, and every extra dollar of that being United's profit. His assessment of Concorde: zero out of three on safe, comfortable and cheap; Boom intends to take all three. On timeline, the target is 4 years, but he says explicitly that ‘fast is more important than predictable’, cannot give a firm date, and only promises to deliver at the earliest time physically possible — which from the outside looks like around 2030. There is a tradeoff worth noting here: a hardware company publicly admitting it is unpredictable, trading certainty for speed.

13:15 Data-center demand is so big they'll auction it
Asked whether the data-center business is a money printer, Blake's answer is ‘it's the most incredible money-printing business I've ever seen’, and he says his inbox holds tens of gigawatts of demand. The first engine fires up next month, and then they plan to auction off all of the capacity. Asked whether he has talked to Elon, or whether this is for Colossus, Blake only says ‘you should ask Elon’. The value of this segment is the anomalous supply-demand signal it gives: for a power product that has not yet reached mass production, demand already far exceeds capacity, and the pricing mechanism has gone from a quote to an auction.

16:19 Break the sound barrier Monday, model in the Oval Office Thursday
Blake recapped the speed of this regulatory push: broke the sound barrier on a Monday, tweeted, Elon retweeted, flew to Washington that night to start the legalization lobbying, and by the time he landed had an invitation from the White House; into the West Wing on Tuesday, and by Thursday the aircraft model was in the Oval Office — and it is still there. From launch to signature, the executive order took 115 days, which he considers slow but admits would be slower under a different administration. His assessment of this administration: ‘I like that it moves fast’. This is the most concrete policy-operations sample in the whole episode: how a single technical milestone gets converted directly into political attention.

item.title: Why renaming a charity is more dangerous than renaming a company
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.description: Mercy Corps became Prosper Global not because the strategy changed, but because the old name could no longer hold what it was already doing — and in conflict zones, a rename can put staff at greater risk.
item.content:encoded:
Mercy Corps became Prosper Global not because the strategy changed, but because the old name could no longer hold what it was already doing — and in conflict zones, a rename can put staff at greater risk.

Medium information density. The first half covers the disaster response and the logic of the rename; the second half, on the erosion of international humanitarian law and AI entering aid work, is worth more.

4:21 The rename isn't a new strategy — the old name can't hold the new business
Jada says an organization's identity grows the way a person's does. The name Mercy Corps described the starting point of aid — rushing in to save people, handing out food, casting itself as the benevolent giver. But what she now discusses with potential donors is cash assistance, seed insurance, identity management on blockchain, and the response she gets is flatly: "That has nothing to do with your name." The rename is not a change of mission; mission and values are the source of continuity, the name is not. Prosper Global is meant to shorten the conversation and put the values up front: we believe every person has the capacity to prosper, not merely to survive.

6:31 Renaming in a conflict zone puts safety on the line
Prosper Global operates in more than 30 countries, many of them remote sub-offices, often in conflict zones. Communities recognize the Mercy Corps colors and know who to look for. A rename means a phased rollout, one country at a time, with local people judging the timing and the context. Jada is blunt: they don't rate armed guards, they don't carry weapons, and their ability to work rests entirely on the trust of the communities they serve. So this is not an ordinary corporate logo swap — in the short term it may make frontline staff less safe. The interesting part: 90% of employees live in the communities they serve, and many program staff were the first to understand the rename — they don't want to be treated as "charity cases."

8:37 Syria is the clearest case for the rename logic
Driving from Aleppo to Damascus, Jada saw rubble the whole way. Syria has just come out of 14 years of civil war and is one of the few countries in the world where the population is flowing back in rather than out, with millions returning at the same time. But many are still living in camps, and the communities they return to have no working water systems and destroyed homes. She tells the story of a woman named Ola: her husband was injured in the war, she hadn't worked before the war, and her community wasn't used to women doing certain things, so she was forced to take over the farming and start cultivating land. Prosper Global helped her set up drip irrigation and repair the local water system, and along the way she learned to ride a motorcycle and brought another group of women along with her. Jada says Syria may be one of the world's rare pieces of good news, and it has been forgotten.

10:44 Oil in Hormuz decides whether African farmers plant at all
Prosper Global published a report called From Hormuz to Hunger, tracking how conflict in the Strait of Hormuz ripples into six fragile countries: Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia, Pakistan, Myanmar and Lebanon. The mechanism: these countries depend on Hormuz for basic fuel, and fuel price spikes hit fertilizer supply directly. When Jada was in Sudan, farmers had only a two-to-three-week window to get seeds in the ground, and fuel costs had already risen 60%. When farmers can't work out what to plant or which inputs they can afford, some decide to abandon the land. This isn't just a problem for now — it cripples next season's food supply too. Meanwhile aid organizations are themselves paying higher oil prices, so the same money serves fewer people.

12:47 Ukraine's grain silos are being bombed on purpose
Prosper Global has just launched a grain storage project with the UN and the Ukrainian Red Cross. Jada says Ukraine actually had a good harvest this year, but Russia is increasingly targeting civilian and economic infrastructure, especially grain silos and storage facilities, with drones. The logic is simple: even with a good harvest, if the silos and storage are bombed out, or the roads and ports are hit so the grain can't move, that season's income is gone. This is a deliberate attack on that kind of infrastructure. What they do includes providing sleeved grain storage bags, helping farmers clear mines, and helping those who lost machinery rebuild or find alternatives. Ukraine was once the breadbasket for many countries, and it needs that grain to feed itself and its own economy.

14:47 Prevention costs about seven times less than response, and nobody wants to fund it
Jada says there is a tendency in the current relationship with the US government to fund only life-saving aid, which is in fact the least efficient way to do it. Her number: doing prevention, trying to avert a crisis before it happens, costs roughly seven times less than intervening afterward. She also notes they had been ready to rename to Prosper Global before the Trump administration took office, but held off to see how things would land — the funding had already vanished and the whole sector was in a hard place. Instead they doubled down on helping Americans understand the nature of humanitarian need and what aid actually looks like today, correcting a lot of misinformation. She says the key to a leadership moment is intentionality: what are you letting go of, and what are you continuing to build on?

19:59 With USAID gone, the sector has to rebuild an architecture
Jada acknowledges they have to do more with less money, but stresses this isn't just about saving money — it's about rebuilding an architecture, in a sense. USAID's offices and missions around the world used to carry a huge amount of coordination and information-sharing, and now all of that is gone. So the question isn't just "can AI help" — it's that the sector's entire coordination layer has been pulled out. She says AI can't physically deliver supplies for you and has limits in knowledge, but it is useful at the program level: accessing best practices, pinpointing more precisely what a community needs, anticipating certain needs. They haven't found that "magic solution" yet, but they're talking to AI companies, hoping to build something together that genuinely changes humanitarian aid.

23:02 International humanitarian law is eroding, starting with Ukraine
Jada says the checks on international humanitarian law are being tested and violated, and that this is part of a broader trend. She sees the first case treated as a deliberate pattern as Russia's invasion of Ukraine — attacks on ports, bridges and other civilian infrastructure that was traditionally untouchable followed quickly. The pattern then spread to the way the war is fought in Sudan, and they believe violations of international law are also occurring in Gaza. She notes it took the deaths and destruction of millions after World War II to bring these rules into being: no collective punishment, people must be able to go to school and have a hospital network, civilians shouldn't pay the price. Now those rules are being violated everywhere. She says even the phrase "international humanitarian law" sounds like Greek to a lot of people.

item.title: In the AI Era the Most Valuable Thing Isn't Intelligence, It's the Audit Trail
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.description: Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever runs the pipes into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.
item.content:encoded:
Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever runs the pipes into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.

Worth hearing for vertical AI founders, investment banking/PE practitioners, and enterprise software investors. The first half's product history is only moderately dense with information; the pricing, audit, and sales mechanics in the back half are worth more.

2:03 Model companies are refineries; vertical companies are chemical plants
Gabe reasons from Dario's line: if tomorrow a whole data center full of geniuses appeared at the door of Goldman, Millennium, Citadel, these institutions would still take a long time to figure out how to change how they work and how to wire it into their systems. So he thinks the biggest challenge for every great investor over the next five years isn't getting access to intelligence, it's wiring AI into the investment lifecycle. That's also why he isn't worried about Anthropic and OpenAI: finance is a collection of niches with wildly different data, definitions, and regulatory requirements, and for Anthropic to stop and pick up this coin would be pulling over on the road from $100 billion in revenue to $1 trillion.

4:04 Applied AI companies have a first-mover disadvantage
Gabe says companies that did applied AI early were actually at a disadvantage: you think you know where the world is going, you build the product for that endgame, but the models aren't there yet, and users try it and just say ‘this is garbage.’ Rogo went through that phase itself. His judgment is that if your read on the endgame is right and you keep building toward it, the moment the models catch up is the magic moment. He ties Rogo's product eras directly to model eras: 01 Pro was the first version reliable enough to at least serve as a search tool; by Opus 4.5, and from late 2025 into early 2026, the models can basically do anything a junior investment or banking professional does, provided you give the right instructions and context.

6:06 The MD annotating on an iPad is the real last mile
Gabe gives an example as concrete as it gets: the typical workflow for an investment banking MD is to email deck comments to an analyst, and Rogo lets that MD email the comments to an AI analyst, get a revised draft back in 20 minutes instead of two days, automatically notify the junior analysts on the deal, and show a full audit trail of every small change. He points out the key thing: this finance professional hasn't logged into a computer in ten years, but he has an iPad, and he knows how to annotate on an iPad. That kind of product detail for a specific end user can only come from someone with a spidey sense for the job.

16:57 The harness matters more than the model itself
Gabe compares Claude Code and Claude Cowork with ChatGPT: the models are actually similar, but Claude's harness and presentation are far better, letting the model exercise more long-horizon capability, and so usage and expansion took off. He extends the analogy to the brain: humans have high agency not just because of raw memory, IQ, and knowledge, but because there are a bunch of microservices in the head — how knowledge is stored, how it's retrieved, how it's triggered, and emotion is one way of triggering a microservice. A great investor's judgment comes from seeing something in the market that triggers a memory of some event, producing a creative decision. Those microservices are what vertical companies have to build.

23:43 Skip straight from per-seat pricing to outcome pricing
Rogo today is classic enterprise software: priced per seat, because buyers are used to comparing it to Bloomberg, FactSet, Capital IQ, PitchBook, and every deal signed needs an AE plus a solutions architect to shake hands and explain the integration. Gabe says Anthropic can sell to them easily, with spend rising exponentially and no human in the loop, because it's a token-consumption model; but many industries can't ride the token-consumption wave, and Rogo is one of them, so it has to build its GTM machine at five times the speed. His pricing judgment is that every company goes through two pricing revolutions: first to usage based, then to outcome based. He'd rather skip tokens and usage entirely and ask the customer directly: how much will you pay me per good investment idea? Per quarterly LP report? Per investment banking CIM?

31:19 Auditability matters more than accuracy
Gabe says accuracy is of course still super important, but auditability matters more than accuracy, and the two get conflated all the time. The logic: if the answer is wrong and you don't know how to check it or see where it came from, then whether it's accurate or not you can't use it, because you don't trust it. Conversely, if it's right most of the time and even when it's wrong you can clearly see the assumptions and the data sources, it's still actionable and still saves time. As tools move from copilot to autopilot — not just retrieving information but having agency, actually making investment decisions or sending emails — you have to be able to look back at why it decided that way, because you need to debug it, just as when an individual investor makes a bad decision you check whether the data input was wrong or someone lied to him. In regulated capital markets, if you can't explain the basis for a decision, you simply don't get through.

34:48 The company brain is called Shrek, and every conversation is recorded
Every conversation inside Rogo is recorded, and new hires are told on day one ‘you are always being recorded,’ and that content is filtered into the company brain, named Shrek because the engineers thought that was funny. There's a dashboard showing the ‘swamp’ of what everyone is working on, connected to the company's various systems, with a very clear sense of company goals, values, what has to be delivered to customers, and the north star metric, so it can shape every answer and deliverable. It's both passive and active: you can go in and ask ‘how should I pitch the value proposition and savings of model routing to a large institution,’ and it pulls the information out; it also proactively reminds you, ‘Patrick, I see you're meeting this private credit firm on Thursday, here's what you should know, the use cases that will resonate, and the ROI metrics companies you've worked with in the past want to hear.’ Gabe says this is the core problem of enablement: suck information in, hand it out when people need it.

42:18 What it's like to be turned down by 40 investors in a row
Gabe says the hardest low point was the A round: at that point there were no star investors on the cap table, David Tisch introduced him to 40 investors, he met Sequoia, Kleiner, Benchmark and others, and all 40 passed. And not the send-a-deck-and-get-no-interest kind — it was ‘interesting, meet Gabe,’ ‘like Gabe, talk for an hour,’ ‘come to IC,’ ‘let's grab a meal,’ ‘come back over the weekend’ — and then ‘we've decided not to invest.’ He says that phase had nothing to do with anything except you, like being dumped by 40 girlfriends, each time you fell in love and each time the other person said it wasn't for you. In the end Thrive didn't invest either; Keith Rabois came about a month after everyone had passed, and Gabe asked Keith back: if this isn't a contrarian bet, why do all your friends say it's a bad idea and none of them believe in me? He sums up three reasons investors didn't invest: they underestimated the finance TAM, the product really was bad at the time, and there weren't enough data points to believe he could chew glass and ship the next version.

item.title: The Rocky Statue Is Not Art, Yet It Became a Landmark Philadelphia Can't Tear Down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.description: A bronze made for a movie was rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, left to sit in a warehouse — and in the end what saved it wasn't artistic merit but the fact that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's status is always granted by its audience, not by the experts.
item.content:encoded:
A bronze made for a movie was rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, left to sit in a warehouse — and in the end what saved it wasn't artistic merit but the fact that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's status is always granted by its audience, not by the experts.

A complete narrative arc in 30 minutes: class, artistic authority, race and monument politics, dense with detail and almost no filler.

4:09 Bronze instead of foam decided its fate
In Rocky III there's a scene: a fictional mayor stands on the museum steps and dedicates a statue to Philadelphia. The production could have had the art department make a prop out of painted plastic and foam and toss it in a dumpster after shooting. Stallone didn't do that — he paid $53,000 to have the artist A. Thomas Schaumburg cast the statue in bronze. Laura Holzman says that choice was crucial: it wasn't made of a material you throw away after filming, it was made of an art material. Stallone went to high school in Philadelphia, called Rocky a "euphemism" for the city, and then offered to donate the 1,800-pound statue to Philadelphia to stand permanently at the top of the steps. It was precisely because it was bronze and not foam that the next fifty years of fighting were even possible.

10:25 The root of the opposition was Philadelphia wanting to be Athens
The museum leadership opposed it most fiercely, and their reasons were far bigger than aesthetics. Philadelphia's glory days had long faded by the early 20th century, and by the 1976 Bicentennial it was the city that could never shake its bad luck: crumbling infrastructure, corrupt local politics. In the 1980s the arts world wanted to remake Philadelphia as a cultural metropolis and restore the title a famous architect had given it — "the Athens of the Western world." They had bet heavily on the city's most important museum, and they didn't see how a nine-foot-tall, sharply abdomened boxer could help Philadelphia get there. Art commission chairman F. Eugene Dixon Jr. wrote to a colleague that the statue standing temporarily on the steps was fine, but putting it permanently in the courtyard — "I hope you're joking." In the winter of 1980 the commission voted 6 to 2 against permanent placement, and the remaining two votes were to ban it from the steps altogether.

12:34 Thousands of signatures are no match for eight people with votes
What brought the statue back to Philadelphia from Los Angeles was a grassroots campaign. Local truck driver Art Gorman was one of its biggest champions — Mark Bowden describes him as a regular Philadelphia guy from a blue-collar neighborhood, thinking: who are these self-appointed sophisticates, these taste gatekeepers, to tell us what we can see on the steps of the art museum? At the end of 1980 he drafted a petition, all in capital letters, knocked on doors for thousands of signatures, and drew a pile of media coverage. The show says it plainly: the story got told as blue-collar Philadelphia versus elite high-culture Philadelphia, a "slobs versus snobs" narrative. But the petition couldn't change the commission's basic position — the snobs were still the ones voting.

13:34 The prop crew bolted the statue into the ground with steel bars
Rocky III opened in May 1982, and the art commission only allowed the statue back on the steps for the premiere; once it was over, it had to go. But the production company simply left it there, the city wouldn't pay to move it, and it was up to the museum to deal with it. Months later the movers finally came and found an obstacle: the statue was bolted to the sidewalk with steel bars driven several feet into the ground — "as if the filmmakers intended it to stay there forever." In the end the statue was pried loose and hauled five miles away to the Spectrum arena in South Philadelphia, where it stood with other athletes' statues. Most people thought the fight was over, but Stallone spent the next twenty-five years repeatedly asking for it to be moved back to the museum, and every time he got the same answer: no.

15:35 One phone call did more than twenty years of aesthetic debate
In 2006 things moved: the mayor was pushing a batch of public space renovation projects, Stallone was about to release his first Rocky film in 16 years, and the statue was sitting in a warehouse because the city was building a new sports complex. Stallone's friend Jimmy Binns — who had appeared in the sequels and was a well-connected Philadelphia lawyer — called the mayor and asked if he'd help get the statue back to the museum. Binns recounted the conversation: he asked the mayor, do those museum board members invite you to their homes for cocktails on Sundays? The mayor laughed and said no. Binns said, then screw them. The mayor said, alright, screw them. With the mayor behind it, even the Philadelphia Museum of Art started to give ground, and the compromise worked out was: the statue returns to the museum permanently, but not at the top of the steps — a little off to the side at the bottom. The only remaining obstacle was the art commission, which held the final vote.

19:46 By 2006 the debate was no longer about art
In May 2006 the commission announced it might move the statue, setting off a new round of public discussion. City official Harris Baum argued against it on a local NPR call-in show, on the grounds that the Parkway was to be developed into a cultural district like Paris's, "but that's not a work of art." The response he got was completely different from the 1980s: listeners didn't want to talk about art. Judy said the statue was the image of the blue-collar spirit; Jack, calling from Lansdale, said ideally he'd want it at the top of the steps, but a bunch of pretentious old guys in wigs would never let that happen, and he flat-out called Baum a snob and insulting. Baum was fighting the battle of twenty years earlier. On September 6, 2006, the art commission voted 6 to 2 in favor, and the minutes read: the majority believed the statue's iconic symbolic meaning had earned it a place in the city's identity. Less than a week later the statue was unveiled, fitted with nighttime lighting, and lifted onto a brand-new granite base.

26:14 The real champion's steps are called the Rocky steps
The 2015 Charleston church shooting, in which nine people died, set off a national reckoning with racist symbols, and the wind reached Philadelphia: the Columbus statue and the statue of former mayor Frank Rizzo — known for violent policing and racist demagogy — became targets. When Monument Lab asked Philadelphians what kind of monuments they wanted to build, some began questioning whether Rocky was appropriate: Philadelphia has a real boxing history, and those boxers were mostly Black, including heavyweight champion Joe Frazier, who beat Muhammad Ali in a fight watched by more than 300 million people. The show points out that the two most famous things in the first Rocky training montage — running up the museum steps and punching raw meat — actually came from Frazier's real training routine. Frazier got a statue in 2015, but many Philadelphians feel the twelve-foot bronze is nowhere near worthy of a real champion: "His image isn't on the tour buses, and the steps he ran are called the Rocky steps."

28:21 In the reckoning over monuments, Rocky became the city's emotional container
After George Floyd was killed in 2020, Philadelphia's largest Black Lives Matter demonstrations set out from the art museum steps every day, with thousands of protesters gathering right beside the Rocky statue. By then it was already a monument, and by rights it should have faced the same scrutiny — a statue erected for a fictional white movie character, taking the place of a real Black champion, its days should have been numbered. But no one tore it down; instead they folded it in: someone hung a sign on it reading "no justice, no peace," early in the pandemic it wore a mask, later a Ukrainian flag, and when the Eagles' Brandon Graham retired, his cleats were hung on it. Paul Farber saw the most contradictory scene: a Black family posing for a photo all raising Black Power fists, and three or four people later, a group of white men in their early twenties raising white power gestures — the two things happening almost simultaneously without conflict.

item.title: Vitamin K injection refusal rates have doubled, and infant brain bleeds are preventable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
item.description: Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular shot drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates have risen from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse have 81 times the risk of late bleeding.
item.content:encoded:
Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular shot drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates have risen from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse have 81 times the risk of late bleeding.

High information density: it covers both the clinical mechanism of newborn bleeding and the history of vitamin K's discovery and how the 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust. The second half, on who refuses and why communication fails, is the most valuable part.

20:34 Every newborn is born deficient in vitamin K
Vitamin K does not cross the placenta effectively, so even if the mother supplements during pregnancy, the newborn's vitamin K-dependent clotting factors do not rise appreciably. Add an immature gut microbiome and very little self-synthesized K2, and breast milk averaging only about 2.5 micrograms per liter, and a exclusively breastfed infant gets less than 1 microgram a day for the first six months. The result is that every newborn is at high risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding. This is not an outlier phenomenon; it is the physiological norm.

22:35 Late bleeding often comes with no warning, straight to brain hemorrhage
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in newborns comes in three types: early, within 24 hours of birth; classic, within the first week; and late, from one week to six months. The late form is the most dangerous: about 60% of cases are intracranial hemorrhage, and there is often no warning bleed beforehand, just a sudden brain bleed, seizures or unresponsiveness. Mortality ranges from 50% to 60% depending on era and country, with modern figures around 20%. That is why the value of a single preventive shot cannot be measured by "the bleeding probability is low."

25:46 One intramuscular shot pushes the risk to near zero
Since 2003 in the US, and in the vast majority of medical societies and public health agencies worldwide, a single intramuscular vitamin K injection at birth is recommended. It provides a stable supply for the first few months, cutting late bleeding risk from 4 to 7 cases per 100,000 live births (some countries report as high as 80) to about 0.4.
