Infants who receive no prophylaxis have 81 times the risk of late bleeding compared with those who do. Oral regimens also significantly reduce risk, but they require multiple doses, are affected by absorption and vomiting, are less effective than injection, and no oral formulation is approved by regulators in the US.

44:27 How the 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust
In the postwar research climate, informed consent and patient protections had not yet entered the picture, and the logic was "vitamin is harmless and possibly beneficial, so give it to all premature infants." In the mid-1950s Britain gave some premature infants up to 60 milligrams of synthetic vitamin K, after which jaundice, hemolysis and kernicterus rates rose and several infants died. The formulation was withdrawn and the dose dropped back to 1 milligram, but confidence had been shaken: of more than 16,000 infants born in Britain in a single week in 1970, only 20% received vitamin K. This history shows that the aftershocks of a single overdose incident can last for decades.

46:31 The 1990s leukemia scare has never fully cleared
In the early 1990s two British studies linked intramuscular vitamin K to later leukemia risk, and the reaction was swift and strong: some countries switched to recommending oral vitamin K and reserving injections for the highest-risk infants, and British injection rates fell from 58% in 1988 to 38% in 1993. But the two studies had small samples and insufficient controls, and a large body of subsequent research and a WHO working group found no association, with IARC also concluding there was no evidence of carcinogenicity. The problem is that bad news travels fast and good news does not, just like MMR and autism: once doubt is planted, the world never fully recovers.

49:35 Refusal rates have doubled, and the 81-fold risk is badly underestimated
US refusal rates nearly doubled from 2017 to 2024, rising from 3% to 5.8%, with some hospitals reporting even higher. Infants whose parents refuse have 81 times the risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a figure that is badly underestimated because the bleeding itself remains rare and communication is inadequate. Research shows most parents, whether they accept or refuse, know vitamin K is related to bleeding, but do not know that this bleeding can cause severe brain injury and a mortality risk above 20%. The information is present, but it is not being effectively conveyed.

50:36 Refusals fall into three categories, and birth attendants matter enormously
Reasons for refusal fall roughly into three categories: distrust of medicine, pursuit of "natural birth," and preference for alternative medical lifestyles. Some believe that if infants needed more vitamin K, evolution or God would have provided it; others interpret a recommendation to supplement vitamin K as "you are not fit to be a mother." Research also finds refusers are more likely to be white, college-educated, over 30, and planning a home or birth center delivery. The birth attendant's stance is critical: in a New Zealand survey, 100% of doctors thought all infants should receive vitamin K, while only 55% of midwives did, and 26% of those would not give it to their own children; in Canada, infants delivered by midwives were 8 times more likely to have vitamin K refused than those delivered by doctors.

55:46 Doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time
Some parents who lost a child or whose child suffered brain injury because vitamin K was not given are doing something very brave: speaking publicly to say "I made this decision, this is the consequence, do not follow me." At the same time, doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time in their careers, and they are raising the alarm in their communities. Some researchers and doctors are pushing to establish a national US registry of vitamin K refusals and administrations, because vitamin K deficiency bleeding is not a notifiable disease and cases are likely undercounted. In a post-pandemic era when expertise is treated as a dirty word, these preventable injuries and deaths will continue to rise.

item.title: US Strategic Oil Reserve Hits Bottom, Venezuelan Oil Won't Save It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-indicator-美国战略石油储备见底-委内瑞拉石油救不了它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-indicator-美国战略石油储备见底-委内瑞拉石油救不了它/
item.description: The salt cavern reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and overuse is dissolving the salt layers and destabilizing the cavern structures; Venezuelan oil is a different type, requires $100 billion in infrastructure investment, and can't get around the deadlock of congressional appropriations.
item.content:encoded:
The salt cavern reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and overuse is dissolving the salt layers and destabilizing the cavern structures; Venezuelan oil is a different type, requires $100 billion in infrastructure investment, and can't get around the deadlock of congressional appropriations.

Information density is moderate, but it explains the physical degradation mechanism of the SPR—something most coverage omits. Suitable for those concerned about energy security and macro.

0:00 Promised to fill it up, but it fell another 30%
In his inaugural address, Trump promised to fill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve "to the top," but since then the reserve has fallen another 30%. The Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz, leaving a massive amount of global oil unable to ship, and the reserve was used as a price buffer to protect Americans from the global supply shortfall. The problem is that this buffer itself is running out. Trump's new answer is Venezuelan oil, which he called "the largest oil deal in our nation's history," saying 65 billion barrels would go to the US. But the show asks: can Venezuelan oil really save the SPR? And what does this mean for ordinary people's wallets?

2:03 The reserve isn't oil tanks, it's salt caverns dissolved out
After the Arab oil embargo against the US in the early 1970s, the US government realized it needed a backup oil supply, and the SPR was born. About 30 countries worldwide have backup reserves—Japan, Germany, and Australia all have them—but the US version is unusual. Siddharth Mishra, a petroleum engineering professor at Texas A&M, says the US government determined that the most efficient way to store millions of barrels of oil was not metal tanks but salt caverns. Engineers pump in massive amounts of water to dissolve underground salt layers and create caverns—these aren't traditional caves you can walk into, they're man-made caverns, each cylinder roughly the size of the Empire State Building or larger. Between Texas and Louisiana, 60 such caverns make up the SPR.

4:10 Overuse is dissolving the caverns themselves
The SPR was first used in 1991 during Operation Desert Storm, and later during Hurricane Katrina, the 2011 Arab Spring, and the 2022 Ukraine war. The 2022 global release saved Americans about 17 to 42 cents per gallon. But the reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and it's dropping fast—down 50% over the past six years, with 85% of that attributed to the Ukraine and Iran wars. The risk isn't just about quantity: the lower the reserve, the more water needs to be injected, the more room there is for oil to be contaminated, and refineries don't like contaminated oil, making it harder to sell; contamination also forms sludge, making rapid extraction harder—and rapid extraction is the entire point of the SPR's existence. As water is continuously injected, the salt layers dissolve, the cavern structures become unstable, and this engineering marvel that once amazed Mishra is being weakened.

5:13 Filling the reserve can't get around Congress paying for it
Joseph Mikit, an energy security expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, says the US is not in a position to simply buy oil to fill the reserve. Under normal mechanisms, Congress must agree to buy oil and bury it underground, and with severe fiscal deficits, that's a tough sell. Previous administrations tried: during the Clinton and Bush years, the royalty-in-kind program—when companies extract oil from federally owned reserves, they don't pay the government in cash but deliver oil directly into the SPR. Now the government is looking at more unusual strategies: in April, Energy Secretary Chris Wright proposed drilling for oil under military bases, but no follow-up was heard; the recent headline plan is Venezuelan oil, with a private company giving the US 20% control of its existing and future oil fields in Venezuela.

6:15 Venezuelan oil isn't the same type as what's in the SPR
Key detail: Venezuelan oil is a completely different type from the oil in the US SPR, so it must go through some kind of trading mechanism—sell one type of oil, buy another. Energy security expert Joseph is optimistic about the Venezuela deal, believing such a trade could work. He says the plan requires many mechanisms to come together, but it adds a source of oil that won't cause massive market disruption, and it doesn't require the US to get Congress to agree to spend big to fill the SPR at a time of high oil prices and fiscal imbalance. In other words, any plan that doesn't require Congress to buy oil looks great. But the challenge is: getting oil out of the Venezuelan ground is notoriously difficult, and after years of underinvestment and corruption, it requires massive infrastructure investment.

7:19 $100 billion, and no one knows who pays
One Latin American energy expert puts the figure at $100 billion over the next decade to restore Venezuelan production to levels of 20 years ago. And it's unclear who would pay—oil companies, the US government, or someone else. Arnab Data, managing director focused on energy markets at Employ America, directly calls the Venezuela plan "a bit of a pipe dream." His question: we can meet demand with domestic and allied production, so why support Venezuelan production? Rather than investing $100 billion in another country, coordinating between agencies, and sorting through Venezuela's political chaos, it would be better to invest that money in the SPR. His exact words: we don't need to go out looking for oil, there's plenty in the fridge, right here.

8:22 The current oil-borrowing mechanism actually works well
Arnab thinks the Trump administration's current strategy is working well: the Department of Energy lends barrels to oil companies, which promise to return them later, with a premium of up to 24%. He sees this as a well-executed way to deliver to the market, while also signaling to the market that there's demand for US barrels. So here's the disagreement: Joseph is optimistic about the Venezuela deal, believing it provides a source of oil that doesn't disrupt the market and doesn't require congressional appropriations; Arnab thinks it's a pipe dream, the existing borrowing mechanism is sufficient, and the $100 billion would be better invested back in the SPR. The show ends with a reminder: global oil supply continues to decline, another strait is under Houthi control and at risk of closure, and Americans don't know how much longer the SPR can shield them from higher costs.

item.title: Making a Child Perform Isn't Connection, It's Depletion
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.description: Connection isn't getting your child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.
item.content:encoded:
Connection isn't getting your child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.

This episode isn't dense — it's a single topic on a parenting podcast. But if you're dealing with relatives pushing your child to perform, or you want to understand what "connection" actually means, it's worth listening to.

1:04 Making a child perform is fast-food connection
A mother writes in that her 17-month-old son can identify shapes and colors, speak in sentences, and name dinosaurs, but his grandmother keeps making him "perform" — repeating what he's learned, clapping — and when he won't cooperate she grabs his arm and does it for him, and recently even kicked him in the butt. Janet says this isn't an isolated case: we often assume connecting with infants and toddlers means getting them to react to us, to imitate us. But this is "fast-food connection." The child may smile because he's getting attention, but no one is truly seen.

4:08 We're performing too
Connection goes both ways: we don't just make the child perform — we're often performing ourselves rather than being who we are. In her forthcoming book Baby Person, Janet writes that she used to dance, make funny faces, and try every trick to get a reaction out of babies in order to bond with them. These surface methods left her exhausted, and the payoff was tiny and fleeting — "I made her laugh" is just a moment. She says this isn't deep connection; it's all surface.

6:14 Performance connection teaches children to be insincere
Janet lists five reasons connection shouldn't be a performance: one, it isn't real connection; two, it teaches the child insincerity — everything we do with our children teaches them something, and this teaches that "connection requires performing rather than being yourself"; three, it wastes energy and effort, and parents can't afford it; four, it doesn't satisfy, and doesn't move the relationship toward trust; five, it subtly belittles the child — why should a child have to perform to hold our attention and interest?

8:19 Charismatic people are charismatic because they're paying attention to you
Janet quotes something she's always remembered: certain people are magnetic to us not because of how they perform or what they put out, but because they're genuinely interested in us and paying attention to us. Children especially need this, because it's harder for them to express themselves proactively and they don't know what to say to connect. They need us to tune in to their subtleties: what they're interested in, what their expressions are saying, who they are.

9:19 Even a parenting expert couldn't connect with her grandchild
Janet read a book by a well-known psychologist regarded as a parenting expert, in which the author — now a grandparent — said she simply couldn't connect with a toddler grandchild and felt the child had no chemistry with her. Janet's immediate read: this grandparent was trying too hard — wanting to initiate games, wanting the child to cooperate, operating rather than connecting. Her method works for every child from infancy on: observe, listen, receive, pay attention.

10:21 Comment on what you see instead of pretending to be interested
The concrete approach: treat the child as a person with depth, talent, interests, and a real point of view worth knowing. Then comment on what you see — "You're looking over there, did you hear a dog?" "You seem really interested in those blocks, I see you lining them up." Not pretending to be interested, but actually becoming interested. Children can tell the difference between "good job" and "wow, that took a while, I saw you thinking about which one goes on top, and the round one rolled down."

12:31 Children can put a grandparent's behavior in context
How do you let go of the fear that "this is bad for the child"? Janet says children are more aware than we think. They know "this is my grandparent, this isn't how my parents are with me, this is just how this person is." So it won't affect how they feel about themselves. Parents have enormous influence, but grandparents are different — even with frequent contact, the child can place it in the context of "my relationship with that person."

14:34 Narrate instead of correcting
Janet advises this mother not to try to teach her mother or correct her, but to connect, reflect, and trust them to handle the relationship themselves. Concretely: if her son does what the grandmother asks, let it go; if he doesn't and the grandmother kicks him, don't say to the grandmother "you shouldn't do that" — instead say to her son, "Grandma really likes it when you do what she asks, she's really into this" — without sarcasm, just stating what's happening. This is called sportscasting, and it helps both the child and the grandmother understand what's going on.

item.title: The Pentagon doesn't lack models — it lacks the chain that puts intelligence on the president's desk
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-五角大楼不缺模型-缺的是把情报送到总统桌上的那条链/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-五角大楼不缺模型-缺的是把情报送到总统桌上的那条链/
item.description: The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft. It was procurement reform, an institutionalized intelligence-analysis shop, and a chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it — APIs alone are not enough.
item.content:encoded:
The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft. It was procurement reform, an institutionalized intelligence-analysis shop, and a chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it — APIs alone are not enough.

The first half uses the U-2 analogy to lay out the bottleneck in government AI integration; the second half's judgments on procurement incentives, token economics and cybersecurity are worth more, but overall it's a loose interview chat with medium information density.

2:02 The U-2's miracle wasn't the plane, it was the procurement and analysis chain
Garrett says the U-2 story is usually told as a technology breakthrough, but what really mattered was three things: procurement reform that let government and industry work together that way, intelligence analysis being institutionalized (NPIC, which later became NGA), and getting judgment in front of the president and other decision-makers. That, he says, is the ‘miraculous’ part of the story. Today's AI problem is the exact inverse: the technology comes from the commercial world and moves so fast that it has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it into systems, workflows and decision processes — so ‘APIs alone are not enough’.

9:06 AI is moving fastest in warfighting, slowest in business systems
Garrett says the Pentagon and other agencies have made visible progress in warfighting spaces like CJADC2: using AI to build situational awareness across the battlefield, identify targets, and push intelligence quickly to decision-makers at the front. But core business systems — logistics, personnel, finance — have seen the least progress. His personal view is that we should stop splitting systems into ‘mission systems’ and ‘business systems’, because supporting the front requires clean, well-organized data usable at the tempo of operations, and those business systems were never built for that tempo.

10:06 One policy rule blocks the data of twenty thousand logistics troops
He gives a concrete example: some business systems' rules say status only needs to be updated once a week. That's policy — someone wrote it down. But decision-makers now want that data daily, which means going to roughly ten or twenty thousand Army supply sergeants and saying ‘you have to enter it daily, not weekly’. That's ‘a big boat to turn around’, and it has to come with clear value. Worse, the systems the government gave them were bad to begin with — making it hard to enter data while simultaneously demanding a big drop in data latency.

14:10 Government has no market competition as a forcing function
The host points out that a company that doesn't do AI gets killed, but the Air Force or the national security apparatus won't be ‘competed out’ — that kind of forcing function only comes along once or twice a century. Garrett agrees, but says we underestimate our own ability to manufacture mechanisms. He argues for using personnel policy and leadership as carrot and stick: reward people who take risks and take weird career paths, and let people who don't move fast enough face career stagnation or removal. He says it sounds ‘crude’, but that's the mechanism you have to follow.

19:18 Second-mover advantage: watch others burn cash and hit the potholes first
Garrett says this time it's the reverse of the U-2: the technology happens in the commercial sector first and then enters government, so government has second-mover advantage and can see what's working. He cites the lesson of token economics: do you open it up like Uber and let everyone burn tokens without limit, blowing the budget in a quarter, or do you understand token economics first and then deploy to employees? Also, as the federal government, if it gets this right it can act as a supersized buyer and negotiate volume pricing.

23:20 Putting GPUs at the edge first means clearing the policy on who signs and who's liable
Garrett says if you put these tools in soldiers' hands, you'd be shocked at how innovatively and cleverly they use them for their actual jobs — which may mean pushing compute to the edge and putting GPUs in service members' hands. But the obstacle is policy: a logistics officer signs for $500,000 worth of chips, and who's responsible if a chip breaks? He says you have to clear the policy and just say ‘we own this risk’ — if it means some GPUs get broken and money is lost, that's worth it, because the capability reaches the edge.

29:26 Intelligence analysis is more tractable than modeling decisions
Garrett thinks using AI to model strategic decisions is very hard, because it needs good data, and the decision process is deliberately murky — you can't get all the private notes, emails and situation-room audio and video. But intelligence analysis is a more tractable project: the intelligence process is structured and rigorous, agencies have their own SOPs and training, there are decades of data, and there are signals of quality, so you can build benchmarks from it. Still, it's only one input to a decision — historically many decision-makers looked at the same intelligence and made completely different decisions.

38:36 Bill by the hour and people will report more hours
Garrett says the government buys a lot on hourly rates by person and seniority, and this time and materials structure has a status quo bias. The logic is plain: if the incentive is for companies to report more hours, and there's no hard delivery requirement at the end of those hours, they'll report more hours. He says there have been signs of change over the past 12 to 18 months, but looking at public spending data, there's no large-scale shift — most spending is still time and materials. He also mentions that top companies spend 10% of their budget on tokens, while the US government is nowhere near that level.

item.title: Procrastination isn't a willpower problem: next time you'll fail with the same plan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.description: Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it hurts you, and about one in five adults does it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need different fixes, but they share one premise: change nothing about the plan and nothing about the result changes.
item.content:encoded:
Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it hurts you, and about one in five adults does it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need different fixes, but they share one premise: change nothing about the plan and nothing about the result changes.

It breaks procrastination into types you can actually treat and hands you a concrete toolbox instead of another self-discipline sermon. Medium-to-high information density.

1:16 The definition of procrastination has reluctance baked into it
Itamar's definition is: we delay something even though we don't intend to delay it and we know it's bad for us. So "I deliberately decided to do it later and I feel fine about that" is not procrastination. The gray zone is: what if you think delaying is good for you but it's actually harmful? His test is whether you could have anticipated that it would be better for you. About 20% of adults procrastinate chronically, and among students it's 50%. He stresses that procrastination doesn't only happen to people who don't care — people who are highly conscientious, genuinely productive, and sincerely want to make an impact procrastinate too.

3:27 Procrastination is several types, not one thing
Treating procrastination as a single phenomenon makes two mistakes at once: you fail to see that it happens to people other than students, and you can't deal with it in practice. A student who procrastinates from distraction, an executive who procrastinates from burnout, and an artist who procrastinates from perfectionism have different drivers and need different solutions. In his book Itamar distinguishes the anxious type, the pulled-away-by-external-temptation type, the burnout type, and a category he calls zigzaggers — closer to ADHD and impulsivity, switching back and forth among internal rather than external distractions.

5:00 Anxiety cuts both ways: fear of the task versus fear of the consequences
The mechanism by which anxiety causes procrastination is: doing this hurts, the brain says I don't want to hurt, so you put it off. But anxiety also has an adaptive side — if what you're anxious about isn't the task itself but the consequences of not finishing it, a little anxiety pushes you to act. The key variables are intensity and self-efficacy: a little anxiety may motivate you, a lot of anxiety paralyzes you no matter what it's aimed at; and if you also believe you're incapable of finishing, anxiety turns into paralysis more easily. Itamar adds one caveat: even when anxiety does push you, it's a dangerous source of motivation, because it brings stress and a worse experience along with it.

9:25 The biggest mistake is believing you'll try harder next time
Itamar says the biggest mistake people make when tackling procrastination is falling into the self-control fallacy: believing that next time, if you just try harder and summon more willpower, you'll get it done. The absurdity is that we watch it fail over and over, and over and over we believe again. The reasons include the bias blind spot (failing to recognize your own biases) and the empathy gap (predicting, while calm, how you'll behave in a hot emotional state). The real harm of this belief is that it offers a superficially simple silver bullet, which stops you from looking for what actually works. Spencer's addition: if nothing changes, the result won't change.

12:45 Design for your future self as if they were someone else
Spencer's approach: don't assume that the you of two weeks from now will get it done on willpower — instead ask "what would help a person a lot like me get this done in two weeks?" Set reminders, make social commitments, add rewards. Itamar says this is exactly an illustration of his core claim: procrastination isn't a time management problem, and even excellent time management can fail; what you should be doing is distance management. Addressing yourself in the second or third person, or using your name instead of "I", or asking "what advice would I give a friend", all create psychological distance and help you enter wise reasoning, seeing through the situation and around your biases.

16:13 Anxious type: decatastrophize, or do it anxious
For the anxious procrastinator, Itamar's first choice is to decatastrophize: catastrophizing means overestimating both the probability that something bad happens and the harm it does to you. For example, "there's a typo in my proposal, so the agent will blacklist me, and will tell everyone else to blacklist me too." The move is to ask: how likely is this really? How bad would it be if it happened? How would I carry on afterward? Spencer offers an almost opposite strategy: notice that this task makes me anxious, sit inside that feeling, feel it, and then do it anyway — he calls it metacognitive awareness. Itamar files it under the umbrella of mindfulness and self-compassion.

21:39 Procrastination is short-term emotional repair, and it reinforces itself
Spencer points out that anxiety generates anxiety: the moment you say "I'm not doing this now", the anxiety usually drops immediately, so you're learning that procrastinating makes you feel better, forming a reinforcement loop. Doing the opposite unwinds it — doing it while anxious functions like an exposure. Itamar says procrastination here is a defense mechanism: because you feel pressure or anxiety about something you should do, you push it away to avoid the painful emotion. It makes you feel better in the short term and worse in the long term, because you haven't solved the problem — you've only arranged to face it again and again later, or to face worse consequences.

26:39 The burnout fix is to do less
Itamar admits this is the last thing burned-out people want to hear: if you're burned out because you're doing too much, or things that drain too much, you probably need to do less and take more deliberate care of yourself — concretely, deciding more deliberately what to do and, more importantly, what not to do. He describes a loop: you're used to performing well, burnout makes your performance worse, so you work even harder, then burn out more, and it keeps getting worse. He calls this "borrowing health and productivity from your future self". He also notes that burnout doesn't come only from hours: reasonable hours spent on high-pressure, meaningless, or otherwise draining tasks will burn you out just the same.

item.title: The cost of RLHF is mode dropping, not alignment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-latentspace-rlhf-的代价是-mode-dropping-不是对齐/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-latentspace-rlhf-的代价是-mode-dropping-不是对齐/
item.description: RLHF forces models to be extremely conservative to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.
item.content:encoded:
RLHF forces models to be extremely conservative to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.

High information density: Diogo goes deep on the trade-offs between RLHF, RLVR, and RLCD, suited to anyone who needs to form a judgment on model training routes.

6:03 The cost of RLHF is mode dropping
Diogo thinks nobody pays attention to RLHF's downsides, especially mode dropping. The mechanism: to generate very long strings without making mistakes, the model must be extremely conservative, because errors are immediately visible while things that look correct but are subtly wrong are very hard to spot; this calibration is "total poison" for the probability distribution over strings. He uses this to explain why Yann LeCun's chart showing "LLMs necessarily make mistakes as sequences get longer" is mathematically obvious but empirically false — when you cover the distribution you aren't over-penalized by outliers; it's mode drop that loses the minority classes.

11:12 Refusing to answer is a type error, not a safety issue
Diogo distinguishes safety alignment from capability alignment: the latter is "doing what the user wants," the former is "following someone else's instructions," as with OpenAI and Anthropic. He thinks safety alignment is reasonable for products like ChatGPT and Claude, but in an API it is "nuts," "completely unacceptable" — if a dependency is running in the background, having your software randomly crash because a user sent a weird message is insanity. He opposes adding restrictions at the technical layer, on the grounds that every overfit fractures intelligence a little more, and today's models are already fractured enough.

18:15 Public benchmarks are a substitute for trust
Diogo says he is extremely anti-public benchmarks because they are extremely gameable: in the early days every lab had a team dedicated to collecting data like MMLU to pump up scores — essentially "benchmarking with extra steps." He admits intelligence has a je ne sais quoi (good model smell), so people need benchmarks to build trust, but in the long run you can only rely on vibes and trust, until you put the model into a concrete workflow and evaluate it there. He also says that if they wanted to make Jev dumb, they could have shipped that a year and a half ago.

27:34 RLCD is a new North Star, not a new algorithm
Diogo says the term RLHF has been conflated: the original work was Paul Christiano teaching a robot to do a backflip, later it was learning to summarize, and only after that came instruction following. What he actually calls RLHF is "instruction following as the North Star," unrelated to the PPO algorithm — just as DPO and its descendants don't use that paper's algorithm yet still count as RLHF. RLCD is the same: a new task direction, programs in the loop, taking the human out of the loop.

40:38 Reliability is a catchall; the North Star is robustness
Diogo defines reliability as a catchall: if AI can't automate something, in the end it's always some kind of reliability problem — it might be type safety, it might be determinism, or it might just be that the model is too jagged. He explicitly opposes making determinism (same input, same output) the North Star, arguing it's only slightly valuable for unit tests; what really matters is robustness — similar inputs getting similar outputs. The test is to stuff nonces like UUIDs into the prompt and see whether semantically identical questions get similar answers. He says that when people get burned by AI decisions, that happens at the robustness layer.

1:17:12 Reliability is more underrated than speed and cost
Diogo thinks the industry has its attention in the wrong place: "people focus too much on speed and cost and not enough on reliability." His judgment is that reliability is what makes people delighted and what makes them dare to trust. He ties this to TFP growth — he expects TFP growth above 3% within five years, and says that is the mark of an economic revolution, and also what the OpenAI charter originally meant to express. He estimates that all current models are still roughly at zero, maybe not even 1%, on valuable work in the world economy.

1:44:10 The optimal dose of RLVR is zero
Diogo says outright that for a model of TypeSafe's shape, the optimal amount of RLVR is zero. His argument is not "RLVR is useless" but that the "pacing the frontier" discussion smuggles in a premise: it assumes everyone must do more RLVR, and RLVR looks dangerous because it lets the model "do anything they want" in the middle of training — the less you restrict it, the stronger the model is on the outside. So the danger is not a side effect, it's the design goal. He calls this a "disillusion of responsibility": treating "we must do more RLVR" as an axiom and then deriving the conclusion "we are heading toward a dangerous world."

2:09:13 The KV cache is a tyranny over coding agents
Diogo wants to explore coding agents "free from the tyranny of the KV cache." The KV cache locks you into one model, and for efficiency you must keep appending, so you can't do state management, abstraction, decomposition — normal software practices. From this he explains several phenomena: why routing is hard, why sub-agents seem not to work, why compaction is a hard problem — because passing state requires intelligence that is much cheaper than reading state. Directions he envisions include: explicitly annotating state for subtasks, searching for relevant context in a tree of subtasks, parallel sub-agents reading each other's state, and coordinating with smart locks rather than basic-ass locks.

item.title: AI will hit an energy wall within three years, and the fix is to build a computer that isn't a computer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-allin-ai-三年内会撞上能源墙-解法是造一台不像计算机的计算机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-allin-ai-三年内会撞上能源墙-解法是造一台不像计算机的计算机/
item.description: Google alone burns through 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.
item.content:encoded:
Google alone burns through 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.

The first half is the energy math; the second half is his first public reveal of a physical dynamics computer prototype and measured efficiency numbers, which is rare hard information. The biology analogy in the middle can be fast-forwarded.

4:45 Energy isn't a cost line, it's the ticket to entry
Naveen's math: Google crosses 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token, a low estimate, that's 12 gigawatts. The US today puts about 40 gigawatts into data centers; the world, under 100 gigawatts. So one company's AI service eats more than a tenth of global data center energy. His call is that we hit the energy ceiling in about three years. More important, the ranking of scarce resources in a data center has flipped: it used to be floor space, racks, networking gear, GPUs; today it's energy — get the power contract first, then figure out how to fill it. And energy is 50% of the cost of serving a token; the rest is hardware capex and site.

7:04 What a squirrel does on 8 milliwatts, a GPU needs watts for
A human brain is about 20 watts. Scale linearly by neuron count down to a monkey brain and you get one watt, exactly your phone in your pocket. Further down, mice and bats are milliwatt-scale. A squirrel leaping between branches, a thousand times out of a thousand, does it on an 8-milliwatt brain. So your phone's battery could run a hundred-plus squirrel brains. Naveen's conclusion is that biology has already built a physical substrate suited to intelligence, while synthetic systems took a different path: the human cortex moves only about 16 billion bits per second, a high-end GPU moves close to 30 trillion bits per second in and out of memory, and inside the chip it's another 10 to 100 times higher. The energy goes almost entirely into moving information, not computing on it.

10:06 Moore's Law stopped, and the abstraction layers still charge rent
Transistor counts are still rising, but frequency stopped scaling long ago, single-thread performance stopped, and now even efficiency no longer improves as process nodes shrink — Naveen flatly says Moore's Law is basically over. His diagnosis is the abstraction layers: digital itself is an abstraction of the physical world, transistors actually have intermediate states and are engineered into 0s and 1s. Every layer of abstraction is lossy and ignores the complexity beneath it. So their approach is to wire the physics of the semiconductor directly to the neural network, skipping the layers in between. His intuition pump is flocks of birds and ant colonies: individuals do something extremely simple, the whole emerges into complex behavior, and the field is called dynamical systems theory.

12:07 Metronomes on a board sync themselves up
Put several metronomes on a rigid board that can roll back and forth, and they synchronize to exactly the same phase on their own, just because each metronome gives the board a tiny push. That's a purely physical dynamical system. Their question was: can this kind of system compute? The answer is yes — they open-sourced an image generation model called UNO built on a set of such oscillators, and it trains and generates images. Define the system state as the phases of all the oscillators, condition on the output, and generating a plane, a car or a bird follows different state space trajectories. It's the first proof that this class of system can be trained at scale and produce useful results.

14:08 Throwing away connections makes the system easier to train
Fully connected is n squared: 10 elements, 100 connections, fine; 1,000 elements, a million connections, not scalable at all. Their sparsity is deliberately discarding some connections and seeing whether the overall behavior can be rescued. The result isn't just that you can throw them away — after throwing them away the system behaves better and is more trainable, and that holds in both simulation and real physical systems. Naveen says this is the rare case where more efficient, more scalable and better performing all hold at once, a holy grail nobody had cracked, provided you frame the problem correctly first.

15:09 The first physical dynamics computer has already generated images
This is Naveen's first public reveal: they built the first physical dynamics computer. The company only formally started in January of this year, with no team at the time; on June 1 they sent the design to tape-out, and the chip is back in the lab and has produced results — the first images generated by this kind of computer. On efficiency, generating an image takes about 500 nanojoules, versus millijoule scale for an ordinary GPU; a nanojoule is 10 to the minus 9, several orders of magnitude apart. The reason is that it doesn't move information at all. Architecturally it's unlike both CPUs and GPUs: those are von Neumann architectures, with memory and compute separated and data shuttled back and forth; in this machine compute and storage are the same thing, there is no memory interface, and every compute unit is itself a memory.

17:09 4D computing: three spatial dimensions plus one of time
They call this 4D computing: physically, die stacking uses all three dimensions vertically and in-plane, and the fourth dimension is time in the dynamics. The objective function is intelligence per watt. There is a thermodynamic limit that can never be crossed; animal brains are only one to two orders of magnitude from it, while today's computing systems are about 10 billion times away. Their plan is to hit the limit of 2D lithography within three and a half years, and the company's overall goal is to beat biology. Naveen expects the result to be a change in form factor: from gigawatt-scale giant data centers to small data centers scattered everywhere, more local, more adaptive, and supporting billions of robots that dynamically combine to solve problems.

19:12 A thousand times cheaper means a thousand times more consumption
Naveen closes with the Jevons paradox: when the underlying cost of an asset falls, consumption grows by more than the price drop. Halve the price, consumption more than doubles; cut the price to a thousandth, consumption grows more than a thousandfold. So he doesn't think efficiency gains shrink the market — they create the largest market in human history. Chamath then presses on the ecosystem — tape-out, packaging and so on need a whole set of people to cooperate. Naveen's answer is a complete product within two years, in the form of a whole rack, as a new data center product, tokens in, tokens out over the network, but with an internal structure completely different from existing computers.

item.title: Strategic Reserves Are Nearly Drained — the Oil Price Crisis Is Only Now Beginning
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.description: Oil hasn't spiraled over the past six months because of three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. All three are now being drained, and the real shock is only just about to reach diesel and prices.
item.content:encoded:
Oil hasn't spiraled over the past six months because of three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. All three are now being drained, and the real shock is only just about to reach diesel and prices.

Medium information density, but breaking down "why oil prices didn't rise" into three buffers and the pace at which they're being exhausted is more useful than reading headlines.

2:03 Close Hormuz and a fifth of the world's oil is gone
The war began with Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz, cutting off roughly 20% of global oil supply outright. This was the move everyone treated as the "nuclear option" — nobody wanted to see it, because it's too bad for every side. Once the strait closed, oil shot from around $70 a barrel to well over $100. But the market didn't spiral out of control from there; it found several buffers that held the price down. The real question isn't "why did it rise" but "why didn't it rise more."

3:09 Three buffers, each less usable than the last
The first is the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve — emergency crude stored in salt caverns along the Gulf Coast after the 1970s Arab oil embargo — plus the commercial inventories refiners hold, which were at high levels before the conflict. The second is sanctioned oil: a large volume of "dark fleet" crude from Iran and Russia drifting at sea, which in March the US temporarily allowed other countries to buy. The third is China — the world's largest oil importer, normally buying about 12 million barrels a day, roughly 10% of global supply, which earlier this year bought about 3 million barrels a day less, effectively ceding that oil to others. Together, these three held oil below $100 and the national average gasoline price just under $5.

6:12 Ceasefire talks slapped every analyst in the face
In June the US and Iran began talks and reached a ceasefire, and market sentiment flipped 180 degrees: from "extreme crude shortage" to "crude surplus," with analysts predicting oil would fall to $70 or even $60 a barrel. But the peace deal collapsed within weeks, Iran closed the strait again, and Trump declared the ceasefire over. So it was back to the state at the start of the conflict. This episode shows one thing: this price contains a large bet on "the war ends soon," and that bet has repeatedly failed.

8:15 Six months of draining, and the buffers are nearly dry
Commercial inventories have been drawn down, strategic reserves have been released — and reserves can't be released at will; the government only authorized a specific quantity. The US has taken more than 130 million barrels out of the strategic reserve, leaving about 280 million, which sounds like a lot but is approaching the authorized ceiling. Worse, this time there's an added refinery crisis: Middle Eastern refineries were struck in the war, and Ukraine, in self-defense, knocked out a large chunk of Russia's refining capacity — and Russia is the world's second-largest diesel exporter. Once a refinery is destroyed, it takes months to restore. So the problem now isn't whether there's crude; it's that there isn't enough refining capacity to produce the fuel the world needs.

9:16 Venezuela can't put out a fire next door
The Trump administration holds Venezuela up as the solution, and its reserves may be the world's largest. But reserves being there doesn't mean production capacity is there: to actually raise output you have to spend money, move rigs, hire people, drill, and ship the barrels out — that's a matter of years and billions of dollars of investment. As for other "miracle solutions," Benoit says there basically aren't any; you can only hope for "small miracles" — like China deciding to raise diesel output, or refinery repairs finishing early. But none of these take effect tomorrow.

10:17 Gas stations haven't blown up yet — diesel blew up first
US consumers haven't yet seen prices spike at the pump; what's actually rising is diesel — the fuel that drives the heavy trucks moving consumer goods from one end of the country to the other. So the question becomes: will businesses cut back on deliveries? When do they pass costs on to consumers? Once diesel rises, every kind of business has to factor it into its pricing. This is the real channel through which this shock transmits from energy markets into the real economy, and why "gas prices are okay" is a misleading comfort.

12:23 Two paths: absorb it, or pass it on
Businesses have only two choices. One is to absorb it without raising prices: Jim Barber, a third-generation farmer in Pennsylvania, has raised his beef price only once in five years — even though the cost of hauling in hay is up 15% to 20%, he eats it himself, because he values his relationship with customers and believes the conflict will end soon and that holding on will be rewarded. A farmer's fuel exposure is triple-layered — fertilizer, hauling in hay, and shipping his own goods out — so energy costs can be paid three times over or more. The other is to pass it on: Ambix, which makes plastic parts, uses resin, and resin comes from oil; some costs rose 30%, 40%, 50%. At first it resisted raising prices, but as the war dragged on it began passing the 60 cents its suppliers added straight to customers.

15:36 Six-dollar diesel in August, and the shock starts embedding in the economy
When energy prices eased this summer, many businesses had a spell of optimism, thinking maybe they were coming out of the woods. Then in August tensions flared again, fuel prices rose again, and recently diesel hit $6 a gallon. Owen thinks this is the moment some businesses and economists began to realize "the price shock is truly embedding in the economy." Meanwhile, JPMorgan's commodity analysts said in their latest forecast that they no longer know how to model it — there's no baseline, because you can't see around the corner. On paper many economic indicators are healthy, but consumers feel terrible about prices, and nobody — oil executives, politicians, or CEOs — can say clearly how long this lasts.

item.title: AI Safety Language Is Destroying the Regulatory Debate: It's a Bug, Not a Demon
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-a16z-ai-安全语言正在毁掉监管讨论-那是-bug-不是恶魔/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-a16z-ai-安全语言正在毁掉监管讨论-那是-bug-不是恶魔/
item.description: Calling an AI failure "misalignment" assigns intent and moral judgment to software, leaving Congress and the public unable to understand what actually happened — when it should be debugged, reported and fixed like a bug.
item.content:encoded:
Calling an AI failure "misalignment" assigns intent and moral judgment to software, leaving Congress and the public unable to understand what actually happened — when it should be debugged, reported and fixed like a bug.

Medium information density, but Sinofsky uses three firsthand episodes — the 1983 hacker arrests, the 1998 virus, and Y2K — to pull "AI safety" back into a software engineering frame. Useful for anyone building products and communicating about policy.

0:00 "Misalignment" just means the software has a bug
Sinofsky's core claim: when AI does something we didn't expect, that isn't "misaligned" — it's software not running as intended, i.e. a bug. He says that back when Word ate files and deleted all their contents, nobody thought a demon had possessed Word and made it act against the user's will; and when a spreadsheet miscalculated, nobody circled up to pray to the alignment gods. Calling an AI failure "misalignment" assigns it properties it doesn't have — that it is "trying to do something," that it "made a moral judgment," that it "has rules and guidelines." And if it's just making decisions based on statistics, that still doesn't change the standard that it should do what you want it to do — a statistical error is a bug in the product.

7:07 A self-driving car running a red light is also a bug
Sinofsky uses self-driving as an example: if full self-driving runs a red light because it recognized a stop sign as a Christmas tree, we wouldn't say it "failed to align with the spirit of the December holidays and road signage" — we'd say it's a bug, and a dangerous one, because that stop sign means something. He points out that both Tesla and Waymo have built in extensive telemetry, diagnostics and extra cameras — things you wouldn't put in a spreadsheet but would put in life-critical software. And AI models are still at the research-project stage, lacking the tools and telemetry that important software is supposed to have.

8:07 Once telemetry ships, there are more bugs than you can fix
Sinofsky recalls that the software industry spent twenty years with no idea why programs crashed, and could only keep a list of crash sites and fix the top ten. Then someone said: why don't we write a program that, when it crashes, tells us over this new thing called the internet? Suddenly there was telemetry, and suddenly there were far more bugs than anyone imagined — the shift from "we have no bugs, we can ship" to "if we stopped all work, we could fix bugs forever." On that basis he says that when people talk about an AI pause, labs should of course slow down: stop adding new things and go build telemetry, tooling, logging and step-through debugging. He read the bug report OpenAI had just published, and the conclusion was clear: they simply don't know.

9:08 Excel wrote "send dogs" to disk
The first version of Excel for Windows in 1987 had a bug: it would write the letters "send dogs" into some Windows settings file on disk. Nobody knew where the phrase came from, and everyone combed through the Excel source and couldn't find it. Finally a tester wrote a script that generated charts continuously for days and printed them on an old dot-matrix printer, and found that after about two days it would write send dogs into that location — it depended on how much memory you had, how long it had been running, and what printer and device drivers you used. Sinofsky says they could easily have concluded that "Excel's brain decided to print send dogs," but they didn't — they actually debugged it, and then added telemetry.

13:10 PC software used to claim it was different from mainframes
Sinofsky recalls that IBM people would look at them and say their software was terrible, that Windows was garbage compared with the mainframe software running banks, airlines and power plants. For a long time their answer was "you don't get it, we're different, this is new and cool, we run in 64K instead of 1MB, we sell for $5,000 instead of $5 million." But in the end they found the only thing they had to do was grow up: once people started using Excel to decide how planes fly, using Word to file briefs with the Supreme Court, using PowerPoint to present on the Challenger space shuttle disaster, the standard changed. His conclusion: once your tools are used in those settings, you no longer get to use "we're new" as an excuse.

14:10 The virus that cost $12 billion in a day
In March 1998, a virus spread across the internet as a worm. Sinofsky got a call that morning from a reporter gasping "I love you, I love you, I love you." The next day's headline was: $12 billion in damage to the US economy in a single day. He says nobody had imagined a bug could cause $12 billion in damage in 12 hours, but it happened. So they held a meeting and decided to pause Outlook development until they understood what had happened. His attitude: the more people use a system, the more damage it can do when something goes wrong, but that's the price of admission, it's what you signed up for — "we're too popular to deal with it" is not an excuse.

16:10 Alignment piles a Google-sized problem on top
Sinofsky points out a concrete problem with alignment: to achieve it you need a huge set of rules defining what alignment is — what may and may not be done, what is safe, what is unfair. And software engineering learned long ago that adding too many constraints to a system makes it stop working and produces endless unintended side effects. You write one rule, and someone asks "what about this case," so you add another rule. He says this starts to look like Google's job of deciding how to present search results — which took them 20 years and thousands of full-time people, and is very, very hard. What AI labs have signed up for is the upgraded version of that problem: they aren't just retrieving results, they're synthesizing them, so they also have to invent a whole pile of things themselves, and no law is going to invent them for them.

17:10 Y2K didn't happen because people did things
Asked whether AI alignment is like Y2K, Sinofsky stresses there is a causal chain here: professionals worried a great deal, then professionals took a great deal of responsibility, and then nothing happened — that's a direct causal link. They rented generators and RVs, moved computers into secure bunkers, and that is why nothing happened. And there was almost no legislation — there were some odd regulations about Y2K compliance, but most of the rules were drafted by industry itself, by a cross-industry coalition of banks, insurers and others. He thinks OpenAI needs to sit down with all the frontier model players and labs and build a far better reporting mechanism; yesterday's report is a decent start, but nowhere near what a third party would need to understand what happened.

item.title: Optimism Is Not a Personality Trait, It's an Explanatory Style You Can Train
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.description: Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself, but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.
item.content:encoded:
Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself, but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.

Seligman himself walks through the full chain from learned helplessness to learned optimism, and in the back half treats agency as a civilizational variable to be quantified — a rare angle.

9:36 The dog doesn't run, and it's not because it never learned to run
In Solomon's lab, on day one the dog was strapped into a hammock and given Pavlovian shocks it could not escape no matter what it did; on day two it was put in a shuttle box where running to the other side would shut off the shock, and the dog just lay there. Seligman's judgment was that what the animal actually learned was not "the tone predicts the shock" but "nothing I do matters." That reading collided head-on with behaviorism at the time, because it required the animal to be a cognitive subject capable of thinking and of integrating experience across time.

13:50 People can be taught to give up by noise too
Hiroto moved the same design onto humans: on day one, headphones played a harsh noise, and for one group no amount of button-pressing could turn it off, while for the other group pressing a button did. On day two they were given a four-foot "human shuttle box" — hand on one side and the noise sounds, move it to the other side and it stops. People who had been through uncontrollable noise the day before simply left their hand in the box. Seligman stresses that the variable doing the work is not the trauma itself but whether there was control over the trauma — and they ran control experiments on exactly this point.

19:00 Helplessness became the model for depression
In 1970 depression was not yet a diagnostic category; there was only "manic-depressive illness." By 1975 the American Psychiatric Association's DSM had for the first time split out "unipolar depression," listing nine symptoms: passivity, cognitive difficulty, sadness, anxiety, sleep problems, food losing its taste, numbness, loss of pleasure, thoughts of death. Seligman compared the nine symptoms against the learned-helplessness literature accumulated by then and found that eight of them could be reproduced in the lab; the only one missing was thoughts of death — presumably because the experiments used noise rather than something more severe. This model went on to become the dominant model of depression, and the drugs that could break helplessness in the lab became the mainstream antidepressants.

22:19 Five out of eight give up, one in three does not
Across the whole helplessness literature the effect is statistical: on average five out of eight people or eight rats become helpless, and about a third do not. From the 1970s on, Seligman kept asking what was different about that third, and it became the turning point of his career. The answer landed on explanatory style: people who explain bad events as permanent ("I'm stupid"), pervasive ("I'm unlovable"), and their own fault become helpless; people who explain them as temporary, local, and not their fault recover quickly.

26:50 West Point's first week already predicts who will drop out
The first six weeks after entering West Point are called Beast Barracks: woken at four in the morning to run ten miles, systematically put through the wringer, with the stated purpose being to "break them," and roughly a third of candidates quit. Seligman's team measured explanatory style on day one, and the ones who dropped out were the pessimists. The same pattern shows up in college grades (optimists outperform their talent, pessimists underperform it) and in insurance sales: MetLife lost 50% of new hires within a year and 90% within four years; they hired 140 "special forces" whose optimism-scale scores were off the charts, and this cohort outsold the whole company and still had 75% on the job after four years, while the ordinary group was down to 10%.

34:17 Agency breaks apart into three beliefs
Seligman defines agency as the opposite of learned helplessness, made up of three parts: efficacy, the belief that you can accomplish a specific goal right here and now; optimism, the belief that you can accomplish it not only now but in the future and the further future; and imagination, the range of possible goals you can picture — the wider the range, the stronger the agency. Full agency is: I can do it now, I can do it in the future, and I can innovate across many different situations.

36:22 The axial age's answer may have been "I can do it"
Between 1000 and 500 BCE, Greece, the Hebrew world, China, India, and Persia all underwent upheaval: the Buddha, Confucius, and Socrates appeared, and technology, medicine, art, literature, and the first political freedoms all erupted together. Seligman's hypothesis is that over those five centuries humanity discovered the concept of agency. The evidence is vocabulary: in the Iliad, Achilles does not decide to act on his own — Athena tells him to act; a hundred years later, in the Odyssey, Odysseus is already a cunning, resourceful man who makes his own decisions, and the gods begin to exit the stage. By 500 BCE, every culture had produced a large vocabulary of human agency.

38:30 In the Old Testament the verbs God commands with are declining
Seligman took the entire Old Testament and counted agency verbs: broadly, in the Pentateuch God commands and people obey, with only a few exceptions like "choose life"; the further along you go, into the Prophets and the Writings, the more words for human agency appear and the fewer for divine agency. You can now have AI score each book for agency volume by book, and plotted against time it comes out linear — from the Pentateuch to the Babylonian exile around 300 BCE, agency increases, and it correlates linearly with human innovation, population, living standards, political freedom, and technology.

item.title: He Never Won Elected Office, Yet He Reshaped All of New York
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-stuffmissed-他从未当选任何公职-却重塑了整座纽约/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-stuffmissed-他从未当选任何公职-却重塑了整座纽约/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Robert Moses stacked appointed positions into power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Moses stacked appointed positions into power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.

This episode is medium-density on information, but how Moses accumulated power through unelected positions, and the exact words from his 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, are valuable for understanding urban governance and how power operates.

1:01 Never elected, yet he held enormous power
Robert Moses was never elected to any public office in his life, yet he accumulated enormous power through appointment to various government positions. According to Encyclopaedia Britannica, his work includes 35 highways, 12 bridges, numerous parks, Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, Shea Stadium, many housing projects, two hydroelectric power plants, and the 1964 New York World's Fair. He has been dead 45 years and remains a divisive figure, and his legacy may be argued over for another century or more.

6:10 His mentor taught him not to anger voters
Moses became chief of staff of the New York State Reconstruction Commission in 1919 and learned a great deal from Belle Moskovitz. Moskovitz understood deeply how to maneuver within government to achieve goals without angering those in power. One example: in an early draft of a report, Moses recommended cutting part of the workforce, and Moskovitz reminded him that every one of those people was a voter, that they could not be angered, and that a way had to be found to cut costs without cutting so many people. This ‘don't anger the voters’ thinking ran through his later government work.

11:11 Parks were the means, highways the end
When Moses took over the parks commission, most green-space plans simply preserved natural wilderness, but he envisioned adding more manicured landscaping and dedicated recreation areas. More importantly, every time he built a new park, he made sure the project included roads connecting the park to highways — that is where the parkway came from. From the start he planned a large state park system for Long Island, all linked by new roads. In just four years in the job, he added 13 parks to Long Island, roughly 9,700 acres in total, where previously there had been only one park.

13:14 His mother lent him $20,000 to save Jones Beach
Jones Beach was originally just a sandbar on the southern edge of Long Island, almost completely submerged at high tide. Moses wanted to turn it into a great park, and most of the government and the press considered it impractical. He first used large-scale dredging to dig about 40 million cubic yards of sand from the seabed, raising the sandbar from two feet above sea level to twelve feet. But the project nearly died when the money ran out, and Moses did something highly unusual: he borrowed $20,000 from his mother, Bella, to keep the work going. He later confirmed that if his mother had not put up the money, the contractor would not have brought the equipment back to finish. Jones Beach finally opened on August 4, 1925, in a dust storm, and an estimated 1.5 million people visited in its first year.

22:31 His only campaign, and he lost badly
Moses ran for public office only once in his life. In 1934 he ran for governor of New York and was thoroughly defeated by the incumbent Democratic governor, Herbert H. Lehman. Lehman received more than 2.2 million popular votes; Moses got fewer than 1.4 million. Reporting Lehman's victory, The New York Times wrote: ‘Meanwhile, his formidable and combative opponent, Robert Moses, will be free to continue his work as the great parks commissioner.’ After this defeat he never tried to run for office again, and instead continued to expand his power through appointed positions.

23:33 235 new playgrounds, only one in Harlem
Beginning in the 1930s, Moses greatly expanded the city's playgrounds, building 235 new ones. But a pattern began to emerge: he ignored the needs of districts with predominantly non-white populations. Of the 235 playgrounds, only one was in Harlem. In the summer of 1936 he opened 11 new swimming pools: 4 in Manhattan (including one in Harlem and one in West Harlem), 4 in Brooklyn, and 1 each in the Bronx, Queens, and Staten Island. The pools had new filtration and chlorination systems, heating, and underwater lighting, and were considered advanced, but they were also designed to be drained in the cooler months and used for other activities, from shuffleboard to roller skating.

24:35 ‘Tear down the slums, just build a road’
In a 1945 article in The Atlantic Monthly, Moses opened by describing how slums form: existing buildings become overcrowded, speculators add tenants, and people are packed into tenements like chickens. But the ‘cure’ he offered was this: clearing slums is in most cities accomplished indirectly — not for public, semi-public, or private housing, but for parks, playgrounds, parkways, highways, boulevards, and other public improvements. He boasted that his ‘little squad of demolition and construction devils’ had torn down more old slums than all the housing experts combined, and that ‘we built nothing but broad highways, flanked by landscaping and recreational facilities.’

33:43 Eminent domain is the only salvation
In the article Moses explicitly endorsed the use of eminent domain to acquire land. He wrote that buying large tracts of land at reasonable prices had become impossible, and that in such a situation, ‘eminent domain is the only salvation.’ Eminent domain must be exercised by the city, state, or federal government for private limited-dividend or redevelopment companies. He also criticized unions as ‘a serious obstacle to financing slum clearance,’ accusing them of insisting on retaining hourly wage rights, striking, and ‘resisting invention and improvement in the building field.’ He said this attitude was ‘unreasonable’ and would not change until a better-educated new generation of union officials appeared.

item.title: Blame Is Not Revenge: A Philosopher Argues We Should Blame Less
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-phibites-责备不是报复-哲学家主张我们该少责备一点/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-phibites-责备不是报复-哲学家主张我们该少责备一点/
item.description: Miranda Fricker argues that retributive blame makes no sense, and that the most valuable blame is "communicative blame" — aimed at getting the other person to genuinely understand the moral significance of what they did, and reaching shared moral understanding.
item.content:encoded:
Miranda Fricker argues that retributive blame makes no sense, and that the most valuable blame is "communicative blame" — aimed at getting the other person to genuinely understand the moral significance of what they did, and reaching shared moral understanding.

In 23 minutes it offers a workable moral framework: distinguishing retributive from communicative blame, and explaining why blaming less is not the same as abandoning responsibility.

0:04 There is no single definition of blame
Fricker points out that the philosophical literature holds a great many different views of blame: some say it is a hostile emotion, some a reactive attitude, some merely a judgment, some a rupture in a relationship, and some a form of protest. She suspects these views are not talking about the same thing at all. She holds that the object of blame can be any agent — an individual, an institution, or even a collective as large as a nation — as long as it has done something wrong, it is a fitting object of blame.

2:05 Retributive blame has no logic to it
Fricker defines retributive blame as: you wronged me, I am at a disadvantage, so I am entitled to even the score by making you hurt a little too — "getting even" is its most apt metaphor. She says she does not believe this logic in interpersonal morality, and does not find it useful. She admits she does not want to say anything specific about criminal punishment, but confesses she is strongly inclined to think the retributive idea there is rather distasteful. She believes genuinely useful alternatives exist.

3:08 Communicative blame wants shared understanding
Fricker holds that the morally most valuable model of blame is the one aimed at getting the other person to fully grasp the moral significance of their conduct. If you blame me for wronging you, perhaps I have not fully understood the moral weight of what I did; you put it into the conversation, and I either come to understand what I did or push back that it was "not that serious," and in the end the two of us reach shared moral understanding of what happened between us. She admits this is an ideal, but one worth pursuing, and calls it "communicative blame."

5:11 Blame is at bottom a judgment of moral wrongdoing
After the functional analysis, Fricker gives her own definition of blame: blame is a judgment of moral wrongdoing, and that judgment is in some sense activated or motivated by a disposition suited to holding someone responsible. She stresses that this is the context of moral blame. The definition is minimalist, and she thinks its advantage is that it transplants across domains — when she studies epistemic blame, for instance, she need not assume the blamer harbours hostile feelings toward the blamed, only that there is an epistemic fault and that the judgment issues from a responsibility-holding stance rather than passive observation.

6:11 An apology must be made to the right person
Fricker points to a key difference between apology and blame: communicative blame can be broadcast anywhere, and conveying the meaning of blame to a third party can be derived from conveying it to the person concerned — both promote shared moral understanding; but apologising to someone you did not wrong is not an apology at all. Apology is essentially second-personal moral address, and must be done to the right person. She also notes that apology's reparative power is tied to an ongoing relationship — if a stranger wrongs you at random, there is no need to chase an apology, and we all have to learn to let things go.

9:12 Sincerity is not all-or-nothing
Fricker rejects treating sincerity as all-or-nothing. She holds that in most apology practices a person need only be "sincere enough" to count as apologising, and sincere enough in the right way to be accepted by the particular person being apologised to. She cites the philosopher Jeffrey Helmich's notion of the "apology stance": an apology is a speech act that not only expresses but "enacts" the appropriate sorry inner state. She adds that an overly florid apology is merely irritating — apology is a social performance, and must fall within the bandwidth of aptness to be accepted.

12:15 Responsibility is a social construction, not metaphysics
Faced with the minority view that genes and environment determine everything and no one is ever responsible, Fricker argues that this line of thought locates the threshold of responsibility in a metaphysical rather than a natural place. She understands responsibility as something that grows out of the practice of human beings living together, for the sake of social coordination and harmony, constructing a shared moral consciousness. She borrows Peter Strawson's approach: whatever the metaphysics, in everyday life we simply cannot help praising and blaming. She holds that separating metaphysics from the practice of responsibility is itself a way of leading people astray.

19:20 Blaming less is a trainable choice
Fricker says that if blame is a judgment of fault, and the judgment issues from a responsibility-holding moral stance, then we can choose how much human behaviour to bring into this "fault-finding" construction. She gives the example of lateness: some people are highly moralistic about others being late, others do not feel offended at all. She confesses she prefers a world in which everyone is a bit more relaxed about lateness of up to 15 minutes, where it need not be constructed as a matter of respect — it is just "you were a little late," and that is all.

item.title: Chinese open-weight models lead, and distillation explains only one to two months of the gap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-interconnects-中国开源权重模型领先-蒸馏只解释一两个月差距/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-interconnects-中国开源权重模型领先-蒸馏只解释一两个月差距/
item.description: Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap; the real reasons are release cadence and task focus, and US companies are already building products on Chinese models.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap; the real reasons are release cadence and task focus, and US companies are already building products on Chinese models.

This is a status briefing on open models written for Congress: dense with data and clear in its judgments, suited to anyone who wants to grasp the US-China open-model landscape quickly.

0:00 Open weights is not the same as open source
An open-weight model releases only the weights and a license; an open-source model also releases the training code and data. America's genuinely open-source models are led by non-profits, such as the Allen Institute for AI's Olmo, OpenAthena's Marin, and EleutherAI's Pythia. Nvidia's Nemotron is more open than most open-weight models, having released a large amount of training data, but because it has not released all of it, it still does not count as fully open source. The distinction matters: when people discuss "open source", what they are actually talking about is mostly open weights.

0:00 Chinese models have crossed the agentic capability threshold
GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3 delivered a step change in commercial viability, crossing an agentic capability threshold similar to the one Anthropic's Claude Code crossed in December 2025. Chinese open-weight models passed the US in these two key areas roughly 18 months ago. On Hugging Face downloads, China took the lead in July 2025, driven mainly by Alibaba's Qwen. Data from the ATOM project, which the author maintains, shows China's download lead has grown to about 1.6 billion out of a total of 3.2 billion, twice that of the US.

0:00 The benchmark score gap is stark
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, as of September 14, 2026, the top three are Chinese models: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash scoring 45 and 42, and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 scoring 44. The US leaders are Thinking Machines' Inkling and Inkling Small, both scoring 26, and Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 23. The top US models were released in June and July 2026, with a lower update cadence than their Chinese counterparts. Chinese labs are closest on tasks with well-defined demand such as agentic coding, and lag further behind on open-ended scientific tasks such as physics and biology.

0:00 Distillation explains only one to two months of the gap
