Distillation is a technique Chinese labs use commonly, training their own models on the outputs of stronger models, but the author estimates that even if distillation were blocked entirely, for example by deploying KYC tools at Anthropic and OpenAI, the gap from the strongest US models to Chinese open-weight models would only widen by 1-2 months. Distillation has the greatest effect in new domains, and cannot easily produce a comprehensively strong final model. Chinese labs release faster and with a narrower task distribution, which slightly inflates scores on public benchmarks, because all labs are improving continuously and later-released models naturally score higher.

0:00 US companies are building products on Chinese models
Harvey, Cursor and DoorDash use Kimi, Airbnb uses Qwen, Perplexity uses DeepSeek. A large number of young Silicon Valley startups use Chinese models to get a low-cost, flexible option. US startups sign enterprise agreements with Chinese model labs to obtain product usage licenses, a new form of cross-border technology cooperation the author has not seen in his career. Chinese models' share on OpenRouter has grown from about 70% to more than 80%, with weekly tokens processed rising from about 1 trillion in September 2025 to about 80 trillion today. On OpenCode, Chinese models account for about 95% or more of inference volume.

0:00 Academia has already been taken over by Qwen
The author scanned papers in the five most popular ML categories on arXiv (cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.LG, stat.ML). In January 2023, papers mentioning any open model were 2%; by September 2026 they reached 50%. In April-May 2023, of about 12,000 new papers, 2,600 mentioned at least one open-model family, 5.5% mentioned Llama and 1% mentioned Chinese models. At Llama's peak in autumn 2024, 23% mentioned Llama and 7.5% mentioned Qwen. Today Llama is still mentioned by about 21% of papers, while Qwen has risen to 30%. Any Chinese open-weight model is mentioned by more than 40% of papers, versus 30% for the US.

0:00 US models see higher adoption at equal capability
Research shows that US models enjoy disproportionately high adoption when capability and scale are comparable. OpenAI's gpt-oss, its first open-weight models after ChatGPT, became one of the most widely adopted open-weight models ever. Google's Gemma 4 is one of the few models whose adoption approaches Qwen's most popular small models. Nvidia's Nemotron, despite being more capable at the same scale, has seen only middling adoption. This shows US models have brand and ecosystem advantages, but not enough to reverse the overall trend.

0:00 Open-model risk requires ecosystem-level preparation
The structural challenge of open-weight models is that there is almost no effective way to stop pieces of open-source software from falling into the wrong hands. If access to China's strongest open-weight models were restricted because of risk, it would be US companies that suffered. HuggingFace once used a Chinese open-weight model to understand a cyberattack, because closed models refused the request. Managing open-weight model risk tends to come down to ecosystem preparation. Open models are becoming an essential tool for AI diffusion, and continuing to invest in US open models is the best path to staying ahead of these risks.

item.title: Poetry Is Not Democracy's Ornament but Its Pillar
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.description: Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free speech just like censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape entirely through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.
item.content:encoded:
Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free speech just like censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape entirely through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.

Not a literature class: a working poet who also heads the largest humanities funder in the country explains why close reading, naming and literacy are political capacities; the back half is harder than the opening.

5:32 The poet went to the scene instead of writing reflections
Rukeyser was not a poet who stayed in the study. At 19, while studying at Vassar, she felt she had to go south to sit in on the Scottsboro trial — staying at school simply wasn't an option; in 1936 she went to Spain to see the anti-Olympics mounted against the Berlin Games, and arrived just as the Spanish Civil War broke out; she also went to West Virginia to write about the Hawks Nest mine disaster — Union Carbide dug tunnels without wet drilling and without giving workers protective gear, the workers were mostly African American, and nearly all died of silicosis, which Alexander says may be the largest corporate industrial accident in American history. The conclusion: writing let more people know what happened, and connected people of different identities on shared human experience.

13:50 Art is democracy's pillar, not its illustration
She breaks democracy down into a question of language: who a collective is, what it values, which voices it contains, all take shape through language, so without language there is no collective. When we talk about free speech we always fixate on journalism, but artists being censored, books being banned, teachers being told what they can teach strike at the same root. Her wording is hard: art is not democracy's explanatory diagram, art is itself part of democracy — one of its pillars. And poetry doesn't just wave a flag for values; it is the thing itself. To judge whether a democracy is healthy, look at whether art can still occupy an unfettered space.

33:37 Close reading is critical thinking, and it can be taught
She describes close reading very plainly: a method, a practice, anyone can learn it, and its other name is critical thinking. Its use isn't limited to poetry — it works for reading the newspaper, for reading the propaganda around you, whether that propaganda comes from above or from advertising and very, very powerful culture. Figuring out how others are working on you is a good thing. And in America many people are nervous about poetry, feeling they ‘shouldn't be able to understand it’; her method is concrete: drop your shoulders, read it again, don't just read it on the page, read it aloud, then you read it to me — the same poem read by a different person, and you hear something different every time.

42:37 Misnaming people is an anti-democratic weapon
She says one of the most powerful weapons against democracy is misnaming people, calling people by the wrong name. There's an American saying, calling people out of their names, which means flattening people, using insulting labels, even smearing the behavior of an entire people wholesale — this is abuse of language, its purpose is to wound and divide, and it is coming from the highest levels of government. She stresses one thing in particular: it has real consequences. Conversely, naming things precisely, saying what you mean, saying who you are, and catching what others say — these are themselves the capacities democracy needs.

47:58 Only by putting grief into language can you hold it
Her husband Fikre died 14 years ago. She wrote a memoir shortly after his death, which surprised even her — she had never imagined writing one or showing it to anyone; it was more a way of landing, of knowing what she was going through: too overwhelming, too unprecedented, and turning some of it into language helped her name the feeling. Writing about him years later was different in kind, became a responsibility: this person was her ‘my person’, who lived a brave, extraordinary, beautiful life and left hundreds of paintings, now shown in museums and galleries. She is wary of herself too: she hopes she isn't wringing this experience dry.

57:30 Writing poetry throws away far more than it keeps
She doesn't start a poem from ‘I want to write a poem about X’ but from a word, an image, a phrase that resonates there, and she can't say why, so she writes it down again and again. She has a day job — almost all poets do — so the real question is: while you're busy with something else, where do you put the thought. Fragments accumulate slowly, and when she has time to sit down, she asks which piece is still vibrating, still alive. How much do you write versus throw away? Her answer is one word: Most. A serious writer throws away many times what they keep, and that takes a little courage, to keep writing even when it's wrong. What really excites her is the editing stage, because ‘the beast is there’ — the outline is already visible.

1:02:17 The cost of college is a problem, learning is not
She directly rebuts the claim that the humanities have no prospects: critical thinking, close reading, extracting meaning from complex texts, communicating persuasively, imagining other people's lives, understanding multiple cultures — these are capacities useful in any career. She doesn't deny that the cost of higher education is a real problem that really needs solving, but she puts the emphasis elsewhere: what's more worrying is the attack on the university itself, interference in its mission, and the loud repetition of the claim that ‘the university is not a valuable thing.’ Her last line is sharp: creating an undereducated populace serves another purpose.

1:07:22 Those who cannot read are the easiest to control
‘free people read freely’ is a line from the poet and librarian Tracie D. Hall, and Alexander says she borrows it all day long. She reads those five words from the African American tradition: under slavery, it was a crime for Black people to learn to read and write, and it was equally a crime for a free white person to teach them — what was being controlled was not text but people. So the line holds two halves: free people read freely, and, free people are meant to read. If a person cannot read, cannot access a mass of information, they cannot understand their own life, and so lose the capacity to act on an understanding of how outside forces work on them. Where literacy is stripped away, there is only one logic: this is how you are controlled.

item.title: Literacy Once Democratised Europe; Now It Is Retreating
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.description: Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are pulling public discourse back toward a pre-literate age.
item.content:encoded:
Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are pulling public discourse back toward a pre-literate age.

Medium information density, but two mechanisms are worth hearing: "writing cools discourse" and "bad ideas are easier to whitewash on film"; the later section on pop music and reading is looser.

8:13 Literacy is historically very recent and very fragile
Marriott stresses that we are so used to literacy that we forget how anomalous it is. By one estimate, in a certain ancient Mesopotamian city-state there may have been only 20 living people who could read and write; literacy in ancient Rome was around 10%. For thousands of years, reading and writing was not a cultural phenomenon but an esoteric code circulating within a wealthy scribal elite — some rulers were literate, some were not. The real turning point was printing: books could be reproduced in quantity, more people could read, and books became more practical; Protestantism then placed extreme emphasis on the written word, pushing more people to become literate in order to read the Bible. These factors fed each other until the "Reading Revolution" historians identify in the mid-to-late 18th century.

11:19 The Reading Revolution really did change the shape of politics
Roberts pushes back: if literacy exploded, why doesn't the world look turned upside down? Marriott's answer is that the spread of literacy has a democratising effect — the more people who can access information and ideas, the more people participate in politics and criticise power. Early 18th-century Europe was ruled by absolute monarchs; political affairs were essentially court secrets, discussed only among a small elite. By the late 18th and early 19th century, newspapers appeared, the standing of absolute monarchs declined sharply, France became a republic, the authority of the British monarch was far weaker than at the start of the century, parliamentary debates were reported, and public affairs were no longer discussed only in court. He calls this the great age of democratic revolution and democratic reform, and ties it directly to the spread of literacy.

16:32 Writing forces bad ideas into logical form
Marriott concedes books are imperfect, but argues that the way a book organises information is more rational and more coherent than conversation, video or TikTok. Writing forces you to polish an idea repeatedly, to externalise part of your mind onto the page and then test it; the reader faces a fixed text and can reread and critically analyse it. More crucially, the book limits the means of non-logical persuasion — you cannot bypass argument with charisma, shouting or tears. He uses the Nazis as a counterexample: Hitler's Mein Kampf is unreadable even for Nazi elites, because Nazism simply does not hold together once it is required to be presented coherently as a written text; yet Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will is treated as an artistic masterpiece, screened in film classes, and considered a powerfully effective argument for fascism. Bad ideas are easier to whitewash on a screen than in a book.

25:05 The Republic of Letters filtered out trolls through writing
The 17th- and 18th-century European "Republic of Letters" was a community of thinkers, philosophers and scientists who wrote letters to one another and ran journals. The economic historian Joel Mokyr rates it extremely highly, even calling it the single cultural fact that explains the Industrial Revolution. Marriott's mechanism is this: if a clever person sits alone in a village, his ideas can only be told to his neighbours, and scientific innovation struggles to accumulate; the spread of literacy let ideas travel further, more and more people joined the conversation, ideas flowed into one central pool, and thought grew more complex. Roberts adds that the key difference is not public versus private but who the participants are — in conversation with Adam Smith, David Hume and Newton, the standard is naturally high; it is a kind of "submission to what cannot be enforced". Marriott concedes that the literacy barrier itself carries a benign elitism: you cannot burst in and shout like a troll on X, because nobody will pay attention to you.

34:49 The novel gives us a passage into other minds
Marriott believes there is a truth about life that only prose fiction can reach: it lets us see the inside of other people's minds. Reading is an active, not a passive, process — you use the words on the page to build images in your head, which is why it is immersive, why it feels like having lived another life. Film cannot do this, because what it gives you is the external world and it cannot enter another mind directly; writing, meanwhile, is precisely the medium we use to express what is in our minds, mind communicating with mind. He also notes that oral poetry has little interest in the subtle differences between human consciousnesses, and that this capacity to "inhabit another mind" appears only in prose fiction. Roberts does not fully agree, arguing that great films can approach it through dialogue, but concedes that film almost never captures the inner activity that is conveyed by more than dialogue.

47:59 The post-literate commentator is more like Homer
Marriott writes that the post-literate commentator does not explain and analyse the world like the print-era public intellectual, but is more like an oral storyteller, weaving strange and unforgettable tales for a captivated audience. Roberts considers this the deepest insight in the whole piece: faced with the mass of absurd, untenable statements online, people habitually interrogate them with the author's standard — "that isn't logical", "where's the evidence?" — but these people are simply not in that line of work. Their job is to entertain the audience; the truth does not matter, what matters is a story that captivates. Marriott goes further: presenting an argument logically, supplying evidence, driving to a rational conclusion — these are not actually natural to human communication; in an oral culture, the more effective way to persuade is to entertain, to move, to make angry. Writing imposes an impersonal, more rational form of communication, and it is not a necessary product of human communication.

53:59 The richness of pop music also feeds on reading
Roberts cites an example from The History of Rock and Roll in 500 Songs: Jagger wrote "Sympathy for the Devil", whose opening is taken directly from Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita — that novel opens with two Russian intellectuals mocking God and belief, after which a suave gentleman appears, they think he is mad, and finally they realise it is Satan. Marriott calls it an example "annoyingly good", and regrets not having put it in the book. He admits it cannot be pushed too far — it is not that you have to move Penguin Classics into the British Library to join a boy band — but Bob Dylan and Paul McCartney are both obviously heavy readers. He cites research saying that over the past 20 years pop songs have become less complex in both lyrics and melody, partly because the environment favours simplicity and immediacy: to go viral on TikTok, a song has to grab you within three or four seconds.

58:17 The future of reading will be deliberate, like fitness
Marriott stresses this is not a new phenomenon: statistics on the decline of serious reading go back to the 1950s and 1960s, television was the beginning of the screen age, and the remote control was the first scroll. Roberts quotes what his father said at the time — books have existed for centuries, television has been a mass medium for only 20 years, let's see whether it holds up — and admits his father should have worried more. Marriott's consolation comes from the analogy with junk food and fitness: McDonald's arrived, many people got fat, but some realised that health could no longer be absorbed naturally from the environment and required deliberate effort, so they started running and going to the gym. He guesses cognitive health will follow the same path: if reading has a future, it will become more deliberate, less "I'm bored at the airport so I'll pick up a book" and more "I value this experience, so I sit down for half an hour to an hour every night". He admits this makes him a little sad, because reading will become more artificial, no longer the unavoidable part of life it once was.

item.title: A Glass of Water Has No Final Truth: Quantum Mechanics Forces Us to Give Up the Single Viewpoint
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.description: Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not new particles, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is many perspectives that enrich each other but never converge.
item.content:encoded:
Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not new particles, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is many perspectives that enrich each other but never converge.

A four-person roundtable crossing physics, poetry, theatre and economics; high density of quotable lines but the argument is loose. Worth listening if you want a few perspectives that can change your judgment; skip it if you want hard information.

2:06 A glass of water has no final version
Rovelli opens with a glass of water the BBC provided: you look from one side, I look from the other, you wear glasses, I see a different colour. This glass of water can be a physical object (mass, velocity, position), it can be temperature and pressure, it can be the chemistry of H2O plus floating particles, it can be the global economy of being bottled in Italy and shipped to England, or it can simply be "we want to drink it". His claim is that all these perspectives are real, none exhausts another, none contradicts another, and there is no "ultimate glass of water". This is anti-Platonic — he does not accept a distinction between a "level of appearances" and a "fundamental level".

6:13 We still haven't digested quantum mechanics
Rovelli says what he is describing was not borrowed from philosophy but grew out of physics itself. Physicists ran into quantum phenomena; quantum mechanics is an enormous revolution, but "we haven't digested quantum mechanics yet" — the newspaper stories about experiments that "confirm what I learned in a textbook in the 1970s" show precisely that we still don't truly believe it. Take quantum mechanics seriously and what it says is this: the Enlightenment dream of "a complete, determinate, clear description of reality independent of the observer" does not hold. The observer here need not be a human; anything that interacts with something counts.

8:19 The deepest level of reality is not more objective
Rovelli turns it around: the reality at the most basic level physics can reach is not essentially different from the reality Lavinia deals with in poetry or James's characters deal with in economics — both are realities that allow different views, not a reality that is "absolutely objective underneath". So quantum physics isn't that hard; it just hasn't been digested. The specific physical phenomena are of course complex, but poetry is complex and economics is complex too.

10:25 Scientists have always used metaphors
Rovelli says Lavinia's words could be lifted line by line into his book. What is an electron? "It's a grain, a grain of sand, but it isn't really a grain of sand." Why is an electric field called a field? Because it is "a bit like a field in the countryside". We think through metaphor, by taking old concepts apart and piecing a new concept out of the pieces. The goal is not to arrive at a final, perfect description of reality — a century ago we thought we could, but it doesn't work — but to get a better understanding, a better way of navigating reality. He adds a crucial qualification: admitting that everything has a perspective does not mean all perspectives are equivalent, nor that there is no better and worse; it is only that the hope of "arriving at the final correct story about reality" is empty — not unreachable, but meaningless.

12:27 Seeking the ultimate morality is itself the error
Rovelli turns from "complexity" to "value": if you ask "what is the ultimate definition of good and evil, what is universal ethics", he thinks this is itself a morally and ethically mistaken approach. Our morals and values are powerful, important and indispensable not because they are outside us, but because they are inside us, and therefore also perspectival. This section connects directly to James Graham's play — whose first line is "what is the good life".

15:30 Don't be afraid to learn a jargon
Lavinia Greenlaw argues for embracing jargon: not everyone has to learn it, but if you are genuinely interested in something, don't be afraid to learn its language — a mechanic has to learn the names of parts, a surgeon has to learn the names of parts, a poet has to as well. It lets you see more clearly, and it lets you see where something has gone wrong. She admits jargon can be exclusionary, but "that depends on the context in which you use it", and "you can perform difficulty, poets and poems are probably very good at that, but that isn't what difficulty means". She gives the example of poems on the underground: before everyone was on their phones, people would read a poem first and only then realise they were reading a poem; that kind of engagement is far more direct and confident than sitting down and being told "now you are going to read a poem".

22:55 Friction is treated as a problem to be solved
James Graham says modern culture has fetishised "efficiency" and stripped out every layer of difficulty as friction. He gives a concrete image: emailing himself a script to save it, a prompt pops up — "this is a long document, shall I summarise it for you?" — and his reaction is "how rude, I want you to sit inside it and read". He connects back to Bloomsbury and Keynes: meaning is found precisely in the friction, in the difficulty, in the process. He also says the collapse of reading is despairing, because reading demands personal investment, and today that investment is treated as a problem to be solved rather than something to be celebrated.

26:05 War refuses to acknowledge complexity
Rovelli uses International Peace Day on 21 September and the statements of the UN Secretary-General and the Pope to connect the argument about perspectives to war: war is to a large extent driven by greed and power games, but it always wraps itself in a hypocritical narrative — there is only one truth, only one good, we are the good ones, they are the bad ones, we tell the truth, they tell lies and propaganda. So war is built on a total refusal to be prepared to accept complexity, perspectives, and worldviews different from our own. The host Adam Rutherford immediately offers a counterexample: we also always need to seek simplicity, and if you embraced difficulty and acted scholarly all day you might get nothing done and enjoy nothing. Lavinia's response pulls the topic back to rhetoric: language therefore matters more than ever, and poetry and poetics can teach people to argue.

item.title: Apple has no frontier model of its own, but wants to win again with a foldable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.description: Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event introduced no new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on the foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.
item.content:encoded:
Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event introduced no new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on the foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.

Mark Gurman is the most accurate reporter on Apple, and this episode strings executive turnover, the AI roadmap, the privacy controversy and foldable predictions into one line, with high information density.

5:09 The biggest difference between Ternus and Cook is a willingness to decide
Gurman says the event was almost interchangeable with the Cook era, with the only difference being that Ternus opened by laying out a view on AI. The mechanism he gives is management style: you bring an idea to Cook and he keeps probing, in many cases not making a single decision, it's collective decision-making; you go to Ternus and he gives you a decision, gives you an opinion, you may hate the opinion, but he has a position. Gurman stresses this is exactly the biggest difference between the two that came out of talking to insiders, and it explains why Ternus talked about AI first thing on stage.

8:20 The 2026 event had not a single new AI feature
Gurman points out that Apple held a big product event in September 2026 yet rolled out no notable new AI features, and the roughly 15-minute opening just retold the Apple Intelligence story of the past two years. His explanation: Apple has gone as far on AI as it can and can only tell the best story with the cards it holds; and Apple has no AI-centric device, so it has to prop up the iPhone as its AI device until a killer device appears and it can switch narratives.

13:29 Under Cook, Apple became an institution
Gurman distinguishes the Cook era from the Jobs era: in the Cook era people's relationship with Apple is a relationship with an institution, one that spans the globe and is enormous, like IBM; the Jobs era was one new product after another redefining categories. He also corrects the host's read on Vision Pro — every time he writes that Vision Pro is on life support, he gets dozens of responses at the level of near death threats, because some people have built businesses around spatial computing and some consumers paid four thousand dollars for it.

20:45 Apple spent five years swapping out the old guard one by one
Gurman reconstructs the rhythm of the handover: in 2023 Cook began saying at every executive meeting that succession had to be taken seriously; at the time the top ranks either had five hundred million in the bank or were billionaires, and were close in age. So they lined up an order and went one by one — at the end of 2024 CFO Luca Maestri retired, replaced by Kevin Parekh; in 2025 COO Jeff Williams retired, succeeded by his deputy; in 2026 the general counsel changed, with Jennifer Newstead poached from Meta; and only at the end of 2026 did Cook hand off to Ternus. Gurman calls this retention strategy Hotel California: you never want to leave.

28:07 The chip chief was kept with a title invented on the spot
Gurman says the second most important person at Apple now is the hardware head, who built Apple Silicon, Apple's key differentiator. In late summer or early autumn last year he went to tell Cook he was quitting, right in the middle of preparations for Ternus to take over. Cook got him to stay through the transition and promised him the title of chief hardware officer, which Apple had never had, letting him keep his existing team and also take over Ternus's side of the business. Gurman judges this is not a long-term arrangement and that the man already wants to leave again — he conquered the Mac, shed Intel and Qualcomm, and Apple has no next goal for him, so he may leave within a year or two, at which point the hardware engineering team will have to be split apart again, because no successor carries his industry weight.

33:15 Willing to spend tens of billions on a modem, yet says it needn't own AI
What Gurman finds most absurd is executives saying in interviews over the past year that ‘we never owned search, we don't need to own AI’. He counters: these are two completely different things, and Apple spent tens of billions to own a cellular modem that had already been commoditized, buying and fixing Intel's modem business — willing to do that for a modem but unwilling to own AI is ridiculous. The internal idea was originally to partner with Google as a stopgap until it could build its own models, but Gurman says he has seen no evidence that Apple is restarting in-house model work, making big AI acquisitions, or paying AI researchers top dollar.

48:53 All-day watch transcription stepped on the privacy landmine
Gurman's reaction to the Apple Watch's all-day listening feature was ‘I can't believe they did it’. The feature only transcribes, doesn't record or store, and a double tap shows you the last 15 seconds of what someone said to you, without their consent. He says Apple knows the next-generation interface needs some degree of always-on capture, but the societal privacy problem is unsolved: technical white papers, private cloud compute and encryption don't hold back the social backlash. He thinks Apple could have put audio and visual intelligence together next year and told one coherent privacy story; as it is, it's boiling the frog slowly.

57:05 Foldables will become the new normal within a decade
Gurman offers a bold prediction: foldables will become the new normal within a decade. He draws an analogy with smartphone penetration — at the end of 2006 smartphones were about 6% of the market, now they're 85%, and within five or six years they were past half; the iPhone itself wasn't that source, but it pulled everyone into the smartphone game, and he thinks the iPhone Duo will do the same for the phone market. He also mentions the iPhone's number migration feature, hinting the future may be a combination of a foldable for work and a smaller, lighter phone for weekends with family.

item.title: The Real Bottleneck in the Treasury Market: Not Size, but Not Enough Intermediaries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-macromusings-美债市场真正的瓶颈-不是规模-是中间商不够用了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-macromusings-美债市场真正的瓶颈-不是规模-是中间商不够用了/
item.description: Primary dealer balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Market makers gave way to high-frequency traders, but those traders collectively retreated in March 2020 — that is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.
item.content:encoded:
Primary dealer balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Market makers gave way to high-frequency traders, but those traders collectively retreated in March 2020 — that is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.

A front-line New York Fed operator explains Treasury market structure, with empirical data from two 2025 papers and the latest TBAC developments. High information density.

11:26 The Treasury market is so big it must attract new buyers
Golay gives the scale: CBO counts $30 trillion in outstanding Treasuries at the end of 2025, and projects another $26 trillion to $27 trillion over the next decade. The market splits into two parts — the cash market (buying and selling Treasuries directly, partly through inter-dealer broker electronic trading, partly dealer-to-client) and the repo market (borrowing against Treasuries as collateral, intermediated mainly by dealers). A market this large and growing necessarily has to attract different types of investors, including high-frequency traders and hedge funds that are more sensitive to price.

14:31 High-frequency traders went from zero to the main force in electronic markets
Golay calls these firms principal trading firms (PTFs), which mostly use high-frequency strategies and trade on electronic platforms. Twenty years ago they were not in the Treasury market at all; today they may account for the majority of electronic cash market trading. The turning point was the 2014 flash rally — yields moved sharply and no one could explain why, and from that the official sector began to truly understand the growth of PTFs in electronic markets, which also ignited the IAWG's work to study market structure and obtain better data.

16:33 Primary dealer balance sheets have not kept up with the growth in outstanding Treasuries
Golay cites a chart from a Darrell Duffie paper: the size of primary dealer balance sheets devoted to intermediating Treasuries has completely failed to keep pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Part of the reason is post-2008 reforms, and part is simply that the growth in outstanding Treasuries itself has been too fast. The result is that the market has had to attract more price-sensitive types of investors. She also corrects a common impression: it is not that PTFs always retreat during volatility — in other volatile periods the official sector has observed PTFs increasing their activity; but in March 2020, everyone retreated.

19:42 The essence of all-to-all is bypassing dealer matching
All-to-all trading is literally that: any participant in the Treasury market can trade with any other participant. This is nothing new in the equity market, but the Treasury market is largely over-the-counter and dealer-intermediated, so it is not. Golay points out that entering the March 2020 crisis, dealers already had a lot of Treasuries piled up on their balance sheets, and when the wave of selling hit there was no intermediation capacity left. If counterparties could be matched without going through a dealer, that might ease things. But she says explicitly that at the time most people were selling, and it is hard to imagine all-to-all perfectly solving that situation — it is just that every incremental improvement helps.

22:51 All-to-all is stuck on the lack of counterparty matching
One of the paper's core findings: in the off-the-run market, if you look at a 15-minute window, almost no one wants to buy the same off-the-run security you want to sell. Stretch the window to a day, and the match rate rises to 60% to 70%. Golay mentions possible directions for innovation, such as an end-of-day batch auction, and some institutions already have this capability. But to date, no case in this area has actually gotten off the ground successfully. She also mentions that expanding central clearing could push the transition to all-to-all, because you would not need to establish bilateral clearing arrangements with every counterparty — you would only need to connect to a central counterparty.

29:06 Off-the-run is 97% of outstanding Treasuries, yet a liquidity backwater
Off-the-run refers to older Treasuries, ranging from those issued three months ago to 29- and 30-year ones, and accounts for about 97% of outstanding Treasuries. The selling in the March 2020 dash for cash was mainly off-the-run, and the off-the-run market is dealer-intermediated, with no all-to-all. Golay and colleagues at the Board of Governors and the New York Fed did empirical work using TRACE data collected by FINRA, in which transaction-level data is visible only to the official sector. The conclusion: the older the Treasury, the worse its liquidity — larger price impact, lower volume, wider bid-ask spreads.

31:15 The cheapest to deliver can revive liquidity
Another finding of the paper: when an off-the-run Treasury becomes the cheapest to deliver into a Treasury futures contract, its liquidity is better than that of comparable off-the-run securities. This suggests the off-the-run problem is partly about trading activity itself — with trading activity, liquidity improves; without it, liquidity deteriorates. On policy implications, Golay mentions that Treasury buybacks can create trading activity around off-the-run securities and improve liquidity; central clearing makes clearing smoother; as for reducing the number of issuance dates and making individual issues larger, the paper reaches no conclusion, because investors also like the finer granularity of monthly issuance.

36:33 TBAC put the brakes on expanding transparency
At a recent TBAC meeting, some members suggested expanding transparency of Treasury trading data: there is already market-wide aggregate statistics, as well as transaction-level data for on-the-run securities; the suggestion was to consider publishing transaction-level data for Treasury bills, and more frequent on-the-run data. But TBAC expressed caution about expanding transparency in other areas, including the off-the-run and TIPS markets. Golay says this is interesting, because data transparency is precisely the focus of the IAWG's work in recent years, and was listed as a priority in 2021. She personally thinks small incremental transparency is beneficial, but understands that in less liquid markets, releasing too much information would make intermediation very difficult.

item.title: Stanford has a secret course that teaches 12 people how to extract value from other people
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-grayarea-斯坦福有一门秘密课程-教12个人如何从他人身上提取价值/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-grayarea-斯坦福有一门秘密课程-教12个人如何从他人身上提取价值/
item.category: The Gray Area with Sean Illing
item.description: The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO on how to extract value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has rewarded all along.
item.content:encoded:
The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO on how to extract value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has rewarded all along.

Not a generic Silicon Valley critique but a specific investigation with course names, dollar figures and named people; if you care about early-stage investing and talent pipelines, the density of detail is high.

5:12 You can take hundreds of thousands before you have a company
Pre-idea funding was the newest layer of the game when Theo arrived on campus: give an 18-year-old who just got there hundreds of thousands, even millions, of dollars, sign a one-page SAFE check, agree that "if you start a company later, come back to us" — otherwise the money never has to be repaid. For a VC that's pocket change; they don't actually believe in these hyped-up teenagers, and they don't need you personally to succeed — they only need one overnight sensation. Meanwhile students are encouraged to make enormous promises and then discover again and again that nobody follows up: lie, and nothing happens.

13:22 The secret course teaches extracting value
Stanford has a course that isn't in the catalog, called How to Rule the World, taught by a Silicon Valley CEO who styles himself a professor, admitting only 12 students a year — merely knowing it exists is a status symbol. Its central assignment is extracting value from people, with a strong whiff of the ends justifying the means. One woman Theo interviewed said the course taught her how to lie to VCs to raise money — she went on to raise millions and drop out of Stanford, despite having already been caught cheating in a computer science class; months later she put out a glossy launch video for a technology that didn't exist, and Silicon Valley still cheered her on, installed her in a mansion, and invited her back to Stanford to speak.

26:46 Ethics isn't a premise; getting caught is what counts
During ethics week in the intro computer science course, the professor presented the case of a software defect that killed four people on a radiation therapy machine, and the TA asked who in the room cared about ethics — Theo was the only one who raised his hand. Weeks later a classmate told him he was taking a business ethics course, and "we're all just there to figure out how they got caught." He didn't sense that these people felt any need to pretend to care; when Sam Bankman-Fried was under house arrest in the house on the Stanford campus where he grew up, students made pilgrimages, threw parties themed around him, and said they wanted to replicate his success minus the final fall. A colleague's summary of the money that mysteriously vanished at Tree Hacks: it's all just a little bit of fraud.

38:01 The real reason the president fell wasn't the data
Board members who ousted Marc Tessier-Lavigne later told Theo that one of the heaviest reasons they gave was his posture — a highly aggressive public stance when challenged, deny, deny, deny, plus the threatening letters sent by the lawyer he hired, Steve Neal, which embarrassed the university. Theo found no evidence that Tessier-Lavigne himself falsified data: the problem was in labs he oversaw, where subordinates fabricated results in papers he co-authored, including the 2009 paper claiming to have found the cause of Alzheimer's, while internally, before publication, results showed its central finding was "at best unreliable." He was asked to retract and refused, dragging it out for a decade. What drove him out was image management, not the data.

39:01 Four days after being ousted, the mansion closed
Four days after the board unanimously removed him, Tessier-Lavigne closed on a 7,600-square-foot mansion in "America's most expensive zip code," valued at over $10 million; eight months later he announced he had raised $1 billion for a new company doing AI biotech. Of the two VCs that led the round, an investor at one messaged Theo two months later to rib him, followed by a winking emoji; an investor at the other offered him money to start a company. Theo says it's the most Silicon Valley thing you could imagine: everything can be monetized, even taking down a university president turns into an invitation.

45:44 Duck syndrome: paddling like mad under the surface
Duck syndrome is a term Stanford coined itself: students glide across the surface like ducks, making everything look effortless, while underneath their legs paddle like mad just to stay afloat. Katie Meyer was its best illustration — captain of the women's soccer team, an NCAA champion, headed to law school, didn't drink, didn't smoke, didn't speed. Months before graduation, late on a Friday night, after every student support office had closed, she received a letter: because six months earlier she had spilled coffee on a football player (she said it was an accident, he said it was deliberate), her degree was suspended. That night she took her own life. Twelve schools later paid tribute to her; Stanford was not among them. The women's soccer team she had just led held a mental health night and didn't mention her name.

52:01 A legendary professor's fraud case, and the school says it never heard of it
Stan Cohen was the first geneticist to move a gene from one living organism into another, and his 1970s recombinant DNA technique gave rise to the model of universities making money from patents; in its last valid year, that patent accounted for 62% of all Stanford patent revenue. In his freshman year, Theo found that Cohen had been found liable for fraud by a court: he had pitched investors on a drug target that might cure Huntington's disease, saying it was already approved to treat another condition, without telling them it had been permanently banned by the FDA in 1976 because it was lethal. He was ultimately ordered to pay $29 million and paid it. Theo asked the university, which replied that it had never heard of the case and had no involvement whatsoever — even though Stanford owned the relevant intellectual property and had been subpoenaed.

55:04 Raising money is easier than an internship, and that's the signal
The saying inside Stanford's inner circles is that it's easier to raise money for a startup than to land an internship — Theo says that's absurd, it shouldn't be that way, but that's the state of things. He describes the moment as a game of AI musical chairs: everyone is waiting to see who's still standing when the music stops and who's left holding the bag. He isn't worried about cash-flow-positive companies like Meta and Google; he's worried about the companies clinging to the AI narrative that have no technology of their own, no revenue, and no ability to generate revenue — they can't hold on, and they will collapse. But he also cautions that Silicon Valley hasn't held power for long, that it's a very immature power system that hasn't grown guardrails, transparency or accountability, and that one collapse doesn't necessarily mean a reckoning.

item.title: America's Manufacturing Hollowing-Out Is Not a Capability Problem, It's a Financial Return Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.description: Chris Power says America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statements, while China manages it like national security; tariffs are just an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing rivals' industrial capacity.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Power says America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statements, while China manages it like national security; tariffs are just an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing rivals' industrial capacity.

Two frontline hardware founders explain the real bottlenecks of American reindustrialization: not technology, but trust, cost, and supply chain definitions. High information density, with the second half's breakdown of tariffs and subsidies being the most valuable.

2:02 The reserve currency is the first step of decline
Chris Power gives a four-step cycle: great powers first have a generative population and the best industrial capacity, then win or prevent a war, then become extremely lazy, and finally outsource the very things that made them successful. He says this cycle repeats roughly every 150 years: the Netherlands gives way to Britain, Britain gives way to America, and each time industrial power is re-traded for financial power, the world's reserve currency changes. This judgment was the starting point for him founding Hadrian: you think you're Mike Tyson at his peak, but your opponent thinks you're the Mike Tyson right before Buster Douglas knocked him out.

9:10 90% of the factory floor is a software problem
Chris Power says the biggest misconception about advanced manufacturing is that seeing people moving things in a factory means it's a humanoid robot problem. In reality, 90% of advanced manufacturing is smart people sitting at computers doing digital engineering, or operating a very dumb computer on the shop floor. Welders or machinists have to stand in front of the machine because the system isn't closed-loop; they're doing trigonometry in their heads to judge whether the tool is about to break. That's why Hadrian positions itself as a software company: it breaks physical tasks into high-judgment fixturing, then hands them off to robots, CNC, or welding systems to execute.

14:14 Software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware in Los Angeles
Tom Mueller says the aerospace talent ecosystem in Southern California is recovering; three or four years after SpaceX was founded in 2002, the aerospace employment curve in the South Bay started trending up. He lists what this area is simultaneously doing: nuclear energy companies, drone companies, defense companies, 3D printing companies, and Anduril in Orange County. The two companies poach from each other and compete for talent; Northrop Grumman is right across the street from Impulse. Tom's summary: software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware in Los Angeles.

15:17 Vertical integration is to learn the problem, not to save money
Tom Mueller explains the real logic of SpaceX-style vertical integration: the first development engine or spacecraft must be built in-house, because you need to learn all the assembly and machining problems during the prototype phase. If you hand it to a machine shop from the start, and the drawings have problems or the parts don't fit when they come back, you learn nothing. Once the design converges, then you outsource. Chris Power adds that every company should keep 10% to 15% of in-house capacity, because there's always a "hot pot" moment when you need a genius to make something within an hour to hit a flight milestone, but scale must happen externally.

16:18 Outsourcing decisions are about trust, not finance
Chris Power says what's bought and sold in manufacturing is trust. Hadrian's vertical integration strategy is to outsource as much as possible to every reindustrialization startup and small business, because there are too many projects to run. But they will vertically integrate the links where they "don't believe you can deliver on time." This isn't a financial trade-off; they'd rather spend an extra two million dollars on equipment and hire a team than bet the risk on a traditional foundry that has been late on every submarine program for the past thirty years. His exact words: most of America is incompetent at trust and scheduling.

19:20 In WWII, America was China
Chris Power uses WWII as an analogy: German engineers crushed America on engineering, but America wore them down with McDonald's-style mass production and better logistics. He says America played the role in WWII that China plays today—not by having the best engineering, but by producing the most. Now the situation is reversed: U.S. missile stockpiles run out in seven days in war games, China built 2,600 ships while America built six. His conclusion: you can have the best Raytheon missiles, but if you can't mass-produce them, you have no options.

21:23 The robot bottleneck is training data velocity
Chris Power says the robot competition ultimately depends on software, and software—especially AI—now depends on the velocity of training data, which in turn depends on physical-world deployment, meaning mass manufacturing. So this isn't a friendly competition between American companies over "whether Tesla sells more Optimuses or Google wins"; it's a civilization-level confrontation. Tom Mueller adds from the space angle: building on the Moon and Mars requires robot legions rather than humans, because the environment is too dangerous and too expensive; a good robot needs three things—dexterous hands, vision which is basically solved, and an AI brain.

29:40 Tariffs are an imperfect corrective tool
Chris Power says manufacturing has four inputs: energy, labor, cost of capital, and export tariffs. He has run the numbers: even if Hadrian's labor costs and energy costs were both zero, importing components from China would still be three times cheaper than buying raw materials in America and making them yourself. He believes China has operated industrial policy as national security since 1985, subsidizing energy, labor, capital, and export tariffs, while America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement returns. The problem with tariffs is enforcement: banning only China and not Singapore means Chinese companies route through Singapore; differences in definitions of raw materials and assembly also hurt American companies importing components from Mexico.

item.title: He Cooked the Chickpea Pasta Into Mush, Then Survived by Telling People to Brew It Like Tea
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.description: Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board — 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said "brew it like tea" and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.
item.content:encoded:
Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board — 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said "brew it like tea" and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.

The founder's account is unusually dense with failure detail: three scrapped production batches, a kidney stone, being thrown out of the factory, a 30% week-over-week sales drop. Worth hearing for anyone who wants to know how you survive a near-death moment.

5:14 The starting point wasn't a business insight, it was a sinus problem
In college Brian's fridge held nothing but hummus, eating was just "fuel" to him, and he cycled between antibiotics and steroids for so long that surgery was nearly on the table. It was his father, an orthodontist, who got him to try an elimination diet, and that's how he found that wheat-based foods triggered his sinus inflammation — one beer and the next day he couldn't breathe. The ENT told him: I don't know what you're talking about, but if it works, keep doing it. That private problem became the product definition: high-protein, high-fiber, gluten-free pasta, doing what Chobani did for yogurt.

10:26 The first recipe had chia in it and was too sticky to look at
He bought Bob's Red Mill chickpea flour on Amazon and followed blogs for combinations. Version one was chickpeas plus eggs plus chia — the chia made it so sticky the result was ugly. No rolling pin, so he used a wine bottle; no pasta cutter, so he used a knife, dusting flour on the table as he cut to keep it from sticking. Version two dropped the chia, leaving just chickpeas and eggs, and was clearly better, but to make it usable for more people he added tapioca starch and xanthan gum back in and committed to a vegan route. His first capital expenditure was an Atlas Mercado hand-crank pasta machine, about $30 on Amazon. He got up at 5 a.m. every day to make pasta, put on country music, and his roommates thought he was insane.

20:49 Going from 200 pounds an hour to 1,000 magnified every mistake
They first found a tiny gluten-free factory in Michigan that could only do 150 to 200 pounds an hour — wildly inefficient, but they could learn as they went. To get into 190 Meijer stores and 2 Eataly locations, that capacity wasn't enough, so they found what was then the largest gluten-free pasta plant in the country, outside Los Angeles. The problem: that plant had only ever run rice and corn pasta, never legumes. Scaled up to roughly 1,000 pounds an hour, the pasta looked fine coming out and turned into total mush the moment it was boiled. Each trial run was 8,000 to 10,000 pounds, and a failure meant the die costs and ingredient costs were gone, and they had only a little over $100,000 on hand.

26:02 He got thrown out of the factory for asking the operator
After several failed trial runs, Brian ignored the other side's objections and went straight to the line operator to ask what was actually going wrong. The worker said "this corn smells weird," and he answered: that's not corn, we're not making corn pasta today, it's chickpeas. He realized on the spot that communication had broken down completely, and right after that he was escorted out of the plant. At the same time the distributor was threatening him: if you don't fulfill this purchase order, you will never work with this retailer again. He later estimated this shipment would cost nearly everything they had.

28:07 The fix was don't boil it — brew it like tea
With nowhere left to turn they started testing: boil one minute, two minutes, three minutes, then stop boiling altogether — bring water to a boil, turn off the heat, and let the pasta steep in the hot water. What came out of steeping was better than what came out of boiling, or at least it didn't fall apart. Brian says he wasn't proud of the product, and it bothered him to sell it under his own brand, but he knew it was life or death. The packaging was already printed, so they made an extra sticker reading "Banza is easier to cook than regular pasta — brew it like tea," and had people hand-apply it to 20,000 boxes. Once that shipment went out, they immediately pulled out of the big plant and went back to the small Michigan factory.

35:18 The box is orange because every pasta box was blue
They noticed that nearly every pasta package on the shelf at the time was blue — Brian put it as "you'd think they'd colluded." Orange contrasts most strongly with blue, and orange was also the color he'd loved since watching Nickelodeon as a kid, so it became the brand color. The packaging copy involved trade-offs too: putting "chickpeas" in the most prominent spot would scare off a lot of people, and so would gluten-free, so the gluten-free certification went on the side while the front led with high protein and high fiber — making consumers feel this was "a product for me," not "a product that isn't for me."

41:31 The glyphosate report cut weekly sales by a third
Moms Across America published a report saying glyphosate residue had been detected in Banza products. Brian saw the Google alert during a one-on-one meeting; he says his heart sank and his mind jumped twenty steps ahead. He wanted to verify first, so he only put out a statement saying "we are investigating" — which was nowhere near enough for the most panicked people. The lab results were delayed again and again, dragging on for three weeks. The final published result was 98% below the allegation, but not zero — still a very low level, and below the EWG's risk benchmark. He decided to make the supply chain 100% traceable and joined the Detox Project's certification program.

52:15 Natural channel recovered far more slowly than conventional
The sales recovery was a mixed bag: some channels came back better than before, but the natural channel recovered much more slowly — and that was exactly the customer base with the best repeat purchase rates and the highest sales per store. Brian says this actually makes sense, because natural channel consumers are the most susceptible to this kind of information. What he does now: he keeps alerts on for anywhere Banza and glyphosate are mentioned, and personally goes on Reddit to reply and add context, with the goal of making it impossible for the story to be seen without its background. He also admits he should have acknowledged what was happening faster and more visibly at the time.

item.title: AI won't replace people — what replaces them is work that was never written down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.description: Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of how work gets done — that "map of work" is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own model.
item.content:encoded:
Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of how work gets done — that "map of work" is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own model.

Daniel Dines breaks down the real bottleneck of AI inside the enterprise from UiPath's front line, with a high density of counter-consensus claims — for anyone trying to judge the actual pace of enterprise AI adoption.

6:17 AI does not change its own weights on the job
Daniel argues the biggest difference between AI and humans is not reasoning ability, but that AI does not change its own weights on the job. A human is changed by a job; AI just writes things into a notebook. He gives the example of two chefs: one who has cooked Japanese cuisine for 20 years, one who has cooked Italian for 20 years — give them the same recipe and what they produce is completely different. This is not something you can replicate by writing the company down on paper, because human judgment comes from years of being reshaped by the work. So on the claim that "there are millions of Einsteins in the data center," Daniel thinks what Dario meant is millions of entities with partial reasoning ability, not Einsteins who can learn on the job the way a person does.

16:29 Probabilistic technology should not do work that demands precision
Daniel raises another limit on AI: precision. Every step AI takes is probabilistic — even if each step is 99% correct, after 100 steps the overall success rate may be only 60%. So have AI do long multiplication over and over and it will eventually get it wrong. His conclusion: the fact that a tool can do something does not mean you should use it for that thing. ChatGPT looks like it is doing arithmetic, but behind the scenes it is calling a computer tool; the precision is not provided by ChatGPT. Extend that logic to the enterprise: all work that demands precision should run on precise technology, and there is no reason for it to run on probabilistic technology.

18:34 Deploying AI hasn't gotten easier; deploying automation has
Daniel points to an asymmetry inside the enterprise: deploying AI agents is no easier than it was two years ago, but deploying automation has become much easier, because you can use coding agents to generate the automation. He lists ChatGPT, chain of thoughts and coding agents as the three main milestones. A coding agent works at "design time"; people use it to build automation that runs precisely every time at "execution time"; and when the automation breaks because an upstream system changed, AI can come back and fix it. The result is that AI is generating the software that runs the company, and that software cannot change its behavior in real time — it can be audited, tested and read by a person. This is the pattern he believes is taking shape in the enterprise right now.

23:46 Blind layoffs cut the people AI most needs
In his book Daniel introduces the concept of the "credentialed middle": companies used to hire for deep domain credentials in some field, and that is exactly the kind of expertise AI helps with most. His judgment is counterintuitive — you will be inclined to cut the people who are not the biggest experts in the domain, but those are precisely the people you will need to supplement expert work with AI. He gives the example of a law firm: it used to hire 25 interns a year, this year it hired only 4. He agrees most roles will need fewer people, but the key question is "which people." His criterion: keep the people with the most initiative, who can maintain client relationships, who can mentor newcomers, who carry the company culture — because AI cannot show initiative in the human sense.

25:51 What decides whether AI can take over is how clear the framework is
Harry argues that work like finance and accounting is highly verifiable, so it is easy for AI to replace. Daniel disagrees outright: it is not a question of verifiability, but of whether the work is framed by a framework someone else has already defined. He says finance is precisely a domain where the framework is unclear — receive an invoice or an order and there can be different ways to handle it, such as whether Nvidia would ship to OpenAI first, and that rule may never have been written down at all. If the rules are not captured by a framework, AI cannot learn them. So a company must first hand the "map of work" to AI: all workflows, all exceptions, all processes, all systems. This is also what he keeps stressing: models are interchangeable, and the map of work and the processes around it are where the real value lies.

29:01 Use agents to interview employees and draw the work as a map
UiPath has launched a technology called cartography, as a discipline that helps companies surface how work actually gets done. Concretely, it uses a product called a cartographer agent to interview real business experts and have them record what they are doing, with the agent following up in real time: why did you change how you handled this invoice because the zip code was different? Why did you choose another path? That is how exceptions get dug out one by one. Then it aggregates data from multiple people to generate a real-time process map. With that "map of work" in hand, you then use coding agents to design how the process should be transformed, and ultimately, through "printing software," push the process from purely manual point A toward a state with fewer people operating systems and more automation and agentic AI operating systems.

34:15 Vibe coding is easy for prototypes and hard for production
Daniel admits UiPath tried vibe coding, and at first it looked astonishing, but pushing it into production hit a wall: connectors, permissions, auditing, security — all of it has to be maintained. He gives his own example of writing a procurement tool: initially it was written entirely by AI, but the database schema was completely wrong and someone had to rebuild the structure. His conclusion is that going from prototype to production is where the real work is, not writing the code itself. In the end you will very likely spend as much as, or more than, the tool you replaced, while also consuming the bandwidth of your best people. So he does not think systems of record like Salesforce will be replaced by vibe coding.

45:34 The opportunity in legal AI is in the process, not the model call
Harry does the math: the US legal industry is a $300 billion market, and if 30% of the labor can be replaced that is $90 billion in revenue. Daniel counters that the $90 billion will not convert into token revenue — maybe only 10%, so a $10 billion token opportunity. His judgment: for legal opinions, open-source models and frontier models are both good enough, and what is actually valuable is the custom workflow built around the legal process. If Harvey and Lagora just help you call a model once to get a legal opinion, that is not a hundred-billion-dollar market; but if they really draw the work as a map, build out the workflow and give you a legal department, the value is far greater.

item.title: Even Legal-Cannabis States Can't Escape: A Federal Ban Is About to Empty the THC Shelves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.description: A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry, and now Congress wants to close it — even legal-cannabis states will feel it when they lose the cheap alternative.
item.content:encoded:
A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry, and now Congress wants to close it — even legal-cannabis states will feel it when they lose the cheap alternative.

Eight minutes on how a regulatory loophole grew into an industry and how it gets cut off in one stroke — for anyone watching policy risk and regulatory arbitrage.

0:00 Legal-cannabis states can't escape a federal ban either
Half of US states have legal recreational cannabis, but the reason THC drinks, vapes and gummies can be sold openly in states that ban cannabis is a loophole left by the 2018 farm bill: it allows low-concentration THC from hemp. After lab processing, that low concentration is enough to mimic a cannabis high, which is how you get Delta 8, Delta 9 — and, as the show jokes, by now Delta 11. Congress now wants to close the loophole, and with a stricter ban. The key is that it's a federal ban, so even if your state has legal cannabis, you get hit.

1:00 What's being banned is a $28 billion industry
The show puts the size at $28 billion and says the industry could disappear before the end of this year. Tennessee has already gone first: since July it has banned most THC hemp products, and a local reporter described herself as already living in a "post-hemp world." State legislators even beat Congress to it, banning full-spectrum CBD and smokable flower first. For retailers, farmers and processors, this isn't a policy debate — it's a choice that has to be made before year-end.

3:07 Farmers are going back from hemp to blackberries and corn
Tennessee farmer Lee Crabtree's farm used to grow mostly CBD-variety hemp, and the new state law makes selling those products illegal, so he's gone back to traditional seasonal crops like blackberries and corn. The family still has the industrial kitchen from its CBD food days, and now his wife Stacy uses that big stainless-steel counter to cut grapes for chicken salad and sell it at the roadside farmers market. Lee says income is down, and if the traditional crops don't sell, he'll have to go find a job. This is what the ban looks like landing on one specific household.

5:08 The regulator's case: consumers don't know what they're drinking
Tennessee Republican Representative William Lamberth uses a drinks analogy: someone buying a Sprite expects a Sprite, not a beer; someone buying a beer expects a beer, not a tequila; someone buying a tequila expects not to get a Sprite. He says the goal is for consumers to know exactly what they're buying. But farmers, even when they agree with the logic, worry the law overcorrects. The show also gives the other side: big companies are laying people off, and some are simply moving across state lines — Emily Schaeferich's company Burning Acre moved from Columbia, Tennessee, to North Carolina to keep growing, and she admits ripping up the entire retail, manufacturing and wholesale supply chain "definitely costs a lot of money."

6:10 Moving to another state may be a wasted move
Hemp economist Beau Whitney calls the nationwide ban taking effect in December an "extinction-level event." His mechanism: cannabis can only be grown in certain states, while hemp can be grown and shipped anywhere, so hemp businesses can build supersized capacity, push costs down and ship nationwide; cannabis, by contrast, needs one supply chain per state and can't get hemp's economies of scale. The result is that hemp-derived foods are far cheaper than their cannabis equivalents. So even in states with legal recreational cannabis, consumers will feel the squeeze when they lose the cheap alternative.

7:13 The ban takes out state tax revenue
The show pulls out economies of scale on its own to explain it: the more of the same good you produce, the lower the unit cost, and the savings can be passed on to consumers. That also explains why hemp-derived foods are cheaper than cannabis products. But consumers aren't the only ones affected. For a lot of state budgets, losing the hemp industry means losing a sizable source of tax revenue — in Tennessee alone, a $54 million budget hole. Beau Whitney also says it could put hundreds of thousands of jobs at risk.

7:13 The delay just moves it from November to December
The White House has urged Congress to delay or amend the ban, the Senate currently supports it, and the House voted earlier this month to delay it too. But those moves only push the effective date from November to December — a one-month delay. For companies that have already moved across state lines and rebuilt supply chains, a month changes nothing — they may have just moved the whole business only to find the industry destroyed in December.

8:14 Those staying behind switch to fiber hemp
Tennessee farmer Bill Corbin, in Springfield, is preparing the first fiber hemp crop for the French company Hemp-It; this kind of hemp goes into rope, packaging and auto parts. He says there isn't a person in the industry who didn't know this day was coming, that he thinks the industry was unsustainable to begin with, and he agrees with legislators' efforts to suppress recreational use of hemp derivatives. But he worries about medical consumers: he himself is older and has arthritis, relies heavily on full-spectrum CBD, and the products left after the ban may not be strong enough for older people or those trying to avoid opioid painkillers.

item.title: The Bat Doesn't Know What It's Like to Be a Bat Either
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.description: The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.
item.content:encoded:
The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.

The second half of episode 400, and listenable on its own. The first half is about theories of consciousness; the second half unexpectedly slides into animal ethics, and the four of them never do settle their disagreement.

1:07 A bat having an inner world is not the same as being conscious
Christopher summarises Dennett's response: he flatly denies Nagel — we can talk about what it's like to be a bat in all sorts of ways (by first ruling out the things bats don't do, for instance), and with enough information we eventually get there, because "what it's like to be a bat" just is the discriminative, dispositional states the bat has. Dylan supplies the step Dennett actually rejects: drawing on von Uexküll's Umwelt and Innenwelt (surrounding world and inner world), Dennett grants that the bat has an inner world, which is not crazy; what he won't accept is the move straight from "has an inner world" to "therefore consciousness exists," and that is exactly the step Nagel uses to prove consciousness exists. Our mode of access is heterophenomenology: treat the bat's behaviour and physiology as a text in need of interpretation.

5:37 Consciousness is not an all-or-nothing property
Christopher reads out a passage from Dennett: are language-less animals not conscious at all? Dennett says the question shouldn't be taken as a given challenge, because it presupposes something "we went to a lot of trouble to get away from" — that consciousness is an all-or-nothing property that splits the universe into two utterly different categories: things that have it and things that don't. That dichotomy is what Dennett wants to dismantle; what he wants is consciousness in degrees. Christopher then offers his own version: he doesn't want to accept property dualism, he wants to deny the hard problem, because subjectivity can perfectly well have a biological and evolutionary explanation — agency and subjectivity co-evolved; a physical process organised from the inside "feeling like something" is a real biological phenomenon.

12:57 The bat doesn't know what it's like to be a bat either
Seth pushes the argument to its extreme: it isn't "we don't know what it's like to be a bat," it's that there is no "what it's like to be a bat, seen from the bat's side" at all; the bat itself doesn't know either, because it lacks the machinery to string experiences into a narrative and give them names. Dylan immediately marks out the cost of this inference: if anything with dynamic activity has its own experience, then atoms count too, and that's panpsychism. Christopher says you don't have to go as far as atoms, but concedes that the direction really does sound like panpsychism — he'd rather use a threshold: you need a feedback loop of perception and action before you can talk about a new way of being.

14:35 Even plants have a perspective in some sense
Mark digs up a line from Dennett's book: the perspective of a conscious observer is a refined descendant of the primitive perspective of the first replicators, which "divided the world into good and bad" — on that account even plants have a perspective in this sense, and "perspective" becomes a metaphor. Christopher then offers gradualism: from sponges to mantis shrimp to humans, subjectivity accumulates layer by layer and gets thicker and thicker, with a fuzzy threshold in between. Dylan wants to nail the threshold down harder: you can't use "complex" as the criterion, since weather is a complex self-maintaining system too; the difference is that living things can replicate themselves and have a wholeness, so the only thing the Earth lacks is its own replication.

19:47 You are a bunch of things, not a soul
Mark finds Dennett's 1994 reply collection Get Real, which uses snakes as an example: a snake has no central representation of "mouse," it just responds to prey through three separate sensory systems. Dennett's point is that the perceptual system we take to be a single whole is really a pile of little homunculi each making its own discriminations; you are not an Aristotelian form, a soul, an organisation that runs you — we are all a bunch of things.
