Christopher objects: failure to integrate information processing doesn't mean there's no self — the two hemispheres of a split-brain patient are also separate, and we don't conclude from that that he has no self; the snake may still have a more ancient, minimal sense of boundary and evaluative experience.

27:39 Reducing experience to discrimination looks a lot like behaviourism
Christopher says he agrees with Dennett 99%, and is stuck on the 1%: when Dennett wants to reduce a person to dispositional states, saying that experiencing red is nothing over and above being able to discriminate red from non-red and being in that discriminative state, it sounds like behaviourism. Seth offers a defence: even if the substrate is just discriminative states, subjective experience, the self, is a composite stitched together out of memory, imagination, representation and symbolic language — it weaves scattered discriminative states into a story with descriptions, meanings and colour, and that story is me. Christopher agrees about the narrative self, but points out that the bat lacks the metacognitive capacity to construct such a self.

38:54 You can club an iguana, but not a rabbit
Mark says "everyone is a world" is a good moral fiction, but he doesn't know how to apply it to animals: Florida has too many iguanas, and he encourages people to go out and club them — he says that's completely fine and humane; swap in a rabbit and he won't accept it. Seth offers an evolutionary explanation: our feelings about animals domesticated over tens of thousands of years, wild animals and reptiles were never the same to begin with, and this doesn't conflict with "the self is a narrative centre of gravity." Christopher anchors it in valence: animals are not reflex machines, they are situated perspectives that evaluate, and that is the reason they enter moral consideration — he says that after reading Lars Chittka's The Mind of a Bee, the way he deals with bees changed.

46:10 Take away caring and nothing is left of pain
Mark turns to where Dennett talks specifically about pain: what is the functional relation of pain? If you take away "caring about it, wanting to get away from it," take away everything else, and leave only the sensation of pain, then nothing is left — your not liking pain is itself part of the pain. Mark says this is exactly Dennett's attitude to philosophical zombies: imagine a being with exactly your biological makeup, reactions and even internal relations, but the light of consciousness never came on — Dennett thinks this is so absurd that it's hard even to explain to scientists.

item.title: Beijing's Central Axis Is Not a Relic. It's a City Operating System Still Running
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-historyhit-北京中轴线不是古迹-是仍在运转的城市操作系统/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-historyhit-北京中轴线不是古迹-是仍在运转的城市操作系统/
item.description: The Ming rebuilt Beijing from a blueprint written two thousand years earlier, and the central axis still dictates the symmetry and growth of a city of twenty million — even the Olympic Bird's Nest sits on that line.
item.content:encoded:
The Ming rebuilt Beijing from a blueprint written two thousand years earlier, and the central axis still dictates the symmetry and growth of a city of twenty million — even the Olympic Bird's Nest sits on that line.

Medium information density, but its strength is restoring the central axis from tourist attraction to a planning logic still in force — suited to anyone interested in cities and organisational design.

7:13 A manual from two thousand years ago is still in use
When the Ming set out to rebuild the capital, they dug up a technical manual written more than two thousand years earlier: the Kaogong Ji (“考工记”). It specified a city four to five kilometres on each side, three gates per side, the palace at the centre, an ancestral temple on one side, the court in front, the market behind, and a Temple of Heaven in the southern suburbs. The historian Jeremiah Jenik says the logic behind this layout was cosmic order: there is a fixed point in the sky, the North Star, so there should be a corresponding fixed point on earth — and the most fitting fixed point is the emperor himself. Put yourself in the palace at the exact centre of the city and you have put yourself inside a cosmic order that revolves around you.

9:16 They actually built it to the drawing
The most astonishing thing is not that the Ming dared to use a blueprint over a thousand years old, but how closely they built to it. Overlay the Kaogong Ji plan on the model at the Beijing Planning Exhibition Hall and the two almost coincide. So Beijing today is still a twenty-first-century city running around a fifteenth-century heart, and that heart follows principles laid down nearly two thousand years ago. Compare London, which grew organically along the Thames: Beijing had the blueprint first, then the city.

11:20 The central axis is a spine, and the city grew out of it
From north to south, the axis strings together the Bird's Nest, the Drum and Bell Towers, Jingshan, the Forbidden City and the Temple of Heaven, ending at Yongdingmen in the south. The episode likens it to a spine: everything is planned and expanded outward from this line. Running true north-south and aligned with the heavens, the line has been Beijing's most distinctive feature for six hundred years, and it determines the shape of the city today.

12:22 The right to tell time is the right to rule
The Drum and Bell Towers were the city's timekeeping centre, and the bell was said to be audible twenty kilometres away. From 1272 until 1924 — the year the last Qing emperor left the Forbidden City — the time struck here was Beijing's official time. The drum was beaten a hundred and eight times every two hours; it was the first sound Beijingers heard in the morning and the last they heard at night. The episode says it is almost as if the emperor were not merely marking time but claiming ownership of time itself.

15:32 Jingshan was piled up from the rubble of the previous dynasty
Jingshan is not a natural hill; it was built artificially by the Yongle Emperor according to feng shui principles. An ideal palace faces south, with water to the south — water that should curve and flow to bring qi and vitality — and a mountain to the north to block the evil qi coming from that direction and to display authority. Beijing is too far from the Yan Mountains to the north, so the Ming used rubble from the old Mongol palaces and earth dug out of new water channels to build a symbolic mountain inside the city.

18:52 The Forbidden City was a super-project of nationwide mobilisation
Ten thousand logs were shipped from 1,800 kilometres to the southwest; the golden bricks of Suzhou came from 1,100 kilometres to the south, with 18 million bricks fired in total; gold leaf came from Nanjing. A million labourers plus more than a hundred thousand craftsmen built it in fifteen years. From the 1420s to the early twentieth century, twenty-four emperors lived here. Today it receives more than fifteen million visitors a year, making it the most visited historic site on earth.

22:55 A nail-free timber structure can take a magnitude 9.5 quake
These buildings are almost entirely wood, and what lets them stand for centuries is the dougong (斗拱): the dou are the bearing blocks, the gong are inserted and interlock very tightly. Wood shrinks and warps, and this system lets it deform flexibly while keeping the overall structure intact; in an earthquake every small piece of wood can slide a little, rather than shearing the bearing blocks or snapping bolts. Scientists have calculated that this construction could withstand a magnitude 9.5 earthquake, the strongest ever recorded.

23:57 It was struck by lightning within a year of completion
The Forbidden City was not fireproof. Less than a year after it was completed in 1421, the three great halls burned to ashes after a lightning strike. Three hundred and eight bronze vats were subsequently installed to store water against the next fire. The detail makes the point: no matter how precise the planning, it cannot stop a single point of failure — you can only add redundancy afterwards.

item.title: Germany's CDU Falls Out of a State Parliament: The Era of the Centre Is Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.description: The CDU won less than 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right hold overwhelming majorities among voters under 35.
item.content:encoded:
The CDU won less than 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right hold overwhelming majorities among voters under 35.

This is a piece of German domestic political commentary, not an interview. Information density is moderate, but it lays out the judgment that "populism has become the mainstream" very clearly. Suited to anyone following the direction of European politics.

0:00 The CDU is shut out of a state parliament for the first time
In the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state election, the CDU won less than 5% of the vote and therefore holds no seats in that state parliament — the first time this has happened in the history of the Federal Republic. In the same election the AfD took roughly 38% of the vote, once again becoming the state's largest party. The author calls this Merz's "final nail in the coffin": he may hang on as chancellor for a few more weeks or months, but his authority has vanished and his capacity to shape the country is completely exhausted — in political language, "a dead man walking."

0:00 The CDU's decline came later than the SPD's but is just as fatal
The CDU is the most important party in postwar German history, governing the Federal Republic for 53 of the past 77 years, and from Adenauer to Kohl to Merkel it left its mark on every aspect of the country. The author points out that in the early 2000s everyone was talking about "the crisis of social democracy," as the SPD fell from over 40% support to record lows; in hindsight, the fate of the centre-left big tent was merely a leading indicator of a broader crisis of the entire political centre, and the CDU subsequently walked the same road. The era of what Germans call the Volksparteien — catch-all parties capable of mobilising most of the vote — is effectively over.

0:00 Populists are not a fringe phenomenon but the most important political force
The author says this is the most-asked question of the past decade: "Will the populist wave last, or is it about to peak?" In the summer of 2016, when Trump became the Republican nominee and Britain voted for Brexit, the answer seemed obvious to him; now the answer is undeniable — the populists are here to stay. What looked abnormal a few years ago has, whether you like it or not, become the mainstream. Populist politicians now hold power in the United States, India, Turkey and many places across the democratic world, and have a very high probability of taking office in France and Brazil in the coming months. Even where they remain in opposition, they are already strong enough to destroy any sense of business as usual.

0:00 The rise of one extremist party is feeding another
In the Berlin state election, Die Linke took 26% of the vote and emerged the big winner. The party descends from the Socialist Unity Party (SED), which ruled East Germany with an iron fist, and after reunification initially appealed mainly to older voters nostalgic for the security of the communist system; in recent years it has reinvented itself in the image of the global illiberal left, which the author considers roughly comparable to Zack Polanski's Greens in Britain or the more extreme parts of the DSA in the United States. During the campaign, some of the party's supporters were filmed chanting "Yalla, Yalla Intifada!"; on election night, the head of a notorious crime family visited the party's election party and cheerfully told the media he felt an affinity with it. The party's leader is now very likely to become the next mayor of Berlin, which would be the first time an heir to the SED has taken power in the capital.

0:00 Voters under 35 have swung to the two extremes
Another notable feature of the two elections is the age distribution. The SPD and CDU, which once dominated Germany's political landscape, now draw most of their support from pensioners. Among voters under 35, Die Linke and the AfD hold unassailable majorities in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. From this the author concludes that the coming years will bring an even larger tilt toward the extremes. This also explains why the collapse of the centre is not a one-off election accident: the structure of the electorate itself is pushing the scales toward the two ends.

0:00 Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's left coalition is just an election accident
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, because a batch of other parties all failed to clear the 5% threshold for entering parliament, a broad left coalition just barely won enough votes to govern. But the author stresses that this is an election accident unlikely to be repeated — a few thousand votes either way would leave the state completely ungovernable. This point is crucial: when centrist parties fall below the threshold, they don't just lose their own seats, they push the governability of the entire state to the edge of a cliff.

0:00 Don't surrender, and don't deny the problem is real
The author explicitly rejects two responses. The first is to urge the centre to surrender: if the political centre can't hold, then moderates might as well defect to the extremists on "their own side." He thinks this is wrong — neither Die Linke nor the AfD can solve the real problems Germany faces, and despite their enormous differences, the two have conspicuous similarities, from their ambivalence toward Moscow to their persistent inability to purge antisemites from their own ranks. The second is to keep denying reality: for a decade the centre has attributed the extremists' success to foreign interference, social media algorithms, some candidate's tactical blunder, or the stupidity, sexism or racism of voters. The author says these ways of blinding yourself to the facts in front of you may be comforting, but they are just as dangerous.

item.title: Going global: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and America — go there first to get big
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.description: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and America once they're big, but it's exactly the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.
item.content:encoded:
Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and America once they're big, but it's exactly the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.

Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas investment experience into four choices, counterintuitive but each backed by cases and numbers, especially the second half on AI transforming organizations and pricing, which is the most information-dense.

1:30 The old cross-border mega-seller path is dead
Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border mega-seller’ popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-style mindset, with dozens or hundreds of accounts; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. A decade ago these companies made money faster than other paths, and many investors loved them. But distribution-style companies are essentially traffic-style companies: the more stores, the more likely to get traffic. When platforms don't have enough goods, distribution isn't opposed; once goods are abundant, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, three red lines: selling goods not as described harms consumers, fake orders harm other merchants, and inserting small cards to build private domains harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel places great importance on consumer experience, and these behaviors hit exactly that protective wall.

4:38 Four choices, region comes first
Wei Zhe says it's not just cross-border e-commerce; all of life is about choices being more important than effort. He gives four choices: region, channel, product category, and brand positioning. On region, he has always advocated seizing the European and American markets first, because of strong purchasing power, high internet penetration, and more importantly, the brand can build momentum. This isn't their invention; when Japanese and Korean brands went global, they all seized Europe and America. On category, they change their advice every three years: the first three years they supported products with universal appeal between China and abroad, where the domestic supply chain could sell overseas without modification, like Anker's power banks, which were almost identical except for voltage; the second three years they advised making overseas-exclusive products, because China's supply chain had gone global and universal products had no differentiation; the most recent three years is product 3.0 — electric, with chips, with algorithms.

12:29 It's not that you go to Europe and America after getting big; you get big by going there
Many companies tell Wei Zhe, ‘I'll go to Europe and America when I'm big,’ and he says it's exactly the reverse: you go to Europe and America to become big. He gives the example of Cupshe, a swimwear company: a husband and wife, with $50,000 of inventory, and their first stop was the US. $50,000 is the goods for sale, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. He recently looked at AI smart hardware, starting from Kickstarter crowdfunding with a thousand or ten thousand products, even taking pre-orders before placing orders, with no capital — that's also a great way to test the waters. He even advises big companies entering the European and American markets to learn from small startups. They always say the needle must be fine enough to pierce; both big and small companies should first do the four singles well: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

20:36 After AI, good companies don't just find demand, they create it
Wei Zhe says with AI, excellent companies don't look for demand, they should lead demand and create demand. He gives the example of a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: originally not electric, they electrified it, added chips and algorithms; the algorithm is actually simple, with GPS positioning, and the map of the universe's movements is regular. He wasn't an astronomy enthusiast but would buy one; at home in Silicon Valley, with one tap, it automatically aligns to Orion for you, tells you the best viewing is at 3 a.m., you set it and go to sleep, and the next day it takes the photos for you. This lets everyone become a good astronomy enthusiast. Another example: a cross-border class student making curtains, which didn't sell well in the US after being electrified because American electricians are expensive, so he put solar panels on the window, turning electric curtains that need an electrician into DIY ones; revenue went from one or two hundred million to four or five hundred million, with profit of one or two hundred million.

24:48 In the AI era, still using subscription fees means you're behind
Wei Zhe says in the AI era, if you still think in terms of subscription fees, you're behind again; they are all advising companies to do back-end charging, software charging, called tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest way, a bit like advertising charging by time instead of by usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services, or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks off this month, isn't subscribing for a month a waste of two weeks? They suggest that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not the old SaaS model of $9.9 per month. An AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and nothing if you don't read; the same with smart bike trainers: after topping up, one dollar per ride, two dollars for two hours.

27:28 Adding AI is more promising than AI plus
Wei Zhe has a view called AI plus or plus AI; he reverses the phrase and says he's more optimistic about plus AI rather than today's AI plus. The difference: plus AI is taking hardware humans have already accepted and making it AI; rather than creating a previously unseen hardware because of AI. It's very hard for humans to accept a brand-new hardware. For example, Oura makes rings, because you first accepted rings; some things that hang a camera under your neck are harder for me, I haven't accepted that hardware. So they are very optimistic about adding AI to already-accepted hardware. They invested in a capacitive stylus that is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad, it doesn't add an extra pen, it just makes your pen AI. He also especially wants to transform one of the top fitness equipment companies going global, replacing the fitness coach on the screen with AI-generated ones — you want a male, it's male; you want a Black person, it's Black; install two cameras and you get AI-guided fitness.

29:43 Channels aren't flat; they're a pyramid
Wei Zhe says channels aren't multiple channels multiple paths, each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and which channel new products launch in first. What is a light-goods channel, what is the main waist volume channel — the pyramid design differs by category and brand. He gives Anker: making power bank mecha seems a bit low, to enter the consumer electronics high ground of Soundcore earphones you have to get into Apple flagship stores; whether it really sells a lot isn't important, but it can transform the brand, Apple is the pyramid's peak. Pop Mart must open on London's Oxford Street, even if it doesn't make money, how much can it lose, but it must be propped up there. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels to sell goods, which definitely won't work; AliExpress is a light-goods channel, when Amazon delists you, you dump it there, you can't sell on Amazon and here too, consumers get confused.

36:14 R&D is 1, marketing is 0
Wei Zhe says he really dislikes spending heavily on marketing. Many Chinese brands going global or cross-border e-commerce are willing to add 2% of revenue to marketing expenses, but consumers don't get it. He says, do you dare to add 2% of revenue to R&D expenses? He has met many bosses with 1 billion or 2 billion scale; a 1 billion boss says 20 million for R&D, I don't know what for. He says, see, there's the problem, you don't know what for. Your 2% on marketing makes the platform happy, consumers don't get it; but 2% into R&D, consumers get it. He has always firmly believed good products speak for themselves, marketing is just — your R&D is 1, marketing is 0; if you have something good you can amplify it, if you don't have that 1, never put many 0s. He gives three judgment signals: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and you crush it by doubling performance; second, you sell at the same high price as it; third, you sell online and hit offline channels to come to you.

item.title: The AI Office Hype Hasn't Settled, and the Personal Agent War Has Already Begun | Breaking Down Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.description: Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and hasn't officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal agent hype, capital is grabbing tickets more than responding to real demand.
item.content:encoded:
Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and hasn't officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal agent hype, capital is grabbing tickets more than responding to real demand.

Four frontline product people break down four paths — Town, Instinct, Grok Bot, Muse — and also explain why that batch of products like Xiaolongxia became martyrs. Information density is high, but the second half is worth more.

0:00 100,000 users support a $10 billion valuation
Instinct only began small-scale invite testing in February this year, and by the end of August it still had fewer than 100,000 users, yet its valuation rose from $50 million at the start of the year to $500 million in August, $2.5 billion at the end of August, and this month market rumors of a new round have already reached $10 billion, with Sequoia and Benchmark both in talks to lead. The founder is a 23-year-old unknown with no big-company experience, no technical patents, no industry background. Pan Luan put it bluntly: what capital is buying is not the entrepreneur or the product, it's the story of the next OpenAI, and it can grab a ticket at the price of the next-generation personal operating system.

15:16 The line between tool and person is initiative
The biggest difference between this wave of agents and the last is that it is no longer another tool, but a person. There are two differences between a person and a tool: first, long-term understanding — a tool needs context re-explained every time, while a person understands what kind of person you are like a friend or colleague; second, initiative — in Manus, setting up automated tasks still depends on prompts, on you spelling out rules and intent, and that is not initiative. True initiative is subjective agency — like the colleague who understands your goal in doing something and proactively comes over to say, "I have a plan, should we discuss it?"

18:09 Office agents organize by project, personal agents organize by person
The core difference is the dimension along which context is built. Cloud Code builds context along a mission or project dimension, and switching to the next project means starting over; this wave of personal agents builds context centered on you as a person, knowing your profile, preferences, and past history. Open Codex or Manus and the list on the left is all the tasks and projects you've sent out; open Grok Bot and beside you are AI companions you can co-drive. In personal scenarios, model capability and the harness layer matter less, because individuals don't have that many complex tasks; office agents care a lot about task completion rate.

30:28 Town first trades email for the user's delegation right
The four products are trying to solve the same problem, just with different approaches. Town has a mobile app, but 70% of its data traffic is on PC, and it focuses on the email scenario, solving one high-frequency scenario well before expanding. It understands which emails you frequently send and receive, automatically archives, learns your writing style, drafts replies for you, and sends automatically after you confirm. It goes deeper in the email scenario than any other agent, and has already achieved fairly viral spread overseas, especially in school-related scenarios. In one sentence: use a high-frequency scenario to build user trust, and bit by bit acquire the user's ultimate delegation right.

39:33 Poke didn't take off not because of technical limits
Poke and Instinct are both agents that live inside IM and don't make standalone apps, but Poke didn't take off. Suki believes it wasn't a technical limit — Browser Use was already very mature by the end of last year, and Poke could have done it completely at the time; the difference was team strategy: Instinct went deeper in the agent direction, taking the full-delegation route, able to access credit cards, screen, microphone, book flights, buy things — things users hadn't seen, which produced viral spread; Poke put its energy into content recommendation accuracy, taking the proactive push route, with email notifications arriving even earlier than the inbox itself, but it didn't do the step of "finishing things for you."

42:39 Cloud agents must handle three environments
Mark says building a cloud agent was a painful lesson: local agents and cloud agents are completely different things. To build personal AI you need it available anytime, anywhere — you can't lose contact just because you close your laptop screen. The cloud must handle three environments — the user's device, the cloud service, and the agent's execution environment — and task state, task interruption and recovery, and context transfer between these three environments are extremely complex systems. They started in February, and just getting the agent to run stably on the cloud took at least two months; excluding detours, polishing a sincere work takes at least three to four months.

50:39 Hiring an assistant and being a middleman are two different businesses
Town started with corporate tax filing, and after pivoting it leans more toward enterprise scenarios, with a relationship more like you paying for a personal assistant, naturally filtering for people willing to pay, with a typical profile of white-collar workers who are extremely busy and have no time or energy. Muse is more like a middleman, shopper, or broker — although it has a paid subscription, the estimated main revenue source is still commission from matchmaking transactions, leaning toward mass users and blending into daily WhatsApp chats. Two completely different logics, cutting different scenarios and filtering out different users.

1:14:07 Bookmarks may be noise to an agent
The story Zuckerberg told when launching Muse was about extracting your favorite ingredients from Instagram saves, generating a shopping list, adjusting the menu by dinner party size and dietary restrictions, then completing shopping and relationship maintenance — turning years of interest profile into money, from a discovery platform into a decision and transaction platform. But Suki suspects this is to save face for the free business narrative: helping users complete transactions is absolutely not in the top scenarios users want to solve; users more want to solve the annoying things they don't want to do themselves. There isn't that much high-quality context in bookmarks; truly high-quality context comes more from offline, IM and email, and Douyin and Instagram saves may themselves be noise to an agent.

item.title: Ten Years of Parenting Taught Me: When Your Kid Won't Listen, the Problem Isn't Your Kid
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.description: On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain — from forcing her daughter to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as truth — each one first learned in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.
item.content:encoded:
On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain — from forcing her daughter to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as truth — each one first learned in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.

For parents who want to interrogate their own parenting methodology. Medium information density, heavy on personal narrative, but the ten reflections are clearly structured, and the back half — on "the village" and the couple relationship — is more valuable than the front half.

6:00 Forcing the medicine won the behavior and lost the relationship
The host recalls her three-year-old daughter refusing antibiotics. She held her daughter down and forced the medicine in; her daughter threw most of it back up. That night her husband Alvin stayed with their daughter in the bathroom for an hour, calmly saying the whole time, "I'm willing to do anything, but we're not leaving until we figure this out." In the end the daughter finished the whole course herself — small sips of medicine with small sips of water, then a small piece of chocolate to kill the taste. The host says the difference wasn't that her husband was more patient, but that he wasn't solving a behavior — he was understanding what would actually help the child do this thing. What the child needed was autonomy over the process, and to feel she was on the same team as her parent, rather than being held down to do something.

9:19 The authoritative parenting framework rests on 146 white kids
The host says she accepted uncritically early on that "authoritative is the best parenting style," because every blog and every study said so. It wasn't until she made the episode on corporal punishment that she found a paper co-authored by Diana Baumrind defending parents' ability to spank their children, and started digging. She found that this framework — cited more than 26,000 times, and defining sixty years of parenting research — was originally based on just 146 white, middle-class preschoolers in the town where Baumrind lived. She calls this evidence of her own insufficient critical thinking, and says she now asks at the macro level, "Does this theory make sense?" and at the micro level, "Does it fit this specific child in front of me?"

17:41 Not punishing your kid doesn't mean being ruled by your kid
The host says she once believed that without punishment and consequences children would run wild — she was already thinking in the shower, when her daughter was four months old, "How do I discipline her without becoming a mean mom?" Clinical psychologist Dr. Houri Parsi admitted in the membership community that she too had treated "obedience" as the goal, and that every tooth-brushing was a battle. Once, recording for the host to see, she deliberately used no threats, no punishment, no rewards — she just asked her two-year-old son, "Why don't you want to brush your teeth?" He couldn't find the words; he just called out "Mama" and buried his head in her chest. She realized what he wanted was time alone with her. She put the toilet lid down, sat down, held her son, and they sang a song together — and he brushed his teeth himself, the whole thing in under five minutes.

21:31 "I need you to take out the trash" is not a need
The host says that looking back, she didn't understand what a "need" was — she thought saying to her husband, "I need you to take out the trash," was a perfectly logical sentence. Before their daughter was born the two of them almost never fought: mountain biking in summer, skiing in winter, because the ad agency they worked for represented resorts and paid them in vouchers. After their daughter was born everything changed: during his three weeks of paternity leave her husband would fetch her anything she wanted, and the rest of the time he was training for a hundred-mile ride and watching the Tour de France. She says it was learning that she had needs for "collaboration, partnership, and having her effort seen" that actually pried open the problems between them; before that she was carrying a large amount of resentment inside her with no idea how to handle it.

24:01 When you're triggered, the problem isn't the person who interrupted you
The host says her biggest trigger is being interrupted — the moment her husband interrupts her she flies into a rage, most recently over how much postage a package needed. She always assumed the cause was simply that her husband interrupted her, and that if he stopped, everything would be fine. In July 2018, recording with intergenerational trauma expert Dr. Rebecca Babcock-Fenerci, she traced it live to her own father, a special education teacher who treated sixteen-year-olds like ten-year-olds and for a stretch lectured her every night. Later, in the car, she interrupted her daughter, and her daughter said, "Don't interrupt me, Mama," and her husband looked at her and said, "She's you." She says that was the moment she realized it had never been only about the two people in the room, and out of it she developed the "Tame Your Triggers" course, which grew from a one-month module to ten weeks.

30:27 The handmade book she made while pregnant was full of expectations for her child
The host describes a book she made while pregnant: three covers, one in the middle and one on each side, opening in both directions, brown book cloth with a beige spine, the word "me" cut out of the board on one cover, and on the reverse cover the word "you" embossed, the concept being "you came out of me." On the "me" side she wrote her own feelings and thoughts; on the "you" side she wrote to Carys, whom she had not yet met. She reads out the earliest batch of "expectations for you": I hope you're smart, or at least average; I hope you're the kind of child who shakes hands with people instead of hiding behind my legs; I hope you like roughhousing and also like pretty things; I hope you don't cry all the time; I hope when you fall you pick yourself up and say "I'm okay." She says looking back now, her biggest mistake was not knowing how to simply be with a person, to let them be their whole self and witness it, without carrying ideas about how they should be.

33:14 Kohn's principle two: reconsider your demands first
The host says she once assumed she'd play the role of "enforcer" — she even wrote "I hope you can love me the way he loves me" on her pregnancy expectations list. She says RIE loosened the soil for her, but what actually planted the seed was Alfie Kohn's Unconditional Parenting. She shares a few of its principles: principle two is to reconsider your demands — "maybe when a child won't do what you ask, the problem isn't the child, it's what you're asking"; principle five is to change how you look, not just how you act — when you see your child do the thing you asked them not to do, your first reaction is curiosity about what they're struggling with, not how to make them stop; principle ten is to "attribute to your child the best motive consistent with the facts you observed," and she says when she quotes it she changes the ending to "consistent with the behavior you observed," because "there are no facts, only what we observe."

39:07 The couple relationship isn't a different subject, it's the same one
The host says she long believed the couple relationship and the parent-child relationship were completely different things — when she started the parenting membership eight years ago she asked Dr. Laura Froyen to write the co-parenting module, because she had no idea how to handle a partner relationship. She says her parenting shift toward collaboration was relatively easy, because she had no ten-year-old habits with her daughter; but she and Alvin had been together ten years without ever learning how to disagree, because they spent most of it doing hobbies they loved, and she didn't mind doing most of the housework. It wasn't until she took Gottman training that she realized this was almost the same work she'd been doing with her child all these years — while also believing the Gottman method itself has a few key flaws. She recruited couples from the membership to record real arguments, using modified tools, and one couple — where the husband had refused to discuss a toxic issue — found that after his wife listened for ten minutes with a genuine intent to understand him, he was willing to talk, and in that same session they reached an agreement to move forward.

item.title: NPR's comment section was mistaken for bots — it was actually a group of middle schoolers
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.description: NPR staff saw a pile of gibberish in the comments and their first instinct was bots, so they reported it. A younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.
item.content:encoded:
NPR staff saw a pile of gibberish in the comments and their first instinct was bots, so they reported it. A younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.

Four independent stories, medium information density, but the generational misread in the first story and the mother-daughter conversation about braiding in the third are both worth hearing.

1:01 The gibberish comments aren't bots, they're kids
Dave Blanchard saw a sudden flood of incomprehensible messages in the Wild Card comment section on Spotify, and his first instinct was bots, so he reported them to Spotify and had the posts deleted. But Hannah Chin, a colleague at NPR ten years younger, opened the screenshots and immediately reached the opposite conclusion: these are children. Her evidence was the display names with emoji you need a special character generator to type, the cartoon avatars she'd never seen before, the back-and-forth short sentences with piles of exclamation marks. Dave wasn't buying it at first, and replied, "That's an interesting theory."

6:05 Using playlists as a group-chat doorway
Hannah kept digging and found how the kids did it: one kid creates a public playlist called Let's Chat Here or New Chat with just one podcast episode in it; other kids see the playlist, click into that episode, and chat in the comments. They also posted Google Forms as little quizzes, writing "only cool people can fill this out." Hannah said bots don't go post Google Forms, but Gen Alpha does, the way her own generation made UQuiz or BuzzFeed personality quizzes. That was the detail that convinced Dave.

8:06 They picked NPR because nobody's in the comments
The show contacted several commenters, and only one, a 14-year-old girl named Ella, agreed to be interviewed; she did it from the car while her father drove. Ella said the core of the group is about 20 kids, many of them in drama club, mostly girls, with strict parents who won't let them use regular social media. They first chatted in the comment section of a podcast that played TikTok videos; after that podcast got shut down, the kids started using playlists to move to new ground. Asked why they chose NPR shows, Ella said: we look for podcasts that don't have many comments, so we don't get mixed up in other people's comments.

11:08 Dave needed a generational translator
After learning the truth, Dave said he felt guilty for reporting them, and also felt old. He said, "I literally needed Hannah to be my generational translator," and that this made him acutely aware of his age and his obsolescence. Ella said she's sure that one day she too will be as completely lost as Dave. The show puts this segment at the top, as the entry point to the whole episode's "intergenerational space travel" theme.

25:35 The wedding toast was a poem nobody heard
At 18, Courtney read a poem she wrote at her mother's second wedding, and her mother held it against her for thirty years. The poem opens with the mother walking in habitual darkness, every breath like her last; the middle has her standing by the counter smoking; and the ending turns to "you found roots, you found a soul worth worshipping." The mother said that on the wedding day she only heard the negative first half and never heard the goodwill at the end; rereading it, Courtney admitted that presenting a bride with that dark a picture on her wedding day really would make it impossible to hear the kind words.

31:52 The body knew the marriage was wrong first
Two days after the wedding, the 49-year-old mother had a massive stroke. Courtney offers a theory: her mother's body, not her mind, had known all along that the marriage was a mistake. The mother agreed, saying she knew when she bought the wedding dress, that she wasn't all that happy then, that she "anticipated this awfulness ahead of time," sensing it in every fiber. The exchange turns all the earlier arguing about the wedding toast into a question about why her mother didn't listen to her intuition back then.

39:05 Only kicking out the stepfather repaired them
Last October, the mother fell in the kitchen Mr. X designed and broke her back; Mr. X was too drunk to help and only handed her the phone hours later so she could call an ambulance herself. The mother was hospitalized for months and gave Courtney power of attorney to go to court and get Mr. X out. Courtney said it was the hardest thing she's ever done, but they won. The mother said it was precisely because Courtney spent so much time here for that, that she realized how much her daughter cared about her. Mr. X pulled them apart, and getting rid of him pulled them back together.

55:41 The mother says braiding shouldn't be the entry to toughness
Myra Flynn locks horns with her six-year-old daughter Avalon every morning over braiding, and she blurted out "sometimes what we need isn't comfortable," then immediately realized those were her own mother's words. She called her mother, Martha Mathis, expecting support, but her mother said: braiding shouldn't be the entry point for making a child tough, because it carries too much racial and gender meaning; and six-year-old Avalon is already the toughest little girl there is. Her mother's advice was to let Avalon handle a small section of hair herself, because "she'll be gentle with herself."

item.title: Robots Are Still at GPT-1, and the Real Signal Is Success Rate, Not Loss
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-crossing-机器人还在-gpt-1-阶段-真正的信号是成功率不是-loss/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-crossing-机器人还在-gpt-1-阶段-真正的信号是成功率不是-loss/
item.description: The Scaling Law signal for embodied intelligence has already appeared, but we're measuring the wrong metric: low loss does not mean high success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.
item.content:encoded:
The Scaling Law signal for embodied intelligence has already appeared, but we're measuring the wrong metric: low loss does not mean high success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.

Xu Mengdi (徐梦迪), assistant professor at Tsinghua's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences, on data, world models and In-Context Learning for embodied intelligence. The middle and later sections on the data loop and the loss trap are the most valuable.

12:15 Pretraining is not everything; adaptation is what matters
Xu Mengdi's CMU best doctoral thesis is called Building Adaptable Generalist Robots, and its core claim is: pretraining is extremely useful, but you cannot hope a robot will succeed 100% of the time on pretraining alone. The defining feature of the open world is that tasks keep changing — at home there are 20 objects today, a week later 30 of different kinds, and people's preferences change too. So the robot must be able to adapt to change in its deployment environment and improve itself. She explored two paths: In-Context Learning and test-time training; the latter changes only 0.5% of the adapter parameters, but change too much and it forgets the pretrained knowledge.

19:22 Why adaptation only became important now
Humans generalize well for two reasons: extremely strong priors, and learning things very fast. The mainstream approach until now has been to scale data and models so that multi-task and instruction-following abilities get stronger — essentially giving the model a strong enough prior first. But Xu Mengdi points out this does not mean adaptation is unimportant — it is just that people only recently realized it. And adaptation places demands on the base model: you don't want the robot's self-learning process in a real setting to be terrifying, like smashing a cup. So starting from pretraining is reasonable.

49:46 Low loss does not equal high success rate
This is the most counterintuitive technical judgment in the whole piece. There is a very tricky point in robotics: loss is not directly tied to success rate. Loss can be very low while the final success rate is not necessarily low — there will be a lot of oscillation. Her example: a task might take 20 steps in total, and the first 17 steps involve no contact with the object. Even if those 17 steps fit extremely well, if step 18, when contact actually happens, has a relatively large error, the task fails easily. This is an imbalance in the time sequence. So a Scaling Law that actually means something should be: as data gradually increases and the model gradually grows, success rate on unseen tasks gradually rises.

50:47 Robots are still at the GPT-1 moment
Today's mainstream embodied models are still ‘pretraining + fine-tuning on the target domain’, which can be compared to the GPT-1 stage of language models — GPT-1 itself also needed targeted post-training to solve the corresponding tasks. What Xu Mengdi really wants to achieve is the GPT-3 moment: giving the model task information through ICL, through prompting, with no fine-tuning needed, telling the model what to do purely through context. That way the weight of fine-tuning becomes much weaker, it scales more easily to more scenarios and more tasks, and ordinary people can use it too.

58:49 The data loop is a chicken-and-egg problem
The hardest point is whether you can give the model a stable data loop. That requires putting the robot into an end-user home or service scenario, having a suitable mentor to teach it, and the robot must show obvious progress after being taught for half an hour — only then will end users be willing to use it, and only then can the data loop start turning. But there is a chicken-and-egg problem here: the base model needs to be good enough and learn fast enough, yet the model also needs to get into the scenario first so users start using it, in order to draw out that base capability. So whether the data loop can be made to work is the riskiest point of all.

1:03:52 Data is defined by working backward from model capability
Data itself gets fed to the model, but the definition of data is not conjured out of thin air — it is defined by the model's capabilities. When people define data, what they are actually doing is: figuring out what capabilities the model needs, and working backward to how the data should be collected. For example, if you need smoother motion, the data should be of the smooth type; if you need fail-recovery ability, the data should be collected with failures and corrections in it. And right now people's definition of model capability is still fairly vague, so the data requirements are vague too.

1:05:54 Each of the four data types has its own place
Xu Mengdi's position is that of a fusionist, because different data teaches the model different things. Teleoperation data is closest to the robot body itself, suited to the post-training stage, making the model more directly relevant to the target domain. Simulation data easily produces position generalization and texture generalization, making the model more robust to visual change, and suits the front end of pretraining or mid-training. UMI data sits in the middle, more like robot data but cheaper to collect. Human data is the cheapest, can be spread widely across different scenarios, and what it teaches is scene variation and task-relevant information, less tied to the specific shape of the morphology.

1:19:02 AI-written papers are obvious at a glance
Robotics papers have recently been doubling in number, and Xu Mengdi's way of coping is to scroll through articles promoted by the researchers she follows, because the author list itself has already done a layer of filtering. She can clearly see that some articles have a very large AI-written component. Her judgment: AI-written articles may pass review and actually get into some conferences, but overall the quality still won't be higher than human-written ones, because they look familiar while in fact many arguments are full of holes and there isn't much content. Once she finds out a paper was written by AI, her interest in it is discounted.

item.title: The Woman Who Killed Marat: Why the Court Would Not Believe She Acted Alone
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-restishistory-刺杀马拉的女人-为什么法庭不信她独自行动/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-restishistory-刺杀马拉的女人-为什么法庭不信她独自行动/
item.description: Corday had her declaration written before the assassination, and after her arrest she insisted she acted alone. The revolutionary tribunal kept pressing her on the "chain of conspiracy" — they could not imagine that provincials thought Marat a monster.
item.content:encoded:
Corday had her declaration written before the assassination, and after her arrest she insisted she acted alone. The revolutionary tribunal kept pressing her on the "chain of conspiracy" — they could not imagine that provincials thought Marat a monster.

High information density, tracing a causal chain from the institutional origins of the Terror through paper-money inflation to the Vendée war, with the assassination details in the second half especially valuable.

0:00 The assassination declaration was written before the act
When Corday was arrested she was carrying a declaration titled "To the Friends of Law and Peace in France." In it she named Marat "the most vile of villains," said he "has been condemned by the universe, and is therefore outside the law," and called on the French to "rise. Strike. Strike." This text was not a post-hoc defense; it was written before the act — what she wanted was not escape but to turn her death into a rallying point.

9:30 Marat was the first modern populist
Keith Michael Baker's new biography positions Marat as the first modern populist. His formula included: constantly invoking the capitalized "People," claiming the people are at every moment in danger of being betrayed by appeasers and traitors; an obsession with conspiracy theory, openly stating that his goal was to keep readers "perpetually alert," lest they be dragged into the abyss by royalists, priests, and the like. The show points out that this "wake up, sheep" language is used by both left and right today.

21:57 Paper-money inflation pushed the poor into the streets
In early 1793 France suffered successive poor harvests, the national grain market collapsed, and the government, lacking money for war, could only print paper money, the assignat, with about four billion in circulation. This caused severe inflation, bread and sugar prices soared, protests occurred almost daily in the markets, and women's marches appeared in the streets of Paris. The show stresses: these were the very same conditions that had sparked the Revolution and the storming of the Bastille, and the poor would think, "The Revolution happened, yet life has not improved, so someone must be scheming."

32:13 The commander's defection confirmed the conspiracy theories
On March 8, 1793, the Austrians counterattacked and decisively defeated Dumouriez at Neerwinden, forcing him to withdraw from Belgium and Holland. He wanted to emulate Sulla and march on Paris as a military dictator, asking his subordinates, "Shall we march on Paris?" They answered no. On April 5 he rode over to the Austrian lines, taking with him a number of senior officers, including the future French king Louis Philippe. A volunteer wrote to his mother: "Whom can we trust now?"

38:27 The Terror machine was improvised
The show stresses that the key institutions of the Terror had no blueprint, no plan; they were built as they went along, only later appearing as a machine, and many who helped build it were eventually swallowed by it. On March 10 the Revolutionary Tribunal was established to try political crimes, with death sentences to be carried out within 24 hours and no right of appeal, located in the Palais de Justice in Paris, with the existing Conciergerie prison in its basement. Danton said: "Let us be terrible, so that the people need not be."

42:37 The Girondins used new rules to strike at Marat, and it backfired
Having just abolished parliamentary immunity, the Girondins, while many deputies were away on missions to the provinces, indicted Marat on April 14, accusing him of inciting insurrection. Marat first went into hiding for three days, then, finding that Parisian street opinion was on his side, turned himself in for trial. On April 24 the trial opened at the Palais de Justice; the chief prosecutor, Fuquietanville, was a Montagnard supporter and allowed Marat a long self-defense. The ten-man jury acquitted him within hours, and Marat was carried back to the National Convention by some 800 people, wearing a crown of roses, with cries of "vive la république, vive Marat." For the Girondins it was a complete humiliation.

1:04:31 Corday buys a knife: a 15-centimeter black-handled kitchen knife
Around eight in the morning on July 13, Charlotte Corday left her hotel, walked to the Palais-Royal arcades, bought a newspaper (which said the Convention would likely sentence the imprisoned Girondin deputies to death), and bought a black Paris hat with a green ribbon, replacing her white Norman-style hat. She entered a cutlery shop called Le Coutelier Badin and bought a kitchen knife with a black handle and a blade about 15 centimeters long. Between 11:30 a.m. and noon she took a carriage to Marat's home on the rue des Cordeliers, but, lacking an appointment, was turned away by Marat's sister-in-law.

1:10:51 The court would not believe a woman could act alone
Corday was arrested on the spot; one of her interrogators was Jean-Baptiste Drouet, the postmaster who had recognized Louis XVI's flight at Varennes. From the start she said she had acted alone. But the revolutionary tribunal repeatedly interrogated her about the "chain of conspiracy," convinced she must be part of a Girondin plot. The interrogator Montané said: it is impossible, because you say Marat is the source of all France's ills, yet Marat is precisely the one who never stopped exposing traitors and conspirators, so someone must have lied to you. Corday replied: you are mad; only in Paris do people see Marat, in the provinces he is taken for a monster. The court could not imagine that provincials would think Marat a bad man.

item.title: Intel's Optane Died Because 3D NAND Was Too Cheap, Not Because the Tech Was Bad
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.description: Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it got squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.
item.content:encoded:
Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it got squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.

A complete history of a storage technology's failure, from RMM in 1970 to the shutdown of Optane in 2022. Medium information density; the back half on data-center deployment and Micron's exit is the most valuable part.

3:07 The physics of phase-change storage is what makes it slow
Phase-change storage writes data by switching a material between its crystalline and amorphous states: the crystalline state has low resistance, the amorphous state high resistance, and the two differ by three to four orders of magnitude. Melting the material and quenching it into the amorphous state is called RESET; the reverse is called SET. SET either melts the material into a liquid and lets it cool slowly into a crystal, or heats it to a temperature high enough to convert it directly to crystalline without melting. The author points out that SET is often the speed bottleneck for PCM. This physical mechanism has not changed since Stanford Ovshinsky discovered the phase-change behavior of chalcogenide compounds in the 1960s.

4:13 Intel built phase-change memory in 1970, then forgot about it
In 1970, RG Neale and DL Nelson of Energy Conversion Devices and Intel's Gordon Moore published an article in Electronics magazine announcing "Read-Mostly Memory," positioned between RAM and ROM, for storing data that programs read often but rarely change. Each cell was a silicon diode plus a layer of phase-change material; Intel supplied the silicon substrate, ECD supplied the material. But in 1970 the minimum feature size was only 10 microns, power consumption was high, SET took milliseconds, and endurance was low. DRAM capacity was growing, EPROM arrived, and RMM disappeared. Years later someone asked the 79-year-old Moore about the article, and he said he had no memory of it at all.

9:25 Numonyx treated PCM as its only shot at a comeback
The rise of NAND sent NOR flash into a long decline, and in 2007 global NOR sales fell 9% year over year. Intel merged its NOR business with STMicroelectronics' flash business, forming the Swiss company Numonyx in 2008, with an investment from Francisco Partners and a bank loan. NOR had none of NAND's growth prospects, so Numonyx could only bet on PCM — PCM combined NOR's fast random reads with NAND's high-capacity storage, and in theory could replace both. In February 2008 Intel announced delivery of its first PCM prototype, Alverstone, at 128 megabit and 90 nanometers.

13:33 Mobile PCM was swept away in one wave by 3D NAND
PCM's entry strategy was to attack the mobile market, replacing the NOR flash that stores boot code while also storing data. In 2009 Samsung announced a 512 megabit PRAM at 60 nanometers, saying that paired with DRAM it could save more than 20% in power. Micron acquired Numonyx in 2010 for about $1.2 billion in stock, and in July 2012 finally shipped 1 gigabit PCM at 45 nanometers, which Nokia put into its Asha feature phones. But in August 2013 Samsung announced mass production of 24-layer 3D NAND, and 3D NAND then set off the steepest cost-decline curve in semiconductor history, and mobile PCM's most compelling rationale was gone. In January 2014 Micron announced it was pulling out of mobile PCM.

17:38 Intel and Micron were split on Optane's positioning from the start
In July 2018 Intel and Micron agreed to a friendly breakup, going their separate ways after completing joint development of the second generation of 3D XPoint. The disagreement was over product direction: Intel initially aimed Optane SSDs at consumer PCs and laptops, hoping to spread wafer costs across volume; Micron wanted to go straight into the data center. Jon Carter hinted back in 2016 that consumer systems did not really need 3D XPoint's low latency, non-volatility and endurance — or at least not enough to pay four to five times the price of NAND for them. In October 2018 Micron announced it would pay $1.5 billion to buy Intel's half of the IM Flash plant in Utah, and Intel shifted to producing it itself.

22:47 Putting Optane in the data center meant redoing motherboards and software
In April 2019 the first DIMM-form-factor Optane DC Persistent Memory went on sale, four years after 3D XPoint was announced, and it required matching Xeon processors, chipsets and motherboards. It had two modes: Memory Mode pooled Optane and DRAM into a single volatile memory pool, working out of the box, but its value depended on DRAM price swings; App Direct Mode was the genuinely valuable mode, letting software write persistent data into Optane so it was still there after a reboot. Restarting an Oracle or SAP database normally takes more than an hour to reload data from SSDs or hard drives, and Optane could eliminate that. One imprecise but directionally useful test showed a 12.5x improvement. But App Direct Mode required programmers to rethink data consistency.

24:51 Only 40% of 582 proofs of concept used the mode that actually mattered
In 2020 Intel updated Optane adoption, saying there were 582 proofs of concept in the pipeline, with SAP HANA and Oracle Exadata the main users and the rest mostly in high-performance computing, infrastructure and some AI analytics. But only 40% used the more valuable App Direct Mode. Intel said it believed the industry would eventually adopt that mode, but it might take years. In the same period Intel announced the sale of its 3D NAND business to SK hynix for $9 billion, with Optane not included in the deal — seemingly an endorsement, but it also let people infer that Optane's implied loss in 2020 was more than $500 million.

25:52 After Micron left, Optane was down to a single supplier
In March 2021 Micron announced it was immediately stopping 3D XPoint development, saying the Utah plant had long suffered from underutilization and dragged $400 million a year off the company, and the plant was later sold to Texas Instruments. Micron attributed the decision to the continuing fall in 3D NAND prices and to the hard changes data centers and applications would have to make to take full advantage of the product. Micron pivoted to betting on the open-standard interface CXL, because machine-learning systems made Micron realize that not just CPUs needed more memory — GPUs and AI accelerator ASICs did too. Micron's public exit severely weakened Optane: customers could rely only on Intel as a single source, and Optane was a proprietary technology. In July 2022, on its earnings call, Intel quietly announced it was shutting down the Optane business.

item.title: Huawei's Ascend chose the hardest road: not compatible with Nvidia
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-touzishizhan-华为昇腾选了一条最难的路-不兼容英伟达/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-touzishizhan-华为昇腾选了一条最难的路-不兼容英伟达/
item.description: For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that doesn't solve a chokehold problem but instead walks into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets more exhausting the longer you do it.
item.content:encoded:
For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that doesn't solve a chokehold problem but instead walks into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets more exhausting the longer you do it.

The first half is about how the book was written, low information density; from the two key decisions at Ascend's founding, Fang Xingdong gives a lot of frontline detail and judgment that only exists in the book.

16:10 Ascend's harshest decision was not being compatible with Nvidia
At Ascend's founding there were two choices. The first was whether AI chips should be specialized or general-purpose; Liao Heng, as chief scientist, judged that AI should be a general-purpose product, and the architectural choice has been proven right today. The second was harder: whether to be compatible with Nvidia. Many domestic chips chose compatibility, with the benefit that Nvidia's existing ecosystem and tools could all be shared. But Xu Zhijun was firm from the start: they had to find another way. Fang Xingdong believes this choice was extremely bold at the time, and that many times along the way it faced enormous challenges — because the entire Chinese IT industry has been a follower industry for three or four decades, and had never developed based on its own root technology.

19:11 Anything you do as a follower gets more exhausting the longer you do it
Fang Xingdong recalls having dinner with Xu Zhijun three years ago, when Xu half muttered to himself: Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets more exhausting the longer you do it. There are two kinds of following: in standardized products, Chinese companies can always close the gap and even overtake, but by the time they overtake, there is no profit left in the industry — 2G to 5G, PCs, phones all went this way; in non-standardized areas, such as competing with Cisco in routers for so many years, the gap has not closed. In Xu Zhijun's eyes, what Huawei did in the past was also following. So Ascend is special among the six products: the other five solve chokeholds, solving survival first, while Ascend was not choked in 2019 — it is a completely proactive compute product.

29:16 Process is choked off, so it can only be made up through system innovation
Each generation of industry chips gains roughly 20% or more performance, mainly from the increase in transistor count driven by advanced process improvements. Huawei lost this premise and can only gain performance through system innovation and breakthroughs — stacked compute, interconnect, higher integration. Fang Xingdong explains with a car metaphor: before, you just had to make the engine stronger and stronger; now the engine is constrained and cannot be enlarged, so you can only make the car run well through architecture, weight reduction, heat dissipation and other factors. Nvidia's solution is to keep working on the engine, because TSMC can still manufacture it. In the interview, Liao Heng uses the metaphor of an 18-story pagoda: many companies are good at only one layer because of the great division of labor, while Huawei is forced to do manufacturing, ecosystem and chip design all at once.

34:21 Huawei has to pull the domestic supply chain up with it
Previously Huawei did design, relied on the global supply chain, had TSMC manufacture, could choose the best international partners for other components, directly buy American products and assemble them, sell at a good price with a brand premium, and profits were decent. Now it cannot cooperate with foreign partners, TSMC cannot process for it, and domestic processes are still lacking in every respect, so Huawei has no choice but to support and drive the domestic supply chain — only then does it have a way to survive, only then can its products be manufactured. So the challenge of the past seven years is not just improving its own capabilities, but also driving the entire supply chain — without driving it, independent autonomy is impossible. Manufacturing is not Huawei's main business, but it has to help companies like SMIC and Yangtze Memory keep advancing process, yield and quality.

37:40 Ascend's significance is not that Huawei survived, but that the industry has an engine
In the past, Huawei's product launches and iterations were still based on American root technology and the industrial ecosystem; the high-value components of a phone were basically foreign. Now Huawei's phones, including Ascend, drive almost 100% domestic supply chains. Fang Xingdong believes the greatest significance of the Tao Law is not that Huawei itself can survive and be autonomous, but that China's entire semiconductor industry and entire IT industry have their own engine, which never existed before. Huawei's rapid development represents the rapid development of the entire industrial ecosystem. He also points out that the market, looking at reports, news or public opinion, has not yet realized that we are at this inflection point — mention Nvidia and people think it is formidable, mention Huawei and they say it is policy that makes everyone use it.

45:47 It is not a question of difficulty, but of cognition and resolve
Fang Xingdong believes doing communications versus doing IT is essentially not a question of difficulty, but of cognition and resolve — whether you dare to do it. The most typical example is the Gauss database: among these six products Ascend stood out, and the least conspicuous may be Gauss, but the database is a half-century-old industry with a relatively stable market, and if it really gets choked off it is deadly. Huawei at the time wanted to acquire or support domestic vendors, but after research found none of them were up to it; domestic companies could only grow in the cracks of American giants, small in scale, weak in R&D, weak in product innovation. So Huawei decided to do it itself, benchmarking Oracle, and starting in 2011 and 2012 invested 1 billion, 2 billion, 3 billion a year, without knowing whether there would be any output in the future.

1:06:04 The future is two centers, not one replacing the other
Fang Xingdong judges that global high tech moving from a single system centered on the US to two centers is the general trend; politics will not allow a continued single center — the US will not allow it, and China will not allow it either. He believes a single center is itself abnormal, and only two centers can create competition — only with two systems does every consumer, every company, every country, no matter how big or small, have a choice, and not be choked into a forced either-or. So the mission of Huawei's six products is to go from second choice to better choice; it is not a simple substitution relationship with Nvidia, but each having its strengths, complementing each other, coopetition. He admits the American system is currently stronger, with its advantage mainly in advanced manufacturing, and that Huawei, under process constraints, relies on the Tao Law to avoid being left behind; once advanced process is also broken through, it can work both ways at once.

1:19:11 The tech war won in the short term, at a greater long-term cost
Fang Xingdong believes the US did indeed suppress Huawei through the tech war, but cannot solve the problem in the long term. He reasons: without the national confrontation of 2017 and 2018, Huawei might have been at least one-third of Nvidia, one-third of Apple, possibly China's largest company by market cap; in 2019 Huawei had already surpassed Apple, and its global shipments briefly surpassed Samsung for one quarter. Nvidia today is dominant alone; if it had been running neck and neck with Huawei in AI chips from the start, it could not be in this position today. He judges that once the side being attacked builds a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, and the other side cannot eliminate it even under the harshest conditions, it will be even harder to eliminate later; it will only grow stronger, turning from one monopoly into two competitors.

item.title: Ads Are Machine Learning 1.0: How AppLovin Earned an 84% Margin
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-allin-广告是机器学习的-1-0-applovin-靠它赚出-84-利润率/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-allin-广告是机器学习的-1-0-applovin-靠它赚出-84-利润率/
item.description: Advertising isn't AI's past tense — it's the earliest and most profitable deployment of deep learning. AppLovin used recommendation models to build an 84% EBITDA margin in the $50 billion mobile game ad market, and became its own best investor with $6 billion in buybacks.
item.content:encoded:
Advertising isn't AI's past tense — it's the earliest and most profitable deployment of deep learning. AppLovin used recommendation models to build an 84% EBITDA margin in the $50 billion mobile game ad market, and became its own best investor with $6 billion in buybacks.

A CEO who almost never gives interviews explains the shared technical roots of ads and AI, the buyback playbook through a 92% drawdown, and why a Chinese engineering team is an advantage. High information density, worth listening to.

1:02 Mobile game advertising is a $50 billion market
Adam says outsiders underestimate the scale of mobile gaming: more than a billion adults play casual mobile games every day, and these people are household decision-makers. Two years ago AppLovin disclosed $11 billion in annual ad spend on its own platform, and it has grown roughly 60% year over year since, which by rough math puts it around $20 billion today. But that isn't the whole market — many other ad companies monetize in this ecosystem, so double that number and the entire mobile gaming ecosystem spends roughly $50 billion a year on advertising. He notes that not long ago social was also just a $50 billion opportunity.

3:02 Advertising is machine learning's earliest and most profitable deployment
Adam calls advertising ML 1.0: it was the first deployment of all the technology that now drives AI. Large language models create more economic value today than advertising, but advertising is an extremely profitable deployment of deep learning models. Recommendation systems and large language models differ in architecture, but their trajectories are highly similar — research in large language models transfers to recommendation systems and vice versa; many LLM researchers spent the early part of their careers looking at ad systems. The beauty of the ad business is that you build a model to predict a future outcome, and the value of that prediction can be converted into money immediately.

6:03 Search ads create no economic expansion; discovery ads do
Adam splits advertising into two categories. One is bottom-of-funnel advertising: the consumer already knows what they want to buy and is just doing research to complete the transaction — that's Google Search's business, and large language models will compete with Google Search almost entirely there. The other is his category: not knowing user intent, and creating demand that didn't exist so the user sees something and thinks ‘this looks really cool, I want to buy it right now’. He stresses that the transaction in search or in an LLM would have happened anyway, so there isn't much economic expansion there; discovery advertising creates economic expansion, which is what makes Meta's ad business strong and what AppLovin wants to do.

8:07 Your phone isn't listening, but your behavior is tracked
Faced with the question of ‘I mention something at lunch and then an ad shows up’, Adam says it's more likely you did something trackable earlier — a search, browsing a website, searching for a product — without realizing it, and then you said something related and started seeing related ads. He states plainly that AppLovin does not track location at all, arguing that tracking precise location to render ads is a very heavy concept, and that the data transfer required to parse microphone content in real time and translate it into ads isn't realistic. But he concedes that if you're on a social network, relationship data between you and others can of course drive the ad experience — for example, a friend searched for something and you might see a related ad, which he thinks is fine.

10:07 From $28 billion to $3.8 billion, then it started buying itself
AppLovin went public in April 2021 with $600 million in EBITDA at a market cap of about $28 billion, peaking at $40 billion. In 2022 the stock fell almost every day, down to a market cap of about $3.8 billion — in a year when the company did $1 billion in EBITDA.
